data_source_notes: Primary data pull worked after correcting the endpoint: the literal URL given in the task (https://api.ransomware.live/v2/victims/sector/Hospitality%20and%20Tourism) returns the HTML API-docs landing page, not JSON (ransomware.live v6 "Aegis" redesign changed routes). The API docs page (fetched via WebFetch on https://www.ransomware.live/apidocs) revealed the correct v2 route is GET /sectorvictims/<sector>. Re-fetching https://api.ransomware.live/v2/sectorvictims/Hospitality%20and%20Tourism (via PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, since the Bash/curl tool had no network egress in this environment) succeeded on the first try (HTTP 200, no rate-limit issue encountered) and returned 771 victim records with all documented fields (activity, attackdate, country, description, group, press, ransom, victim, data_size, url, claim_url, plus bonus fields like discovered/domain/infostealer). Only 5 of 771 records had a non-null "ransom" field and only 41 had "press" detail; most records are bare leak-site claims. Step 2 supplements were only partially successful: the ransomlook.io query URL returned HTTP 400 Bad Request (endpoint/parameter format likely changed or requires different query encoding) and was not retried further; ransomwhat.telemetry.ltd/posts.json 302-redirected to https://ransomwatch.telemetry.ltd/ (a project rename), which returned only the site's landing page rather than a raw posts.json feed, so no corroborating victim-post data was retrievable from that source in the time available — both are noted as failed/unavailable rather than fabricated. All 8 example incidents and all aggregate stats were independently verified via WebSearch against named news/vendor sources (BleepingComputer, Cyber Daily, SecurityWeek, Malwarebytes, CNBC, Chainalysis, Sophos, Coveware, Verizon, IBM, Maine AG breach-notification filings, etc.), not solely from ransomware.live. No industry-specific (hospitality-only) breakdown was found in Sophos, Coveware, IBM, Verizon or Chainalysis 2025 reports — those vendors publish overall or retail-sector figures rather than an "Accommodation/Food Services/Arts and Entertainment" specific cut, so retail figures are used as the closest disclosed proxy and are labeled as such.
data_sources_used: WebSearch news coverage (BleepingComputer, Cyber Daily, SecurityWeek, CNBC, Chainalysis blog, Malwarebytes, Help Net Security, Forbes, TechTarget, Infosecurity Magazine, PYMNTS, Cybernews, The Register, Sun-Times, casino.org, Maine AG data breach notice filings)
Sophos State of Ransomware 2025 / State of Ransomware in Retail 2025
Chainalysis 2026 Crypto Crime Report (2025 ransomware data)
IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025

example_incidents.summary: Scattered Spider used a vishing/social-engineering attack against MGM's IT help desk to obtain credentials, then deployed ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware, forcing MGM to shut down casino floor systems, digital hotel room keys, slot machines, ATMs, restaurant/payment systems and websites across 30+ properties for roughly 10 days.
example_incidents.financial_impact: MGM disclosed an estimated ~$100 million negative impact to Adjusted Property EBITDAR for Las Vegas Strip and Regional Operations, plus under $10 million in one-time remediation/legal/incident-response costs; company said it expected to be largely covered by cyber insurance. A related shareholder/consumer class-action settlement was reached in 2025.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: MGM has stated it did not pay a ransom (unlike sister-incident Caesars); no confirmed dollar figure for a demand specific to MGM has been publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Core systems (slot machines, digital key cards, reservations, payment processing) were down for approximately 10 days before full restoration.
example_incidents.data_impact: Personal information (names, contact details, driver's license/SSN/passport numbers for some) of roughly 37 million MGM Rewards members was compromised.

example_incidents.summary: Attackers compromised a third-party IT support vendor via social engineering to breach Caesars' network and exfiltrate the ~6TB Caesars Rewards loyalty database before Caesars negotiated and paid a ransom; the attack occurred just before, and is closely associated with, the MGM incident by the same threat-actor ecosystem.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Caesars disclosed the incident in an SEC 8-K; ongoing consumer class-action litigation (Caesars Entertainment Data Breach Litigation). Specific total incident cost beyond the ransom payment not publicly broken out.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Attackers initially demanded $30 million; Caesars paid approximately $15 million in cryptocurrency. The FBI later tracked and froze a portion of the payment as it moved through crypto exchanges.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Caesars stated its hotel, casino and online operations were not significantly disrupted (unlike MGM); recovery was largely on the data-breach/notification track rather than an operational-outage track.
example_incidents.data_impact: Loyalty program database of more than 65 million Caesars Rewards members exposed, including driver's license and Social Security numbers for a subset of members.

example_incidents.date: April 2026 (initial access April 14; discovered/blocked April 22; disclosed publicly ~mid-May 2026)
example_incidents.summary: ShinyHunters used social engineering to trick a Carnival employee into granting IT system access, then used the compromised account to copy personal data from a limited portion of Carnival's systems before being blocked; the gang later claimed 8.7 million stolen records and published data on its leak site.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a specific dollar figure by Carnival; the company began offering two years of complimentary TransUnion credit monitoring to affected US residents, an ongoing cost. Litigation/regulatory exposure likely given the scale of records.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed; ShinyHunters is an extortion-focused (data-theft, not necessarily encryption) group and threatened to publish/sell the data if terms were not met.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No major operational/cruise-booking outage reported; this was primarily a data-theft/social-engineering incident rather than an encryption/downtime event.
example_incidents.data_impact: Data breach notice filed in Maine listed 5,995,277 affected individuals; ShinyHunters claimed 8.7 million records stolen. Exposed data included names, addresses, emails, phone numbers, dates of birth, and government ID numbers (driver's license, passport).

example_incidents.victim: Compass Group Australia (Sydney-based catering/support services group)
example_incidents.date: September 2024 (first attack disclosed Sept 4; second Medusa-affiliate attack later in September, data posted Sept 18, 2024)
example_incidents.summary: Medusa ransomware affiliates breached Compass Group's Australian IT network twice within the same month, exfiltrating close to 1TB of data combined, including employee wage records and scanned passports/driver's licenses of contractors, then threatened publication on Medusa's leak site.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed by Compass Group; company activated its incident response plan and notified employees, clients, suppliers and regulators.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: First attack: Medusa demanded US$2 million to delete/not publish the ~785.5GB of stolen data (with a US$100,000/day deadline-extension fee). Second (separate) attack: ransom demanded was US$100,000. Not publicly confirmed whether any payment was made.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Specific downtime duration not publicly detailed in press coverage; company stated it secured systems and launched an investigation with external cybersecurity specialists.
example_incidents.data_impact: Near 1TB combined across both incidents; data included employee wage declarations and scanned passports/driver's licenses of contractors and staff, with the threat actor threatening publication on its dark-web leak site.

example_incidents.group: Unclaimed / unattributed (no group publicly took credit)
example_incidents.date: March 2024 (outage began March 22, resolved around March 26, 2024)
example_incidents.summary: A ransomware attack encrypted numerous Panera Bread virtual machines, taking down point-of-sale systems, online/mobile ordering, the loyalty (MyPanera) program, and internal phone systems across the chain's roughly 2,160 cafés; stores stayed open but had to fall back to cash-only transactions during the outage.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed by Panera; the company did not release financial figures. Independent security analysts estimated such multi-day enterprise ransomware disruptions typically cost tens of millions of dollars in lost sales and recovery, but no Panera-specific figure has been confirmed.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed; no group claimed responsibility and Panera did not comment on any ransom demand or payment.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Approximately one week (March 22-26, 2024) of major IT outage across point-of-sale, online ordering, loyalty and phone systems before restoration.
example_incidents.data_impact: A subsequent notice confirmed an employee data breach tied to the March incident (SSNs and other employee personal data); customer payment-data exposure was not confirmed.

example_incidents.country: Norway/Scandinavia (200 properties across Scandinavia, Finland, and the Baltics)
example_incidents.summary: Conti ransomware hit Nordic Choice Hotels' central IT systems, disabling reservation, check-in/check-out, room key-card and payment systems across its ~200-property, 16,000-employee hotel network; staff fell back to manual processes while replacement systems were rolled out property-by-property.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a specific dollar figure.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Nordic Choice stated it deliberately did not contact Conti and had not received (or did not intend to pay) a ransom demand; no payment reported.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Replacement/workaround solutions were in place at most hotels within days of the attack (over the following weekend), with normal operations restored within about a week.
example_incidents.data_impact: Guest booking data and Nordic Choice Club (loyalty) member data were confirmed potentially exposed; no indication passwords or payment card data were affected.

example_incidents.victim: Rivers Casino Des Plaines / Rush Street Gaming
example_incidents.group: Cicada3301 (2023 breach discovered Nov 2023; Cicada3301 also separately claimed Rivers Casino Philadelphia data in a later 2025 extortion post)
example_incidents.summary: Hackers accessed files containing personal data of customers and employees at Rivers Casino (Illinois); the breach was discovered months after the intrusion, leading to consumer notification, class-action litigation, and a separate 2025 Cicada3301 extortion claim against the related Rivers Casino Philadelphia/Rush Street Gaming entity.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; the casino faced a class-action lawsuit over the data breach.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: For the 2025 Rivers Casino Philadelphia/Rush Street Gaming Cicada3301 claim, an undisclosed ransom was demanded with a stated deadline (Feb 15, 2025); no payment publicly confirmed. No ransom figure disclosed for the 2023 Illinois breach.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No major operational outage publicly reported; this was primarily a data-theft/notification incident rather than an encryption/downtime event.
example_incidents.data_impact: Names, birth dates, contact info, driver's license/government ID numbers, Social Security numbers, bank account and tax ID information, and passport numbers for a subset of customers and employees (at least 8,151 individuals per Comparitech); the 2025 Cicada3301 claim alleged 2.56TB of data stolen from Rush Street Gaming.

example_incidents.date: June 2025 (claimed on leak site June 20, 2025; group teased on social media June 12)
example_incidents.summary: Anubis ransomware claimed the largest data leak in Disneyland Paris's history, alleging the data (obtained via breach of a construction/renovation partner company rather than Disneyland directly) included ~39,000 files of park construction and renovation plans, exposing images/videos of attraction designs (Crush's Coaster, Frozen, Ratatouille, Buzz Lightyear, Phantom Manor, etc.). Disneyland Paris had not publicly confirmed the claims as of the reporting.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; Disneyland Paris had not acknowledged the breach in public statements found.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed/unclear whether a ransom was demanded of Disneyland Paris directly versus its partner firm.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No park operational disruption reported; this was a third-party/supply-chain data-exposure incident rather than an IT outage at the park itself.
example_incidents.data_impact: Approximately 64GB / ~39,000 files of construction and renovation-related documents and media allegedly exposed via a Disneyland partner company, not confirmed to include guest personal data.

example_incidents.summary: On November 8, 2023, Inspired Entertainment, Inc. detected a ransomware attack that disrupted its corporate IT systems. The company initiated response protocols and engaged cybersecurity experts, later discovering that personal data had been exfiltrated on November 15, 2023.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The affected IT systems have now been substantially restored to full operational capabilities.
example_incidents.data_impact: Company data, including personal data, was exfiltrated.
sources: United States Securities and Exchange Commission

example_incidents.summary: On January 18, 2023, Yum! Brands, Inc. announced a ransomware attack that impacted certain information technology systems. The company initiated response protocols and engaged cybersecurity professionals, while confirming that less than 300 restaurants in the UK were temporarily closed but are now operational.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Less than 300 restaurants in the United Kingdom were closed for one day; all stores are now operational and systems are expected to be largely restored in the coming days.
example_incidents.data_impact: Data was taken from the Company's network; no evidence that customer databases were stolen.

example_incidents.summary: England Hockey is investigating a potential data breach after the AiLock ransomware gang listed it as a victim on its data leak site. The threat actor allegedly stole 129GB of data and threatened to publish the files unless a ransom is paid. The organization is prioritizing an inquiry with both internal teams and external experts to understand the situation.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Washington Hotel in Japan disclosed a ransomware infection incident that compromised its servers, exposing various business data. The hotel brand has engaged cybersecurity experts and is assessing the impact while confirming that customer data is likely safe due to separate storage. The attack occurred on February 13, 2026, and has temporarily affected operations at some properties.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The incident is impacting operations at some Washington Hotel brand properties, including the temporary unavailability of credit card terminals. The firm says it recorded no significant operational disruption.
example_incidents.data_impact: various business data; customer data is unlikely to be exposed

example_incidents.summary: The Toronto Zoo experienced a ransomware attack in January 2024, resulting in a data breach that exposed personal and financial information of employees, volunteers, and donors. The Akira ransomware group claimed responsibility for the attack and published the stolen data on their dark web site, which included sensitive information from transactions dating back to 2000.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: impacted individuals' names, street address information, phone numbers, e-mail addresses, last four digits of credit card numbers, associated expiration dates

example_incidents.summary: The Play ransomware gang claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on Krispy Kreme, impacting its business operations and online ordering system. The gang alleged that they stole sensitive data from the company's network and threatened to publish it unless a ransom was paid.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Krispy Kreme experienced operational disruptions, particularly with online ordering, and took measures to contain and remediate the breach.

example_incidents.summary: Bologna FC confirmed a ransomware attack by the RansomHub group, which resulted in the theft and online publication of sensitive data. The leaked data includes personal and confidential information of players, financial records, and medical records, among other details.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: The Grand Palais Rmn in France suffered a cyberattack during the Olympic Games, which was identified as a ransomware attack. Although operational disruptions occurred, the museums under its management continued to operate normally, and there were no signs of data exfiltration, despite a ransom note being left by the attackers demanding payment in cryptocurrency.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: operational disruptions were reported, but a solution allowed stores and boutiques to operate autonomously

example_incidents.summary: Christie's, a British auction house, notified clients of a data breach involving the RansomHub ransomware gang, which accessed and extracted customer files between May 8 and May 9, 2024. The auction house is offering affected individuals a free twelve-month subscription to an identity theft monitoring service and has taken steps to secure its systems following the incident.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: at least 500,000 clients' full names, addresses, ID document details, and various other sensitive personal information

example_incidents.summary: The Daixin ransomware gang claimed a cyberattack on Omni Hotels, threatening to publish sensitive customer information unless a ransom is paid. The attack caused a nationwide IT outage affecting various systems, and the gang has claimed to have stolen over 3.5 million visitor records.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Certain systems were brought offline, most of which have been restored. Omni quickly launched an investigation with a leading cybersecurity response team, which is ongoing.
example_incidents.data_impact: 3,539,089 records of Omni Hotels visitors with sensitive information, including names, email addresses, and mailing addresses.

example_incidents.summary: Omni Hotels Resorts confirmed a cyberattack caused a nationwide IT outage affecting its locations. The hotel chain is currently restoring encrypted servers from backups and has taken down impacted systems to protect its data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Systems are being manually restored from scratch, with some systems expected to be available again on Thursday.

example_incidents.summary: The MGM Resorts service desk was hacked through sophisticated social engineering tactics, allowing attackers to gain unauthorized access and deploy ransomware across the network. This incident caused significant operational disruptions and highlighted the need for improved security measures at helpdesks.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: widespread system outages and operational disruptions

example_incidents.summary: Gallery Systems, a software solutions provider for museums, suffered a ransomware attack on December 28, 2023, leading to significant IT outages. The attack encrypted certain computer systems, preventing them from operating, and the company is working to restore access while notifying law enforcement and conducting an internal investigation.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Systems taken offline to prevent further encryption; working to restore access with last available backup.

example_incidents.summary: Gellyberry Studios, the indie game developer of 'Ethyrial: Echoes of Yore,' suffered a ransomware attack that encrypted all data on their main server, including local backups, resulting in the loss of 17,000 player accounts. The developers opted not to pay the ransom, fearing that it would not guarantee the return of their data, and are instead working to manually restore the lost accounts and items.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Server availability returned late on Friday; developers are manually restoring affected accounts and data.
example_incidents.data_impact: 17,000 player accounts affected; in-game items and progress lost.

example_incidents.summary: The FBI has issued a warning about ransomware gangs targeting casinos through third-party gaming vendors. The Silent Ransom Group (SRG) has been involved in data theft and extortion attacks, tricking victims into installing malicious tools that allow them to exfiltrate sensitive data without encrypting files.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: personally identifiable information of employees and patrons

example_incidents.summary: LDLC ASVEL, a French professional basketball team, confirmed a data breach following a ransomware attack by the NoEscape gang. The attackers claimed to have stolen 32 GB of sensitive data and are threatening to publish it unless a ransom is negotiated. The club is currently assessing the impact of the breach and has reported the incident to the national data protection authority.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 32 GB of data stolen, including personal data of players, passports, ID cards, financial, taxation, and legal documents, NDAs, contracts, and confidential letters

example_incidents.summary: Motel One was targeted by the BlackCat/ALPHV ransomware gang, which claimed to have stolen nearly 24.5 million files, including sensitive customer data. The hotel chain reported that while the attackers infiltrated their network, the impact was minimized due to effective protective measures. However, the threat actors have threatened to leak the stolen data if a ransom is not negotiated within five days.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 150 credit cards, customer addresses, booking confirmations for the past 3 years

example_incidents.summary: A ransomware operation has targeted Russian players of the Enlisted multiplayer first-person shooter by distributing trojanized versions of the game through a fake website. The ransomware, which mimics the notorious WannaCry, encrypts files and demands a ransom from victims within three days.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Yum! Brands, the owner of KFC and Pizza Hut, experienced a ransomware attack on January 13, 2023, resulting in the theft of personal information of employees. The attack led to the temporary closure of around 300 restaurants in the U.K., but the company reported no evidence of customer data being affected.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: 300 restaurants shut down temporarily for one day
example_incidents.data_impact: personal information of employees including names, driver's license numbers, and other ID card numbers

example_incidents.summary: Crown Resorts confirmed it suffered a data breach after its GoAnywhere secure file-sharing server was compromised by the Clop ransomware gang. The gang is extorting Crown Resorts, claiming to have stolen data from its networks, although the company states there is no evidence of customer data being compromised.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: IceFire ransomware has expanded its operations to target Linux systems, previously focusing on Windows. The ransomware encrypts files on compromised systems and employs a strategic approach to avoid complete system shutdowns. The group has been active since at least March 2022 and has recently resumed attacks using a new variant of their malware.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: The Play ransomware gang claimed responsibility for a cyber attack on H-Hotels, resulting in communication outages for the company. The attack involved the use of ransomware to encrypt devices on the network after gaining access through vulnerabilities in Microsoft Exchange.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: communication outages

example_incidents.summary: The Hive ransomware gang claimed responsibility for a cyber attack on the New York Racing Association (NYRA) on June 30, 2022, which compromised member data. The attack did not affect day-to-day racing operations, but the association's website faced accessibility issues, and the hackers published a link to download stolen files.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: NYRA's website remains out of reach, but core operations were not interrupted.
example_incidents.data_impact: personally identifiable information of NYRA employees and their beneficiaries

example_incidents.summary: The San Francisco 49ers experienced a data breach due to a ransomware attack by the Blackbyte gang, affecting over 20,000 individuals. The attackers accessed and stole personal information, and the team is working on restoring their systems while enhancing security protocols.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The 49ers are still restoring systems, indicating that the breached devices were likely encrypted.
example_incidents.data_impact: 20,930 individuals affected; personal information including names and Social Security numbers.

example_incidents.summary: The ALPHV ransomware gang has launched a dedicated website allowing employees and customers of a hotel and spa in Oregon to check if their data was stolen during a ransomware attack. They claim to have stolen 112GB of data, including sensitive employee information for 1,534 individuals, and are using this site to pressure the hotel into paying a ransom to prevent public exposure of the data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 1,534 employees affected; sensitive information including names, Social Security Numbers, date of birth, phone numbers, and email addresses

example_incidents.summary: A new ransomware named 'WannaFriendMe' has been discovered, which sells its decryptor on the Roblox platform using in-game currency. This ransomware variant, related to Chaos ransomware, encrypts files and demands payment in Robux for decryption, targeting young gamers. Roblox has since removed the Game Pass and the account responsible for selling the decryptor.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

exposure_categories.description: Core operational software that, if encrypted or disrupted, halts check-in/out, room assignment, and bookings, causing immediate revenue and reputational loss.
subcategories: Property Management Systems (PMS) for hotels/resorts
Central reservation systems (CRS) and channel managers (OTA integrations)
Digital room-key / electronic lock systems
Restaurant/venue reservation and table-management platforms
Ticketing and admissions systems (theme parks, museums, theaters, sporting/entertainment venues)
Event and conference booking platforms

exposure_categories.description: High-volume, PCI-DSS-regulated transaction systems across hotels, restaurants, casinos, and venues that are prime ransomware/extortion targets due to payment card data and operational criticality.
subcategories: POS terminals and back-office POS servers (restaurants, bars, retail outlets, cafés)
Payment gateways and card-present processing systems
Gift card / stored-value and mobile-order-ahead platforms
Casino cage, kiosk, and cashless-wagering systems
ATMs and self-service payment kiosks on-premises

exposure_categories.description: Large repositories of sensitive personal and financial data accumulated through loyalty programs, bookings, and identity verification, making this sector attractive for double-extortion data leaks.
subcategories: Loyalty/rewards program databases (names, contact info, tier/points data)
Government ID data (passport, driver's license, national ID numbers) collected for check-in/KYC/casino compliance
Social Security / national insurance numbers (employee and, in some jurisdictions, guest records)
Payment card and billing data
Health/dietary/accessibility data (spas, cruise lines, event catering)
Minors' data (theme parks, family resorts, youth programs)

exposure_categories.description: Specialized OT/IT-blended systems unique to the gaming vertical within this sector, where downtime directly halts revenue-generating floor operations.
subcategories: Slot machine and cashless wagering networks
Surveillance and physical security systems (often networked to IT)
Player-tracking / rewards-card systems
Sports betting and online gaming platforms
Regulatory/compliance reporting systems (gaming commissions)

exposure_categories.description: Extensive outsourcing and franchise/partner relationships common to hospitality, food service, and entertainment create indirect exposure when a vendor, franchisee, or partner is compromised.
subcategories: IT help desk / managed service providers (a common initial-access vector, e.g., MGM/Caesars)
Third-party booking, ticketing, and OTA platforms
Food & beverage supply chain and distribution/logistics vendors (e.g., Blue Yonder-type SaaS incidents)
Construction, renovation, and facilities contractors with access to internal systems/data (e.g., Disneyland Paris partner breach)
Staffing agencies and payroll/HR outsourcing providers
Franchise and multi-brand management companies operating shared back-office systems across many independently branded properties

exposure_categories.description: Smart-building and physical-plant systems increasingly networked to corporate IT, creating an OT-adjacent attack surface distinct to physically large hospitality/entertainment venues.
subcategories: HVAC, elevator, and building-management systems
Digital signage and in-room entertainment systems
Wi-Fi and guest network infrastructure
Access control and key-card provisioning systems
Ride/attraction control systems (theme parks) and AV/production systems (theaters, arenas)

exposure_categories.description: Back-office systems common to any large multi-site employer, holding data attractive for extortion beyond guest-facing systems.
subcategories: Employee HR/payroll records (SSNs, banking details)
Corporate financial/ERP systems
Email and collaboration/communication platforms
Franchise financial reporting and multi-property accounting consolidations

hazard_categories.description: How ransomware/extortion actors most commonly breach organizations in this sector, reflecting its large, high-turnover, geographically distributed workforce and heavy vendor reliance.
subcategories: Help-desk / call-center social engineering and vishing to reset MFA or credentials (Scattered Spider-style attacks on MGM, Caesars)
Phishing and callback phishing (e.g., Silent Ransom Group-style tactics)
Compromised or purchased credentials, often sourced via infostealer malware from employee or third-party devices
Exploitation of internet-facing PMS, booking, or POS software vulnerabilities
Compromise of third-party IT support/managed service providers with privileged remote access
Compromise via franchise/partner networks with shared or federated access to corporate systems

hazard_categories.description: The mix of pressure techniques ransomware/extortion groups apply against hospitality, food-service, and entertainment targets, which have historically shown high willingness to pay to avoid guest-facing outages during peak periods.
subcategories: Encryption of operational systems (PMS, POS, reservations) causing immediate, highly visible service disruption
Data exfiltration and double/triple extortion (threatening publication of guest/loyalty PII, ID scans, financial data)
Direct harassment of executives, guests, or loyalty-program members with stolen data
Publication of sensitive operational or IP-like materials (e.g., unreleased attraction designs, menus, pricing) as leverage distinct to entertainment/theme-park operators
Timing attacks to coincide with peak seasons, holidays, or major events to maximize revenue-loss pressure and increase likelihood of ransom payment
Pure data-theft extortion without encryption (e.g., ShinyHunters/Scattered Spider-linked groups increasingly skip encryption and threaten-to-leak only)

hazard_categories.description: Unlike pure back-office IT sectors, hospitality/entertainment venues integrate IT with physical operations, so a ransomware event can directly disrupt guest safety, access, and physical service delivery, not just data confidentiality.
subcategories: Casino floor and gaming-machine network disruption
Digital door-lock and access-control system failures stranding guests or preventing check-in
Point-of-sale/payment terminal outages forcing cash-only operations
Ride/attraction control and building-management system exposure at theme parks and large venues
Kitchen, ordering, and inventory system outages disrupting food safety and service continuity

hazard_categories.description: The sector's heavy reliance on franchising, outsourced IT, shared SaaS booking/POS platforms, and contractors creates concentrated single points of failure that can cascade across many brands and properties.
subcategories: Managed service provider (MSP) / IT help-desk vendor compromise (root cause of MGM and Caesars incidents)

SaaS booking, PMS, or supply-chain platform compromise affecting many downstream hotel/restaurant brands simultaneously (mirrors Blue Yonder-type incidents Verizon DBIR flagged for accommodation/food services)
Construction, renovation, or facilities contractor breaches exposing sensitive operational data (Disneyland Paris partner breach)
Franchise/master-licensor shared infrastructure compromise cascading to independently owned locations
Payment processor or gift-card platform compromise

hazard_categories.description: High employee turnover, seasonal/temporary staffing, and broad front-line system access (POS, PMS, key systems) common to this sector elevate both malicious-insider and credential-hygiene risk.
subcategories: High staff turnover creating stale/orphaned credentials and inconsistent access de-provisioning
Seasonal and temporary/contract staff with broad system access and less security training
Front-desk/POS-level social engineering targets (staff empowered to make account/reservation changes)
Shared or weakly managed credentials across large, decentralized property networks

hazard_categories.description: Data-protection, payment-card, and consumer-protection obligations that shape breach costs and downstream liability specific to guest-data-heavy businesses.
subcategories: PCI-DSS obligations for any entity processing card payments (hotels, restaurants, casinos, ticketing)
State/national breach-notification laws (frequent driver of disclosed incident detail in this sector, as seen in Maine AG filings)
Gaming-commission and casino-regulator compliance obligations
GDPR/international privacy law exposure for globally operating hotel chains and cruise lines
Consumer class-action litigation risk following large loyalty-program or guest-data breaches (MGM, Caesars, Marriott)
Brand/reputational risk disproportionate to direct financial loss, given guest-trust-dependent business models

industry: Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment
overview: The Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment industry (ransomware.live sector tag "Hospitality and Tourism") is a high-frequency, high-visibility ransomware target: 771 victims have been tracked on ransomware.live's leak-site monitoring platform since roughly 2018, spanning hotels, casinos, restaurants, theme parks, cruise lines, museums, theaters, and travel/tour operators across 65+ countries (with the US, GB, FR, ES, CA, AU, DE and IT most represented). The sector is attacked by a broad spread of ransomware groups -- LockBit (in its 2/3/5 variants), Qilin, Akira, Play, Medusa, IncRansom, RansomHub, DragonForce and Clop are the most prolific -- and has produced some of the highest-profile ransomware incidents in history (MGM Resorts, Caesars Entertainment) due to the combination of large, valuable guest/loyalty databases, PCI-regulated payment systems, IT/OT-blended physical operations (casino floors, digital key/lock systems, POS), heavy third-party/franchise dependency, and a business model highly sensitive to even brief guest-facing downtime -- all of which make organizations in this sector both frequent targets and comparatively willing payers.

industry: Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Food Production
overview: The Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Food Production sector is a designated critical-infrastructure sector (Food & Agriculture / FA) that has become one of the fastest-growing ransomware targets. It spans a "farm-to-fork" chain of primary producers (crop farms, livestock/poultry, dairy, aquaculture/fisheries, forestry/timber), cooperatives and grain elevators, agri-input suppliers (seed, fertilizer, agrochemicals), food and beverage processors/manufacturers, cold-storage and logistics providers, and grocery/food distributors. The sector's defining risk characteristic is an extraordinarily low tolerance for downtime: perishable inputs and finished goods spoil, livestock require continuous feeding/climate control, and processing is time-and-temperature critical, so an IT outage rapidly cascades into physical, food-safety and food-security consequences. This combination — thin IT/OT security maturity, seasonal/just-in-time operations, heavy automation (SCADA in plants, precision-ag telematics, automated milking/feeding), and consolidation that concentrates single points of failure (a handful of meatpackers, one dominant grocery distributor) — makes victims unusually likely to pay ransoms. Ransomware.live's 'Agriculture and Food Production' sector tag returned 1,219 tracked victim postings (2019–2026) at time of pull, dominated by LockBit, Akira, Qilin, Play, Cl0p, Black Basta, RansomHub and DragonForce, with the United States (321), Canada, Brazil, Italy, France, Germany, UK and Spain most represented. Independent tracking by the Food and Ag-ISAC recorded 212 sector incidents in 2024 (5.8% of all attacks) rising to 265 in 2025, part of an 82% year-over-year surge in overall ransomware volume.

hazard_categories.description: How threat actors gain first entry, shaped by the sector's dispersed sites, legacy systems, seasonal/temporary workforce, and heavy reliance on third-party integrators and remote support.
subcategories: Phishing / business email compromise targeting procurement, logistics and finance staff (single-click compromise, as in the Ahold Delhaize USA breach)
Exploitation of internet-facing/edge devices and unpatched VPNs, RDP and firewalls at remote farms, elevators, plants and cold-storage sites
Mass-exploitation of zero-day/managed-file-transfer and enterprise software vulnerabilities (Cl0p-style campaigns against the sector)
Valid/stolen credentials sourced from infostealer logs (ransomware.live records infostealer-linked exposure for many food/ag domains)
Compromise of third-party IT/OT integrators, MSPs, ag-tech SaaS and remote maintenance access into plant networks
Weak segmentation between corporate IT and plant OT allowing lateral movement from an office foothold into production

hazard_categories.description: The mix of leverage attackers apply. In this sector the physical perishability and food-security angle amplifies pressure to pay quickly.
subcategories: Encryption of production/ERP/warehouse and ordering systems that halts slaughter, processing, packing, invoicing and dispatch (JBS, KP Snacks, UNFI)
Double extortion: exfiltration of data plus threat to leak (Conti/KP Snacks; INC Ransom/Ahold Delhaize; BlackMatter/NEW Cooperative)
Perishability-driven time pressure — spoilage of raw materials, finished goods and livestock welfare used as urgency leverage
Food-security / public-safety framing to raise reputational and regulatory stakes on a critical-infrastructure victim
Re-extortion and data-recycling (e.g., 2026 'coinbasecartel' posting reusing JBS data years after the original event)
Triple extortion / harassment of customers, growers, and downstream retailers whose shelves empty during an outage

hazard_categories.description: Operational-technology exposure specific to farms and food plants where cyber impact becomes physical and food-safety relevant.
subcategories: Plant SCADA/PLC and process-control systems for slaughter lines, pasteurization, cooking, canning, milling and bottling
Cold-chain and refrigeration/HVAC controls where downtime causes spoilage or food-safety failures
Automated milking, feeding, ventilation and climate systems in livestock/poultry/dairy operations (animal-welfare risk)
Precision-agriculture and equipment telematics (GPS-guided machinery, grain-drying, irrigation, environmental controls)
Building-management and food-safety monitoring systems (temperature logging, HACCP-linked sensors)
IT/OT convergence and flat networks that let office ransomware reach production floors

hazard_categories.description: The sector's consolidation and just-in-time structure mean one victim's outage propagates widely; conversely, victims are exposed through their many upstream vendors.
subcategories: Concentration risk in dominant nodes (few large meatpackers, a single primary grocery distributor such as UNFI supplying 30,000+ stores)
Cooperative/shared-platform risk where one hub serves many farms (NEW Cooperative claimed to touch ~40% of US grain production)
Downstream disruption to retailers and food service (empty shelves, salad-kit and crisp shortages) creating contractual and liability exposure
Upstream dependency on agrochemical, seed, feed, packaging and logistics vendors as attack conduits
Ag-tech / SaaS and cloud ERP dependencies (SoilMap-type platforms, farm-management software)
Cross-border, multi-plant footprints that let a single intrusion affect operations on several continents (JBS US/Canada/Australia)

hazard_categories.description: Compliance and liability hazards triggered by an incident, heightened by critical-infrastructure designation and personal-data holdings.
subcategories: Critical-infrastructure reporting obligations (CISA/CIRCIA in the US, NIS2 in the EU) and national food-security scrutiny
Data-breach notification and privacy liability (state AG filings, GDPR) for employee, grower and customer PII/SSNs (Ahold Delhaize 2.2M individuals)
Food-safety regulatory fallout when process/monitoring systems are compromised (FDA/USDA, HACCP records)
Sanctions/OFAC risk when paying groups linked to sanctioned actors
Securities-disclosure exposure for public companies (SEC 8-K / 6-K materiality; Dole and UNFI quantified impacts in filings)
Contractual penalties and litigation from retailers, distributors and cooperative members affected by supply failure

hazard_categories.description: Human and organizational weaknesses characteristic of the sector.
subcategories: Large seasonal/temporary and low-turnover-training workforce increasing phishing susceptibility
Historically thin cybersecurity budgets and staffing, especially at farms, co-ops and mid-size processors (DHS records noted JBS's pre-attack security as unusually poor)
Legacy and end-of-life systems in plants and back-office (Dole: half of legacy servers affected)
Limited backup/recovery testing and lack of manual fallback procedures for automated operations
Dispersed rural sites with inconsistent monitoring and slow patch cycles
Insider access at co-ops and family/closely-held businesses with informal IT governance

exposure_categories.description: The plant-floor and field systems whose disruption stops physical output and threatens food safety and animal welfare.
subcategories: Processing-line SCADA/PLC/DCS (slaughter, milling, pasteurization, cooking, canning, bottling)
Cold-storage / refrigeration / HVAC and environmental controls
Automated milking, feeding, ventilation and livestock climate systems
Precision-ag equipment, telematics, GPS guidance, irrigation and grain-drying controls
Food-safety and quality monitoring/sensor systems (temperature logging, HACCP instrumentation)
Warehouse automation, robotics and conveyance in distribution centers

exposure_categories.description: The business systems that, when encrypted, halt ordering, invoicing, dispatch and payment even when the physical plant is intact.
subcategories: ERP / MRP and inventory-management systems
Electronic ordering, EDI, invoicing and payment systems (UNFI outage crippled ordering/invoicing)
Warehouse-management and transportation/fleet-management systems
Corporate email, file repositories and Active Directory/identity infrastructure
Back-office finance, HR and payroll systems
Legacy and end-of-life servers and end-user computers

exposure_categories.description: The data whose exfiltration drives double-extortion leverage and regulatory liability.
subcategories: Employee/grower PII including SSNs, driver's licenses and passports (Ahold Delhaize: names, DOB, government IDs)
Customer and loyalty/pharmacy data at grocery-affiliated operations
Financial, banking and payment-card records
Proprietary R&D, recipes, breeding/genetics data and agronomic IP (BlackMatter stole NEW Cooperative's SoilMap source code)
Contracts, pricing, supplier and cooperative-member records
Food-safety, traceability and compliance documentation

exposure_categories.description: External entities and shared platforms whose compromise or whose reliance on the victim creates propagating exposure.
subcategories: Grocery retailers, food-service buyers and downstream distributors dependent on continuous supply
Cooperative members and affiliated farms sharing a common platform/hub
Upstream input suppliers (seed, feed, fertilizer, agrochemicals, packaging)
Logistics, cold-chain and 3PL transportation providers
Ag-tech / farm-management SaaS, cloud ERP and remote-support MSPs/integrators
Payment processors and banking partners

exposure_categories.description: Sector-unique tangible exposures that convert cyber downtime into direct physical loss.
subcategories: Perishable raw materials and finished inventory at risk of spoilage during outages
Live animals dependent on automated feeding, watering and climate control (welfare and mortality risk)
Cold-chain integrity across storage and transit
Seasonal/time-critical processing windows (harvest, slaughter, planting) with no slack to absorb downtime
Manual-workaround capacity and business-continuity/backup infrastructure
Brand/reputation and consumer-trust assets tied to food safety and availability

example_incidents.summary: The world's largest meat processor was hit by REvil, forcing shutdown of beef and pork slaughterhouses across the US, Canada and Australia and disrupting roughly a fifth of US meat capacity. Internal DHS records later characterized JBS's pre-attack cybersecurity as unusually poor. Ransomware.live also tracks a later 2026 'coinbasecartel' posting recycling ~3TB of JBS data, illustrating re-extortion.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Direct operational disruption to global meat supply; JBS did not publicly quantify total losses beyond the ransom. Widely cited as one of the most consequential critical-infrastructure attacks of 2021.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: REvil initially demanded $22.5 million; JBS negotiated and paid $11 million in Bitcoin.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Multiple North American and Australian plants shut for roughly a day-plus; JBS said the majority of facilities were operational again within days, choosing to pay to avoid prolonged disruption and possible data exfiltration.
example_incidents.data_impact: JBS said it paid partly to ensure no data was exfiltrated; no large-scale data leak was confirmed at the time.

example_incidents.summary: North America's largest grocery distributor and primary supplier to Whole Foods was forced to take core systems offline after a June 2025 cyberattack, crippling electronic ordering and invoicing across its 53 distribution centers serving 30,000+ retail locations and emptying shelves nationwide. One of the largest quantified financial hits in the sector.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Estimated $350–$400 million reduction in fiscal-2025 net sales; net income impact of $50–$60 million and adjusted EBITDA impact of ~$40–$50 million. Included ~$20 million in manual-workaround costs and ~$5 million in remediation. Company said it expects insurance proceeds to be adequate to substantially offset losses.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Systems taken offline in early June 2025; company ran manual workarounds and said the operational impact was mostly contained to the quarter, with phased restoration over subsequent weeks.
example_incidents.data_impact: Not detailed publicly; impact framed primarily as operational/supply disruption.

example_incidents.summary: One of the world's largest fresh-produce suppliers suffered a February 2023 ransomware attack that hit about half of Legacy Dole's servers and a quarter of end-user computers, briefly shutting North American operations and causing widely reported packaged-salad shortages on US store shelves.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Total incident impact of $10.5 million for the quarter ended March 31, 2023 (of which $4.8 million related to continuing operations); CEO warned the financial impact would not be fully recoverable through insurance.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: North American operations briefly shut down; most disruptive to Fresh Vegetables and Chilean businesses. All impacted servers and end-user computers were subsequently restored or rebuilt with third-party IR support.
example_incidents.data_impact: Dole later disclosed the attack breached data of almost 3,900 US workers.

example_incidents.victim: Ahold Delhaize USA (Giant Food, Hannaford, Food Lion, Stop & Shop, The Giant Company)
example_incidents.summary: The US division of the multinational grocery/food retailer detected unauthorized access on Nov 6, 2024, disrupting pharmacies and supermarket network systems. INC Ransom claimed the attack in April 2025, asserting up to 6TB of stolen data; the incident became one of the largest food-retail data breaches on record.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not separately quantified in dollar terms publicly; costs include breach response and two years of free credit monitoring/identity protection for 2.24M affected individuals.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: No ransom reported paid — attackers published ~800GB of data on their leak site, indicating non-payment.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Network issues across US pharmacies and supermarkets in November 2024; systems restored over following weeks.
example_incidents.data_impact: Breach affected 2,242,521 people; leaked data included names, postal/email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth and government IDs (SSNs, driver's licenses, passports).

example_incidents.summary: An Iowa farm cooperative providing feed, grain and crop-protection services was hit by BlackMatter, which locked systems used to manage food supply chains and animal-feeding schedules. The co-op said ~40% of US grain production runs through its software and warned the attack could 'break the supply chain very shortly,' making it a landmark food-security incident.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; the co-op proactively took systems offline to contain impact rather than pay.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: BlackMatter demanded $5.9 million, escalating to $11.8 million if unpaid within five days. Reporting indicated the co-op did not pay.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Systems taken offline proactively to contain the threat; operations managed via workarounds while remediation proceeded with law enforcement and security experts.
example_incidents.data_impact: BlackMatter claimed theft of financial information, HR data, R&D information and source code for the 'SoilMap' agricultural technology platform.

example_incidents.summary: The UK snack maker (Hula Hoops, McCoy's, KP Nuts, Tyrrells, Butterkist) discovered a Conti ransomware attack on Jan 28, 2022 that disrupted IT systems so severely it could not safely process orders or dispatch goods, prompting warnings of crisp and snack shortages through at least March.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; disruption to order processing and distribution for roughly two months with supply-chain knock-on to retailers.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Conti operated double-extortion with a leak-site countdown; ransom amount and any payment not publicly confirmed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Order placement and delivery disrupted from late January with no normal service expected until at least end of March 2022.
example_incidents.data_impact: Conti published samples including credit-card statements, birth certificates, and spreadsheets with employee addresses and phone numbers on its leak site.

example_incidents.summary: One of Canada's largest packaged-meats and food producers suffered a November 2022 outage attributed to Black Basta ransomware, causing a system disruption that affected operations and order fulfillment across its network; recorded in the ransomware.live sector dataset as a Black Basta victim.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Company acknowledged the outage would cause operational and financial impact and expected full resolution to take time; specific loss figure not itemized publicly.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed; Maple Leaf publicly indicated it would not accede to criminal demands.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: System outage began early November 2022 with recovery efforts extending over subsequent weeks while the company used workarounds to maintain supply.
example_incidents.data_impact: Not detailed publicly at scale; primarily an operational-disruption event.

example_incidents.summary: Dole Food Company confirmed a ransomware attack in February 2023 that accessed employee information. The attack led to the shutdown of production plants across North America and caused delays and shortages of products in stores.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Production plants across North America were shut down, and all shipments were on hold.
example_incidents.data_impact: Employee information of an undisclosed number of employees was accessed.

example_incidents.summary: AGCO, a leading US-based agricultural machinery producer, was hit by a ransomware attack that impacted some of its production facilities. The attack was attributed to the LockBit ransomware group, which has been involved in various cyberattacks recently.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

Food and Ag-ISAC / IT-ISAC 2024 & 2025 Ransomware Reports (via Industrial Cyber, The Record, AGDAILY)
Financial/breach press coverage: SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Cybersecurity Dive, The Register, CNBC, Washington Post, Computer Weekly, CyberScoop, Grocery Dive, Industrial Cyber, CPO Magazine
data_source_notes: STEP 1 (ransomware.live): The documented endpoint https://api.ransomware.live/v2/victims/sector/Agriculture%20and%20Food%20Production returned an HTTP 302 redirect to the site's HTML /api docs page (the site is on a 'v6.0-beta Aegis' redesign) and did not serve JSON; WebFetch also could not parse it. After testing endpoint variants, the working path was https://api.ransomware.live/v2/sectorvictims/Agriculture%20and%20Food%20Production, which returned a valid JSON array of 1,219 victim records with fields activity, attackdate, claim_url, country, data_size, description, discovered, domain, group, infostealer, press, ransom, screenshot, url, victim. One earlier call to /v2/sectors hit an HTTP 429 rate-limit; retried successfully via a distinct endpoint. Data was fetched with PowerShell Invoke-RestMethod (curl returned HTTP 000 in this sandbox). STEP 2 supplements both FAILED: ransomlook.io/api/search returned HTTP 400 Bad Request; ransomwhat.telemetry.ltd/posts.json 302-redirected to ransomwatch.telemetry.ltd and the redirected posts.json returned HTTP 404 — neither corroborating source was usable, so victim/group corroboration relied on the ransomware.live dataset plus mainstream news. STEP 3 incident financials were verified against news reporting and, where available, SEC filings (Dole, UNFI). No figures were invented; where a detail was not publicly reported it is marked 'Not publicly disclosed.' The JBS record inside the ransomware.live sector dataset is a 2026 'coinbasecartel' re-extortion posting rather than the original 2021 REvil event (illustrating data recycling); the 2021 incident details come from contemporaneous reporting. Maple Leaf Foods financial detail is limited in public sources.

overview: The Construction sector (general contractors, engineering/design firms, infrastructure operators, homebuilders, specialty trades, and building-materials suppliers) is one of the most heavily and consistently targeted industries by ransomware groups. Ransomware.live's full victim dataset shows 1,362 distinct Construction-sector victims posted to ransomware leak sites from 2019 through mid-July 2026, with volume climbing sharply from 2021 onward and 2025 alone accounting for 513 posted victims - more than any prior full year (2026 already shows 267 through mid-July). The sector combines several features attackers find attractive: large numbers of small/mid-size subcontractors with weak security maturity sitting inside supply chains for very large general contractors and government owners; time-sensitive, contractually penalized project schedules that increase pressure to pay quickly; large transient, multi-employer workforces with sprawling credential/access footprints; and high-value intellectual property (design/BIM data, bids, proprietary engineering methods) alongside sensitive employee PII (payroll, SSNs) in HR/finance systems. Victims range from small regional contractors to the world's largest construction and infrastructure firms (Ferrovial, Balfour Beatty, Bechtel, Kier Group, Kajima, AECOM, Turner Construction), and the sector has repeatedly been swept up in mass, single-vulnerability exploitation campaigns (e.g., Clop's 2025 Oracle E-Business Suite zero-day campaign) that hit many unrelated construction firms simultaneously through shared enterprise software.

hazard_categories.description: How attackers first get into construction-industry networks, shaped by distributed jobsites, subcontractor sprawl, and reliance on shared enterprise/file-transfer platforms.
subcategories: Phishing/BEC targeting project managers, estimators and accounts-payable staff (construction's high-value, milestone-based subcontractor and supplier payments make it a prime invoice-fraud/BEC target, often paired with or following a ransomware intrusion)

Exploited perimeter and file-transfer/ERP vulnerabilities in widely-used enterprise software (e.g., Clop's 2025 Oracle E-Business Suite CVE-2025-61882 zero-day campaign hit multiple construction firms, including Bechtel and Kier, within days of each other)
Compromised VPN/RDP credentials, including access issued to jobsite trailers and temporary site networks with weaker controls than corporate HQ

Infostealer-harvested credentials from employee and third-party devices (Ferrovial's July 2026 AiLock incident was linked to over 100 compromised employee and third-party credential sets surfaced via infostealer telemetry)
Compromised or over-privileged subcontractor/vendor remote-access accounts on shared project extranets

hazard_categories.description: How ransomware groups pressure construction victims to pay, once inside.
subcategories: Double extortion: encryption plus exfiltration and leak-site publication of stolen files (the dominant model seen across Qilin, LockBit, Akira, Play, DragonForce, INC Ransom incidents in the dataset)
Triple extortion / regulatory and reputational threats (AiLock explicitly threatens to notify regulators and competitors and gives victims a 72-hour response window)
Pure data-theft extortion without encryption (Everest has shifted toward this model; used against Turner Construction)
Threats to leak competitively sensitive bid, pricing and design data to rival bidders or competitors ahead of tender awards

Mass 'name-and-shame' campaigns where dozens of victims across many industries (including construction) are listed together after a single shared-software exploit, increasing pressure via public exposure even before individualized negotiation

hazard_categories.category: OT, IoT and Jobsite/Facilities Technology Risk
hazard_categories.description: Physical and operational-technology exposure distinct to construction and post-construction facilities management, generally less targeted today than pure-IT systems but a growing concern.
subcategories: Building Management/Automation Systems (BMS/BAS) for HVAC, elevators and life-safety systems on projects under a firm's ongoing facilities-management or warranty-service contracts
Connected heavy-equipment telematics and fleet/GPS tracking systems
Jobsite IoT sensors (structural/concrete-cure monitoring, environmental sensors)
Site security systems - cameras, badge/access control - on active construction sites
Potential physical-safety and schedule-disruption consequences if OT/jobsite systems are affected, distinct from pure data-confidentiality harm

hazard_categories.description: Construction projects run through deep, multi-tier subcontractor and design-partner networks and shared platforms, creating single points of failure that can cascade across many unrelated firms.
subcategories: Shared collaboration/BIM platforms (e.g., Procore, Autodesk Construction Cloud/BIM 360) linking general contractors, architects, engineers, and dozens of subcontractors
Common enterprise software creating simultaneous multi-victim exposure (Bechtel and Kier Group were both hit within the same week during Clop's Oracle EBS campaign, despite being unrelated companies)
General contractor -> subcontractor -> sub-subcontractor credential and data flows, where the weakest link in the chain can expose the whole project
Architecture/engineering design partners and geotechnical/survey consultants with access to shared project data
Owner and lender portals used for draw requests and project financing, exposing financial data outside the contractor's own perimeter

hazard_categories.description: Construction's large, transient, multi-employer labor force creates distinctive access-management challenges.
subcategories: Shared or generic site-login credentials used across union labor, day laborers and rotating temp/subcontractor staff
Weak or inconsistent offboarding across multi-employer jobsites when subcontractor personnel change frequently
Disgruntled former employees or terminated subcontractors retaining VPN/portal access
Field staff use of personal/BYOD devices for project apps, increasing infostealer and credential-theft exposure outside corporate IT control

hazard_categories.description: Legal and contractual consequences specific to how construction firms hold data and are bound by project agreements.
subcategories: Employee PII/payroll breach notification obligations (AECOM's 2021 incident exposed employee SSNs and bank routing/account numbers and required notification to the California Attorney General)

Government-contractor obligations (major defense/energy/critical-infrastructure contractors such as Bechtel and AECOM handle DoD/DOE and critical-infrastructure work, raising CMMC/DFARS-style breach-notification and controlled-technical-information exposure)
Professional liability/errors-and-omissions exposure if stolen design, CAD/BIM or structural-engineering data proves defective or is misused after a leak
Contractual delay-damages/liquidated-damages exposure if ransomware-driven downtime in scheduling, procurement, or payroll systems cascades into project schedule slippage
Bid-integrity and antitrust-adjacent exposure if leaked tender/pricing data undermines competitive bidding processes

hazard_categories.description: How ransomware translates into operational and financial disruption specific to project-based construction work.
subcategories: Disruption to estimating, scheduling and project-management software halting active bid submissions or project coordination
ERP/accounting/payroll system outages disrupting subcontractor and supplier payments, risking mechanic's-lien and cash-flow disputes
Procurement and material-ordering system outages delaying material delivery to active job sites

Indirect (rather than physical-site) downtime: unlike manufacturing OT shutdowns, ransomware in construction more often stalls back-office/coordination functions than the physical build itself, per Sophos data showing lower rates of data-theft/encryption combination in construction/property/energy versus manufacturing

exposure_categories.description: The core intellectual property of a construction or engineering firm, of high value both for extortion leverage and to competitors.
subcategories: CAD and BIM (Building Information Modeling) files
Architectural drawings and blueprints
Structural, MEP and civil engineering calculations
Geotechnical and site-survey data
Proprietary construction methods and engineering IP

exposure_categories.description: Commercially sensitive project economics and the financial systems that manage them - a favored ransomware and extortion target.
subcategories: Tender/bid documents and competitive pricing data
Contract terms and subcontractor pricing schedules
Procurement and vendor/supplier data
ERP and accounting systems (e.g., Oracle E-Business Suite - the shared platform exploited in the 2025 Clop campaign that hit Bechtel and Kier)
Banking and wire-transfer details, a frequent target for invoice-fraud/BEC layered on top of ransomware intrusions

exposure_categories.description: Personal data held on large, often multi-employer workforces.
subcategories: Payroll systems (SSNs, bank account/routing numbers - exposed in AECOM's 2021 breach)
HR files and personnel records
Union membership and labor records
Licensing, certification and background-check records for skilled trades
Badge and physical access-control credentials

exposure_categories.description: Technology deployed at or connecting to active construction sites, often with weaker security posture than corporate headquarters.
subcategories: Project-management/collaboration platforms (Procore, Autodesk Construction Cloud/BIM 360, PlanGrid)
Jobsite security cameras and access-control systems
Equipment telematics and fleet-management/GPS tracking systems
Connected/automated heavy machinery
Temporary site networks and trailer-based IT infrastructure

exposure_categories.description: Operational technology exposure that persists beyond project completion, for firms with ongoing facilities-management, warranty or operations contracts.
subcategories: Building Management/Automation Systems (HVAC, elevators)
Life-safety systems (fire, alarm) in occupied buildings under warranty/FM contracts
Toll-road, transit and infrastructure operational systems for firms that also operate (not just build) infrastructure assets (e.g., Ferrovial's toll-road and mobility operations)

exposure_categories.description: External parties and shared infrastructure that extend a construction firm's attack surface beyond its own perimeter.
subcategories: Shared extranets/portals used by subcontractors, architects and engineers
Owner and lender draw-request/financing portals
Common enterprise software shared industry-wide, creating correlated multi-victim exposure
Managed IT/security service providers used by smaller subcontractors

exposure_categories.description: Sensitive project data held on behalf of government and critical-infrastructure clients, elevating national-security and export-control considerations for some firms.
subcategories: Defense, energy and critical-infrastructure project data (Bechtel and AECOM both handle large DoD/DOE and critical-infrastructure programs)
Potentially export-controlled or classified-adjacent technical data for defense/energy construction work
Public infrastructure and toll/transit operational data

example_incidents.summary: AiLock, a double-extortion RaaS group active since March 2025, claimed Ferrovial - a global infrastructure and mobility operator involved in construction and design plus toll-road concessions - on its leak site. AiLock's model gives victims a 72-hour response window and up to five days to pay, threatening regulator notification and competitor disclosure if unpaid.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; no company financial statement or disclosed cost found.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.data_impact: Per HudsonRock infostealer telemetry referenced on the incident's ransomware.live page: 147 compromised employee accounts, 16 compromised user accounts, 106 third-party employee credentials, and 27 external attack-surface exposures identified. Underlying stolen data types/volume from the ransomware group's own leak were not detailed in available sources as of this writing (incident is very recent/still developing).

example_incidents.date: October 12, 2025 and April 8, 2026 (two separate claimed incidents)
example_incidents.summary: Balfour Beatty, a leading UK-headquartered international infrastructure group delivering construction, engineering and support services across transportation, power, buildings and civil works in the UK, US and other markets, was claimed by two different ransomware groups within a six-month span: INC Ransom in October 2025 (targeting US operations) and CoinbaseCartel in April 2026 (UK).
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed for either incident.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed for either incident.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Not publicly disclosed for either incident.
example_incidents.data_impact: Leak size described as 'unknown' in available secondary reporting for both incidents; no confirmed data-type breakdown found in public sources.

example_incidents.country: United States (privately held, one of the world's largest engineering/construction/project-management firms, major US government contractor)
example_incidents.summary: Bechtel was named by the Clop ransomware group as part of a large-scale extortion wave exploiting a zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2025-61882) in Oracle E-Business Suite. Clop posted roughly 39 victim organizations across many industries within a 24-hour window in this campaign; Clop had earlier exfiltrated data via the Oracle EBS flaw in August 2025 and followed up with mass extortion emails in late September 2025 before publishing leak-site listings in November.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed by Bechtel; no company statement located.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.data_impact: Specific data types/volume exfiltrated from Bechtel were not detailed in available sources; the broader Oracle EBS campaign is understood to have exposed enterprise financial, HR and procurement data (the standard EBS module set) at affected organizations generally.

example_incidents.country: United Kingdom (major listed construction, property and infrastructure services company, LSE:KIE)
example_incidents.summary: Kier Group, a leading UK construction, civil-engineering, property and infrastructure services company operating across defence, transportation, health, education and utilities, was claimed by Clop as part of the same Oracle E-Business Suite CVE-2025-61882 mass-exploitation campaign that hit Bechtel days later.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed; Clop threatened to release data absent negotiation.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.data_impact: Per secondary reporting citing infostealer-derived telemetry on the incident record: 4 employees, 120 users, and 23 third-party employee credentials referenced as compromised/exposed; specific stolen-file categories from the Clop leak itself were not detailed in available sources.

example_incidents.country: United Kingdom / continental Europe operations of Kajima Corporation (Japan, one of the world's largest construction firms)
example_incidents.summary: Qilin, one of the most prolific ransomware groups globally in 2025 (claiming roughly 800 victims across 50+ countries since January 2025, and dominant in Europe with 65 Q3-2025 victims per Cyble), claimed Kajima Europe, the European arm of major Japanese construction group Kajima Corporation, exfiltrating a large volume of corporate and project data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Not publicly disclosed/documented in available sources.
example_incidents.data_impact: Approximately 400 GB of data reported exfiltrated, including engineering documents, CAD designs and blueprints, financial and investment records, construction contracts and procurement documentation, internal communications, subcontractor lists and payment schedules, employee HR files/credentials, and project-management files.

example_incidents.country: United States (Fortune 500 global engineering, design and infrastructure-consulting firm)
example_incidents.summary: AECOM was compromised in a payroll-system hack attributed to the Pysa (Mespinoza) ransomware group's double-extortion operators; AECOM subsequently notified current and former employees that their personal data had been exposed and reported the incident to the California Attorney General's office. This is one of the better-documented incidents in the sector because it produced a formal breach notification rather than only a leak-site claim.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Specific incident-response, remediation or credit-monitoring costs were not publicly disclosed; no stock-impact or insurance-payout figures found in public sources.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.data_impact: Personal information of present and former AECOM employees was exposed, including names, addresses, Social Security numbers, and personal bank account and routing numbers, via compromise of the US payroll system; exact number of employees affected was not confirmed in available public sources.

example_incidents.country: United States (one of the largest construction management firms in the US)
example_incidents.summary: Turner Construction Company was listed as a victim by the Everest ransomware group, a double-extortion (and increasingly pure data-extortion) operator active since December 2020 that has targeted government, healthcare, manufacturing and IT-services organizations across North America, Europe and Asia. Turner's inclusion illustrates the group's willingness to target top-tier construction management firms.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.data_impact: Specific data types/volume were not detailed in available public sources beyond the leak-site listing itself.

example_incidents.summary: The Donut extortion group has been confirmed to deploy ransomware in double-extortion attacks, targeting various enterprises including the multinational construction company Sando. The group uses customized ransomware that encrypts files and appends a specific extension, while also engaging in theatrics with their ransom notes and marketing strategies.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Knauf Group, a multinational building materials producer, was targeted by the Black Basta ransomware gang on June 29, 2022. The attack disrupted business operations, leading to a complete shutdown of IT systems while the company investigates and responds to the incident. Black Basta claimed responsibility and leaked 20% of the stolen files, indicating ongoing negotiations for a ransom payment.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Knauf's global IT team shut down all IT systems to isolate the incident and is in the process of forensic investigation, incident response, and remediation.
example_incidents.data_impact: 20% of the files allegedly exfiltrated included email communication, user credentials, employee contact information, production documents, and ID scans.

example_incidents.summary: A new ransomware operation named 'Lilith' has emerged, targeting a large construction group in South America as its first victim. The ransomware performs double-extortion attacks, stealing data before encrypting files and threatening public exposure if the ransom is not paid. The incident highlights the growing threat of this new ransomware strain in the cyber landscape.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
