example_incidents.victim: PowerSchool (SIS vendor serving K-12 districts in the US, Canada and elsewhere)
example_incidents.group: Not a named ransomware brand - single-actor extortion; US DOJ charged Matthew D. Lane, then a 19-year-old student at Assumption University
example_incidents.summary: The defining edtech aggregation event. An attacker used compromised credentials to access PowerSchool's PowerSource support portal and exfiltrate student and teacher data from the hosted SIS environment. PowerSchool paid an extortion demand in exchange for a video purporting to show deletion of the only copy of the data. The deletion proved worthless: in May 2025 the same data was used to extort individual school districts directly in Canada and North Carolina, with attackers sending samples to schools. PowerSchool stated it did not believe this was a new intrusion because the samples matched the December theft. This is the clearest available demonstration that paying for a deletion promise transfers no risk downstream, and that a single vendor compromise generates thousands of correlated district-level losses.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Total programme cost not publicly disclosed. PowerSchool offered two years of identity protection and credit monitoring to affected students and educators; class-action litigation followed. Individual district remediation and notification costs were not publicly itemised.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Approximately $2.85 million in bitcoin demanded and PAID by PowerSchool, per US Department of Justice court documents made public 20 May 2025. Amounts sought in the subsequent district-level extortion attempts were not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No mass encryption event - this was exfiltration-only extortion, so districts did not suffer the closure pattern typical of encryption attacks. Recovery centred on notification, credit monitoring, credential resets and multi-jurisdiction regulatory response, extending well beyond a year and reopening when re-extortion began in May 2025.
example_incidents.data_impact: The attacker claimed data on 62.4 million students and 9.5 million teachers across approximately 6,505 school districts in the US, Canada and other countries. Exposed fields included names, addresses, dates of birth, contact details, and for some individuals Social Security numbers and medical/grade information. Affected populations are overwhelmingly minors, whose identity exposure persists for decades.

example_incidents.date: 2026-05-01 (intrusion 29-30 April 2026; second breach within roughly two weeks)
example_incidents.summary: Described in reporting as the largest education-sector breach on record. ShinyHunters exploited Instructure's Free-For-Teacher (FFT) programme - which allowed educators to create Canvas accounts without institutional verification - to reach production data, then breached the platform a second time within about two weeks. After Instructure missed the initial 7 May negotiation deadline, the group escalated by defacing Canvas login portals at roughly 330 institutions and pivoting to direct school-by-school extortion with a final 12 May deadline. Instructure reached a payment agreement on 11 May, one day before the leak deadline. The incident is the purest example of LMS vendor concentration risk: Canvas is used by 41% of US higher education institutions, so a single platform intrusion simultaneously exposed thousands of otherwise unconnected insureds.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Institutional costs spanned incident response, forensic review, portal remediation after defacement, and notification across thousands of schools.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Ransom PAID by Instructure under an agreement reached 11 May 2026; the amount was not publicly disclosed. Attackers reportedly returned the data and supplied 'shred logs' as claimed proof of destruction - the same unverifiable deletion assurance seen in the PowerSchool case.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Instructure took Canvas, Canvas Beta and Canvas Test offline on 7 May 2026 for investigation and restored service the following day; Canvas Data 2 and Canvas Beta had been in maintenance since 1 May. The Free-For-Teacher account programme was permanently shut down as a remediation measure. Roughly 330 institutions additionally had to remediate defaced login portals.
example_incidents.data_impact: ShinyHunters claimed 3.6TB covering 275 million users across approximately 9,000 institutions (reporting also cites 8,809 universities, education ministries and other bodies) - figures Instructure has not confirmed. Instructure confirmed exposure of names, email addresses, student ID numbers and some private messages between Canvas users, and stated there was no evidence that passwords, financial data or SSNs were taken. Attacker leak-site copy claimed billions of private student-teacher and student-student messages.

example_incidents.group: noescape (per ransomware.live leak-site attribution; press reporting did not definitively confirm the group)
example_incidents.summary: A university research-archive breach that illustrates how higher education accumulates liability for populations who were never students or staff. Attackers reached data from the Multiethnic Cohort (MEC) Study, a longitudinal epidemiological study established in 1993, plus files from three other diet-and-cancer studies. Compounding the event, the university did not notify affected study participants for roughly four months - a delay that drew specific public criticism and independent regulatory risk. Notably, the university PAID to prevent publication, making this one of the few education cases with a confirmed payment decision.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Costs included ransom payment, third-party forensic and recovery support, and notification plus remediation for up to 1.15 million individuals.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Ransom PAID - the centre worked with third-party cybersecurity experts to obtain a decryption tool and paid to prevent publication of the stolen data. The amount was not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Encrypted data was recovered using a decryption tool obtained through the payment. Specific outage duration was not publicly disclosed. Notification lagged roughly four months behind discovery, with the centre compiling names and addresses for study participants well after the August 2025 intrusion.
example_incidents.data_impact: Up to 1.15 million individuals affected (some reporting cites approximately 1.2 million). Exposed data included Social Security numbers and driver's licence numbers sourced from the Hawai'i State Department of Transportation, and City and County of Honolulu voter registration records from 1998. Much of the affected population were research study participants rather than students or employees.

example_incidents.group: Not publicly attributed (district confirmed ransomware; FBI engaged)
example_incidents.summary: The canonical K-12 operational-disruption case. Highline, a Washington state district of 34 schools serving roughly 17,500 students and 2,000 staff, detected the intrusion on a Saturday and immediately isolated critical systems - then closed every school and all activities for three days because core instructional and safety systems could not be trusted. It demonstrates the sector's defining characteristic for insurers: a school district has no degraded operating mode, so business interruption manifests as total closure of an essential public service, with statutory make-up obligations and knock-on effects to transport and meal programmes.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Costs included district-wide re-imaging of all student and staff devices, third-party forensic engagement, and three days of lost instruction across 34 schools.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed - the district declined to say how much was demanded, citing the ongoing investigation, and did not publicly confirm any payment.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: All schools and activities closed for three days, from Monday 9 September through Wednesday 11 September 2024, reopening Thursday 12 September. Network systems remained disrupted into October 2024, when all student and staff devices had been re-imaged - roughly a month of degraded operation after classes resumed.
example_incidents.data_impact: The district confirmed that highly sensitive personal, financial and medical data was breached. The precise number of affected students and staff was not publicly disclosed in the reporting reviewed.

example_incidents.summary: The UK's national library, described as one of the worst cyber incidents in British history. Rhysida rendered almost all VMware ESXi servers unavailable, taking down the website, on-site services and Wi-Fi; the library remained physically open but could accept only cash payments. The institution refused to pay and Rhysida published the stolen material. The case is the reference point for catastrophic recovery severity in a public, non-commercial education/research body: the recovery cost dwarfed the ransom demand by an order of magnitude, and the library had to consume roughly 40% of its financial reserves - a funding mechanism with no analogue in the commercial sector and a key consideration for public-institution insureds.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Approximately GBP 6-7 million in recovery costs, funded from roughly 40% of the library's financial reserves - about ten times the ransom demanded.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: 20 bitcoin demanded, approximately GBP 596,000 at the time. NOT PAID - the library refused, and Rhysida published the data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Services were severely disrupted for months. The main catalogue returned online on 15 January 2024 in read-only format, roughly two and a half months after the attack, with other services expected to remain unavailable for months beyond that. Recovery was complicated by legacy infrastructure and constrained funding, documented in the library's own transparency reporting and subsequent academic analysis.
example_incidents.data_impact: Approximately 600GB of material leaked publicly after refusal to pay, including internal documents and staff and user data. Full affected-individual counts were not publicly itemised in the reporting reviewed.

example_incidents.group: Not publicly attributed to a named leak-site brand; triple-extortion tactics consistent with groups active against UK/US higher education in 2023
example_incidents.date: 2023-06-05 (intrusion began 5 June 2023; detected 9 June; containment from 14 June)
example_incidents.summary: The clearest illustration of research-data liability in higher education. Attackers reached a research archive holding NHS patient records gathered from more than 200 hospitals for medical research purposes - including major-trauma patient reports and treatment records for victims of terrorist attacks - alongside current student and alumni data. Attackers then emailed students and staff directly threatening to sell their data, a triple-extortion pressure tactic. The incident triggered questions in UK health and education policy about universities holding national-scale clinical datasets under research governance rather than clinical security controls.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed. No public confirmation of payment; the university worked with the ICO, NCSC and National Crime Agency.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Detected 9 June 2023 with containment beginning 14 June. Specific outage duration and full recovery timeline were not publicly disclosed; response ran in parallel with ICO and NCSC engagement.
example_incidents.data_impact: Around 250GB of data accessed. Included NHS records relating to 1.1 million patients across more than 200 hospitals, gathered for medical research - with NHS numbers and the first three letters of patients' postcodes among the fields, plus major-trauma and terrorist-attack victim treatment data. Separately, student and alumni data was leaked including names, contact details, gender, dates of birth, university ID numbers and fee status. Students and staff received direct threats to sell their data.

example_incidents.victim: Minneapolis Public Schools (Special School District No. 1)
example_incidents.summary: The reference case for extortion harm to minors and for notification failure. Medusa demanded $1 million with a 17 March deadline, posted the district on its leak site with a countdown, offered to sell the data to any buyer for $1 million, and offered the district the option to pay $50,000 per additional day of delay. The district refused and restored from internal backups - but Medusa then published the files. Analysts confirmed the leaked corpus included school security blueprints, a physical-safety exposure that cannot be remediated by notification or credit monitoring. The district publicly characterised the event as an 'encryption event' and did not notify the 105,617 affected individuals until September 2023, seven months later.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Costs included forensic investigation, restoration from backups, and notification plus credit monitoring for 105,617 individuals.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: $1,000,000 demanded by Medusa with a 17 March 2023 deadline; the leak site also offered a $50,000-per-day deadline extension and listed the data for outright purchase at $1 million. NOT PAID - the district restored from internal backups and Medusa published the stolen files.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Widespread digital disruption following the 17 February 2023 encryption event; the district recovered encrypted data from internal backups rather than paying. Precise system-restoration duration was not publicly disclosed. Notification took seven months, completing in September 2023.
example_incidents.data_impact: 105,617 people notified as affected. Nearly 200,000 individual files containing sensitive student and educator information were released publicly, including student psychological and welfare records. Cybersecurity experts confirmed campus security maps and school security blueprints were among the leaked material - creating ongoing physical-safety risk to students.

example_incidents.date: 2022-09-03 (attack 3 September 2022; leak-site posting 30 September 2022; data published 2 October 2022)
example_incidents.summary: The attack that made K-12 ransomware a national policy issue in the US. Vice Society - the group that dominated education targeting in this period, ranking fourth all-time in the Education dataset with 63 victims - dwelled in the network of the second-largest US school district for over a month, from 31 July to 3 September 2022. LAUSD publicly refused to pay on the principle that 'dollars must be used to fund students and education' and that paying never guarantees full recovery, following FBI guidance. Vice Society published the full 500GB trove in retaliation. The leaked data's contents - student psychological assessments, health and COVID-19 test data, and prior conviction reports - established the template for how education extortion inflicts harm on minors specifically.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a single figure. The district funded incident response, credit monitoring for affected individuals including contractors whose SSNs were exposed, and a subsequent security programme uplift.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Demand amount not publicly disclosed. NOT PAID - LAUSD publicly refused, stating public dollars are better spent on students than on criminals, and Vice Society published the data on its leak blog on 2 October 2022.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The attack disrupted district systems in early September 2022 at the start of the school year, though schools remained open. Threat actors had persistent access from 31 July to 3 September 2022 before detection - a dwell time of over a month. Full remediation timeline was not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.data_impact: 500GB of data stolen and published. The trove included student psychological assessments, health information including COVID-19 test data, and prior conviction reports. LAUSD separately confirmed that contractors' Social Security numbers were among the stolen data. Passport data and other sensitive identifiers were also reported as potentially included.

example_incidents.summary: The Interlock ransomware attack utilized a new malware strain called Slopoly, which was likely generated using AI tools. The attack involved data theft and extortion, with the threat group Hive0163 being responsible for the incident, which affected the Texas Tech University System.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: The University of Hawaii Cancer Center experienced a ransomware attack in August 2025, resulting in the theft of data affecting nearly 1.2 million individuals. The university confirmed that it paid the attackers for a decryption tool and to ensure the destruction of the stolen information.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: paid to obtain a decryption tool and secure destruction of the information
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: caused extensive damage and delayed restoration efforts
example_incidents.data_impact: approximately 1.2 million individuals affected, including names and Social Security numbers (SSNs), driver's license numbers, and health information

example_incidents.summary: La Sapienza University in Rome experienced a cyberattack that caused significant operational disruptions and led to the shutdown of its IT systems. Reports suggest that the attack is a ransomware incident linked to a pro-Russian group called Femwar02, which may have resulted in data encryption.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The university's website remains offline, and technicians are working to restore systems from backups.

example_incidents.summary: Kyowon Group, a South Korean conglomerate, confirmed a ransomware attack that disrupted its operations and potentially exposed customer information. The attack occurred in January, affecting approximately 600 out of 800 servers, and the company is currently investigating the extent of the data breach while working to restore services.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The company is working to restore its online services, a process that is reportedly in its final stages.
example_incidents.data_impact: Over 9.6 million accounts registered, corresponding to about 5.5 million people may have had their information exposed.

example_incidents.summary: Baltimore City Public Schools experienced a data breach in February 2025, affecting over 31,000 individuals. The breach involved unauthorized access to sensitive documents, including social security numbers and student data, and has been linked to the Cloak ransomware group. The school district is providing credit monitoring services to those impacted.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: over 31,000 individuals affected, including sensitive data belonging to roughly 1,150 students, current and former employees, volunteers, and contractors

example_incidents.summary: The Pennsylvania State Education Association (PSEA) experienced a data breach on July 6, 2024, affecting over 500,000 individuals. The Rhysida ransomware gang claimed responsibility for the breach, demanding a ransom of 20 BTC and threatening to leak the stolen data if not paid.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 517,487 individuals affected; personal, financial, and health data including driver's license or state IDs, social security numbers, account PINs, security codes, payment card information, passport information, taxpayer ID numbers, credentials, health insurance and medical information

example_incidents.victim: Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center
example_incidents.summary: The Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center suffered a cyberattack in September 2024, impacting the data of 1.4 million patients. The attack was claimed by the Interlock ransomware group, which leaked 2.1 million files totaling 2.6 TB of data on their extortion portal.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: temporary disruption to some computer systems and applications
example_incidents.data_impact: 1,465,000 people; Full name, Date of birth, Physical address, Social Security number, Driver's license number, Government ID number, Financial account information, Health insurance information, Medical information, Billing/claims data, Diagnosis and treatment information

example_incidents.summary: The Toronto District School Board (TDSB) experienced a ransomware attack on its software testing environment, prompting an investigation into potential exposure of personal information. TDSB has confirmed that all systems remain operational and that they are working with law enforcement and cybersecurity experts to assess the situation.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: All systems are operational and none of their operations are disrupted.
example_incidents.data_impact: Approximately 247,000 students and 40,000 staff members potentially impacted; sensitive information may have been exposed.

example_incidents.summary: The University System of Georgia was impacted by the Clop ransomware gang's MOVEit attacks, resulting in the exposure of sensitive data for 800,000 individuals. The organization began notifying affected individuals in April 2024 after determining that Clop had stolen sensitive files from its systems.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 800,000 individuals affected; Full or partial Social Security Number, Date of Birth, Bank account number(s), Federal income tax documents with Tax ID number, Driver's license number or identification card number

example_incidents.summary: Stanford University experienced a ransomware attack that resulted in the theft of personal information belonging to 27,000 individuals. The attack was discovered on September 27, 2023, and was attributed to the Akira ransomware gang, which claimed to have stolen 430Gb of files from the university's systems and published the data on their dark web leak site.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 27,000 individuals; personally identifiable information (PII) including date of birth, Social Security number, government ID, passport number, driver's license number, biometric data, health/medical information, email address with password, username with password, security questions and answers, digital signature, credit card information with security codes

example_incidents.summary: A ransomware attack on Truman State University caused several days of shutdowns and required the engagement of external security teams. The attack highlights the vulnerabilities educational institutions face, particularly regarding the protection of sensitive personal data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: several days of shutdowns

example_incidents.summary: The Colorado Department of Higher Education disclosed a massive data breach following a ransomware attack on June 19, 2023. The attack compromised sensitive data affecting students, past students, and teachers, with the threat actors having access to the systems from June 11 to June 19, 2023. The stolen data includes personal information such as social security numbers and addresses, prompting the CDHE to offer identity theft monitoring to those impacted.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: CDHE took steps to secure the network and have been working with third-party specialists to conduct a thorough investigation into this incident. CDHE also worked to restore systems and return to normal operations.
example_incidents.data_impact: The data stolen includes full names, social security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, proof of addresses (statements/bills), photocopies of government IDs, and for some, police reports or complaints regarding identity theft. The breach impacts students, past students, and teachers who attended public institutions in Colorado between 2004 and 2020.

example_incidents.summary: On May 30th, 2023, the University of Waterloo experienced a ransomware attack targeting their Microsoft Exchange email service. As a result, the university mandated a mass password reset for staff, faculty, and students, affecting approximately 42,000 individuals. The reset process was scheduled to be completed by June 22nd, 2023, to mitigate potential security risks.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Hawai'i Community College admitted to paying a ransom to prevent the leaking of stolen data. The incident involved the data of approximately 28,000 individuals being at risk due to a ransomware attack.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Colorado State University confirmed that the Clop ransomware operation stole sensitive personal information of current and former students and employees during the MOVEit Transfer data-theft attacks. The breach impacts data from as far back as 2021, affecting personal identifiable information such as names, dates of birth, and social security numbers.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Des Moines Public Schools confirmed a ransomware attack that occurred on January 9, 2023. The BlackCat ransomware gang claimed responsibility for the attack, which involved data theft. The school district had to take all networked systems offline as a result of the incident.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: forced to take all networked systems offline
example_incidents.data_impact: data of not publicly disclosed number of people

example_incidents.summary: The Avos ransomware gang hijacked Bluefield University's emergency alert system to threaten students and staff with the release of stolen personal data unless a ransom was paid. The incident led to the postponement of examinations and the release of some stolen data, including sensitive documents.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: All examinations were postponed; remediation and system restoration efforts are still underway.
example_incidents.data_impact: 1.2 TB of files, including admissions data from thousands of students, W-2 Tax Form for the University's President, and a document related to their insurance policy.

example_incidents.summary: The Medusa ransomware gang claimed a cyberattack on the Open University of Cyprus, disrupting operations and leading to the offline status of critical systems. The group demanded a ransom of $100,000 and published data samples to prove their claims, affecting sensitive information of students and contractors.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Several central services and critical systems went offline; extensions for assignment submissions were provided by academic staff.
example_incidents.data_impact: Student lists with personally identifiable information, financial details of research contractors, and more.

example_incidents.summary: Technion - Israel Institute of Technology was hit by a ransomware attack from a group called DarkBit, which demanded a ransom of approximately $1.7 million. The attack was reportedly motivated by protests against tech layoffs and anti-Israel sentiments, and the university is actively responding to the incident while maintaining normal campus operations.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The university is currently carrying out incident response activities and has blocked all communication networks. Some technical systems are gradually being restored, but the incident response is ongoing.

example_incidents.summary: The Clop ransomware gang has developed a Linux variant that targets Oracle database servers, allowing victims to recover their files for free due to flaws in the encryption scheme. This variant was first spotted in December 2022 during an attack against a university in Colombia, highlighting its early development stage and weaknesses that make it less effective than its Windows counterpart.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: The Vice Society ransomware gang claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on the University of Duisburg-Essen in November 2022. The attack forced the university to reconstruct its IT infrastructure, a process that is still ongoing.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: ongoing reconstruction of IT infrastructure

example_incidents.summary: The Royal ransomware gang claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on the Queensland University of Technology, leaking data they allege was stolen during the breach. The university experienced significant service disruptions and shut down all IT systems to contain the attack, while also warning students and staff about potential risks.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Campuses reopened on January 3, 2023, but system disruptions are expected to continue for some weeks.
example_incidents.data_impact: 10% of the data stolen includes HR files, email and letter communications, ID cards and documents, and financial and administrative documents.

example_incidents.victim: Cincinnati State Technical and Community College
example_incidents.summary: Vice Society ransomware claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on Cincinnati State Technical and Community College, leaking data allegedly stolen during the attack. The college informed its students and staff about the cybersecurity incident, indicating that online services and restoration to regular operations will take time.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Restoration of on-campus networks and email, partial internet access, and classroom computers; however, voicemail, network printing, VPN access, and shared drives are unavailable, causing significant disruption.
example_incidents.data_impact: 10,000 students and 1,000 staff members affected; leaked documents contain personally identifiable information (PII).

example_incidents.summary: Vice Society has been targeting the education sector with multiple ransomware strains, including a recent attack on the Los Angeles Unified School District. The group is known for exfiltrating data before encryption and threatening to leak it if ransom demands are not met. Microsoft has reported that Vice Society has been active in the U.S. education sector since at least July 2022, using various ransomware families and tactics.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: The Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) was hit by a ransomware attack attributed to Russian hackers over the weekend of July 16-17, 2023. Following the attack, the agency activated its cybersecurity protocols and isolated several research centers to control the situation, with most still offline as recovery efforts continue.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Most centers still disconnected; just over 25% online as of the latest update.

example_incidents.summary: Maastricht University experienced a ransomware attack in December 2019, leading to the payment of a ransom to decrypt files. The attack was linked to the hacker group TA505, and the university later recovered the ransom amount through law enforcement efforts.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: approximately 4,500 employees' data including research, educational, and staff data, as well as salary payment information

example_incidents.summary: The Vice Society ransomware gang claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on the Medical University of Innsbruck, causing significant IT service disruption and the alleged theft of data. Following the attack, the university reset all account passwords and began restoring services, while the gang leaked documents on their site, indicating a potential dead end in ransom negotiations.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The university experienced an IT outage on June 20, 2022, and gradually restored its online services in the days that followed.
example_incidents.data_impact: 3,400 students and 2,200 employees; extensive list of documents allegedly stolen.

example_incidents.summary: A ransomware attack on Battelle for Kids exposed the data of nearly 500,000 students and over 56,000 employees of the Chicago Public Schools. The breach involved personal information and assessment scores from the school years 2015-2019, with CPS learning about the breach four months after it occurred.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 495,448 students and 56,138 employees; personal information and assessment scores

example_incidents.summary: Lincoln College, a liberal-arts school in Illinois, announced its closure after 157 years due to the financial impact of a ransomware attack in December 2021. The attack disrupted admissions activities and hindered access to institutional data, leading to significant enrollment shortfalls and ultimately the decision to cease all academic activity by May 13, 2022.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: All systems required for recruitment, retention, and fundraising efforts were inoperable until fully restored in March 2022.
example_incidents.data_impact: no personal identifying information was exposed

example_incidents.summary: Austin Peay State University suffered a ransomware attack, prompting the institution to shut down parts of its network for investigation. The attack was confirmed in late April 2022, and the university took measures to mitigate the impact on its operations.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: shut down portions of their network while investigating the attack

overview: The Energy and Utilities sector (ransomware.live tag "Energy," ~826 indexed victim records at time of research) spans oil & gas exploration/production, pipelines and midstream transport, refining, oilfield services, electric power generation/transmission/distribution, gas distribution, and water/wastewater utilities. It is a top-tier ransomware target because it blends two high-leverage traits: (1) it is critical national infrastructure where downtime has cascading physical, economic, and public-safety consequences, giving attackers extraordinary extortion leverage; and (2) it runs a large, aging, and often flat-networked mix of IT and operational technology (OT/ICS/SCADA). Even when malware only hits corporate IT, operators frequently shut down OT preemptively out of caution (as Colonial Pipeline and Conpet did), so IT-only intrusions still cause operational and physical-world disruption (fuel shortages, offline payment at fuel retail, halted shipment planning). Financially the sector is among the most expensive to recover: Sophos put mean recovery cost for energy/oil-gas/utilities at ~$3.12M (2024), IBM put average energy-sector breach cost at $4.83M, and the sector reports the highest ransom-payment propensity (61% pay) and lowest backup-restoration rate of any industry. Dominant groups observed against the sector include DarkSide/BlackCat(ALPHV) lineage, RansomHub, Qilin, Akira, DragonForce, LockBit, Everest, and Handala (hacktivist/geopolitical). Attacks cluster around stolen credentials/infostealers, VPN/remote-access and edge-device exploitation, and third-party/supply-chain footholds, with double- and triple-extortion (encryption + data theft + regulatory/press pressure) now standard.

hazard_categories.description: How ransomware actors first get into energy/utility environments. Credential-based and edge-device intrusions dominate; the sector's large geographically distributed remote-access footprint (substations, wells, pump stations, SCADA remote sites) widens the attack surface.
subcategories: Stolen/compromised credentials (IBM: #1 vector at 16%; e.g., Conpet infostealer on an IT admin's personal device)
Infostealer malware harvesting VPN/WSUS/RDP credentials from employee or contractor devices
Internet-facing VPN, firewall, and remote-access appliance exploitation (Fortinet/Citrix/Ivanti-class edge devices)
Phishing / business email compromise (energy/utilities are hit harder by email-borne attacks than most sectors)
Abuse of legitimate internal infrastructure (e.g., WSUS/patch-management to push a malicious 'fake update' at Conpet)
Exploitation of unpatched internet-facing enterprise apps and public-facing customer/billing portals
Third-party/vendor and MSP remote-access compromise

hazard_categories.description: How actors monetize access. The sector's criticality makes public/regulatory pressure especially potent, so exfiltration-led multi-extortion is now more common than pure encryption.
subcategories: Encryption of IT systems (production planning, shipment tracking, billing, ERP)
Data exfiltration + leak-site publication (double extortion; e.g., ALPHV 150GB from Creos/Encevo, Qilin ~1TB from Conpet)
Triple extortion: added pressure via press/regulators, and threats to customers/partners whose data was stolen
Threat/harassment of executives, employees, and Petro-Points/loyalty-style customer bases
DDoS as an added coercion layer
Auctioning/selling stolen files to highest bidder (RansomHub model)
Geopolitical/hacktivist extortion and 'name-and-shame' with no intent to decrypt (e.g., Handala targeting Gulf oil majors)

hazard_categories.description: The defining hazard of this sector: the interface between enterprise IT and operational technology (ICS/SCADA/DCS) controlling physical energy flows. IT-only ransomware routinely forces OT shutdowns, and OT-capable malware threatens physical damage.
subcategories: Precautionary OT shutdown after an IT-only breach (Colonial Pipeline 6-day halt; Conpet isolated systems)
Flat/poorly-segmented IT-OT networks allowing lateral movement into control systems
SCADA / DCS / HMI / historian compromise and loss of view or loss of control
OT-specific/ICS-tailored malware (e.g., FrostyGoop manipulating Modbus TCP/502; EKANS/Snake targeting ICS processes)
Legacy/unpatchable OT assets and long OT maintenance windows
Safety-instrumented-system (SIS) risk and potential for physical damage to turbines, pipelines, transformers
Dragos: 25% of observed OT ransomware cases involved full OT-site shutdown, 75% caused some operational disruption

hazard_categories.description: Energy relies on dense webs of vendors, EPC contractors, oilfield-service firms, software providers, and interconnected operators, so one compromise cascades across the value chain.
subcategories: Oilfield-services and drilling contractors as chokepoints (Halliburton disruption rippled to E&P customers)
ICS/automation vendors and remote-maintenance access (e.g., Schneider Electric compromise affecting industrial customers)
Managed service providers and shared IT platforms across utility groups
Software/firmware supply-chain and update-mechanism abuse
Fuel-retail and payment/POS processors (Suncor/Petro-Canada payment outage at 1,500+ stations)
Interconnected grid/pipeline operators and shared SCADA telemetry
Metering, AMI, and smart-grid device supply chain

hazard_categories.description: Privileged operators, field technicians, and contractors expand exposure; personal-device and credential hygiene gaps are recurrent root causes.
subcategories: Privileged IT/OT administrator credential theft (Conpet root cause)
Use of personal/unmanaged devices for work access
Contractor and seasonal/field-workforce access sprawl
Weak MFA coverage on remote-access and OT jump hosts
Malicious or negligent insiders with SCADA access

hazard_categories.description: Energy is heavily regulated as critical infrastructure; incidents trigger mandatory reporting, sanctions-screening on ransom payment, and public/political scrutiny.
subcategories: NERC CIP (bulk power) and TSA pipeline security-directive obligations
CISA/CIRCIA and national-CERT incident-reporting mandates; SEC 8-K materiality disclosure (Halliburton)
OFAC sanctions exposure when paying ransom to sanctioned/Russian-linked groups
Data-protection/privacy penalties (GDPR in EU; customer PII breaches)
State/national-security scrutiny and geopolitical targeting of energy assets
Litigation and shareholder/stock impact from disclosed material incidents

exposure_categories.description: The physical-process control estate unique to energy/utilities — the crown-jewel exposure whose compromise or precautionary shutdown halts energy delivery.
subcategories: SCADA systems and RTUs/PLCs at pipelines, substations, wells, pump/compressor stations
Distributed control systems (DCS) at power plants and refineries
Human-machine interfaces (HMIs), engineering workstations, and OT historians
Safety-instrumented systems (SIS) and protective relays
Modbus/DNP3/IEC-61850 industrial protocol networks
Grid/AMI smart-meter and distribution-automation infrastructure

exposure_categories.description: Corporate systems that, when encrypted, stop planning, dispatch, trading, and revenue — the layer most ransomware actually hits.
subcategories: Production-planning and shipment/logistics-tracking systems (Halliburton)
ERP, SCM, and asset-management platforms
Energy-trading, scheduling, and settlement systems
Billing, metering-to-cash, and customer-information systems (CIS)
Email, identity/Active Directory, and VPN/remote-access infrastructure
Backup and disaster-recovery systems (targeted to force payment)

exposure_categories.description: Public-facing and downstream retail exposure, particularly acute for utilities and fuel-retail operators.
subcategories: Fuel-retail POS and electronic-payment systems (Suncor/Petro-Canada: 1,500+ stations to cash-only)
Customer web portals and mobile apps (Creos/Enovos portals knocked offline)
Loyalty/rewards platforms and member databases (Petro-Points)
Outage-reporting and customer-service systems
Prepay/smart-meter customer accounts

exposure_categories.description: Data types whose theft drives extortion, regulatory penalties, and national-security concern.
subcategories: Customer PII and payment/loyalty data
Employee PII, HR records, passport/ID scans (Conpet, Creos)
Confidential contracts, agreements, invoices, financial records
Engineering diagrams, pipeline/grid schematics, and control-system documentation (national-security sensitive)
Geophysical/seismic, reserves, and exploration IP (oil & gas trade secrets)
Plaintext credentials and access secrets found in exfiltrated document troves (2,270+ credential-bearing files at Creos)

exposure_categories.description: External entities and links whose compromise transmits risk into or out of the operator.
subcategories: Oilfield-service, drilling, and EPC contractors
ICS/automation vendors and remote-maintenance channels
Fuel/payment processors and retail franchisees
Interconnected pipeline/grid operators and shared telemetry
MSPs, IT outsourcers, and shared group-IT platforms
Software/firmware/update supply chain (WSUS abuse, vendor patches)

example_incidents.summary: The largest refined-fuels pipeline in the US (Houston to the Southeast) was hit by DarkSide ransomware on its IT systems. Colonial proactively halted ALL pipeline operations to contain the attack. The 6-day shutdown interrupted fuel distribution to 17 states, triggering panic-buying, fuel shortages, and the highest average US gasoline price in over six years (~$3.04/gal by May 18). It is the defining cyber-physical energy ransomware case and prompted new TSA pipeline security directives.
example_incidents.financial_impact: No single official total disclosed by the company; national gasoline price spiked to a 6+ year high (~$3.04/gal). Ransom of $4.4M paid (see below). Widespread regional economic disruption from fuel shortages.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: $4.4M paid (75 bitcoin) within hours, overseen by the FBI. On June 7, 2021 the DOJ announced seizure/recovery of 63.7 BTC, then worth ~$2.3M (lower than paid amount due to BTC price drop).
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: All pipeline operations halted May 7; systems and operations returned to normal by May 15 (~6-day shutdown). Decryptor tool from DarkSide was slow, so recovery largely relied on Colonial's own restoration.
example_incidents.data_impact: Attackers exfiltrated roughly 100GB of data prior to encryption (double-extortion); primary impact was operational/physical rather than a large PII breach.

example_incidents.summary: One of the world's largest oilfield-services companies detected unauthorized access to corporate IT on Aug 21, 2024 and precautionarily shut down certain applications, including production-planning and shipment-tracking systems used in customer delivery. RansomHub claimed the attack and listed the company on its leak site; Halliburton confirmed data was stolen. Disclosed via SEC Form 8-K (Aug 23) and 8-K/A.
example_incidents.financial_impact: ~$35M direct pretax cost reported in Q3 2024 results (filed late Oct 2024); ~$0.02 adjusted-EPS impact for the quarter from lost/delayed revenue during system unavailability.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed — Halliburton did not confirm whether a ransom was demanded, negotiated, or paid.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Precautionary shutdown of parts of IT infrastructure caused client-system disconnections and temporary inability to generate critical business documents; company described operational impact as limited and restored systems over subsequent weeks. Exact downtime not itemized.
example_incidents.data_impact: Data exfiltration confirmed; company stated information was taken from its systems. Specific record counts/data types not fully disclosed publicly.

example_incidents.summary: A cybersecurity incident at Canadian integrated-energy giant Suncor disrupted its Petro-Canada retail subsidiary (1,500+ stations). Many stations went cash-only, unable to accept credit/debit or rewards; the Petro-Canada app, Petro-Points login, and car washes were unavailable at various sites. Illustrates downstream retail/payment-system exposure in vertically integrated energy firms.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly quantified as a single figure; disruption spanned 1,500+ retail sites over a weekend plus remediation costs (Suncor replaced employee laptops/computers as part of response).
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed; Suncor characterized it as a 'cybersecurity incident' and did not confirm a ransom.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Payment-system disruptions began ~June 21 and were largely resolved over the following days; Suncor swapped out employee computers as a remediation measure, extending internal recovery activity.
example_incidents.data_impact: Unauthorized party accessed basic information of Petro-Points loyalty members; affected members and privacy regulators were notified. No large-scale financial-data theft publicly confirmed.

example_incidents.summary: Luxembourg's main energy supplier/distribution group — network operator Creos and supplier Enovos, under parent Encevo — was hit overnight July 22-23, 2022 by ALPHV/BlackCat (the DarkSide/Colonial lineage rebrand). Customer portals of Creos and Enovos were knocked offline, though electricity and gas supply and breakdown services continued uninterrupted. Demonstrates data-exfil-led extortion against European grid infrastructure.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a dollar figure; operational impact limited to customer-portal outages (no supply interruption).
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Ransom amount not publicly disclosed; ALPHV threatened to publish stolen data if unpaid.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Creos and Enovos customer portals were rendered non-operational following the July 22-23 intrusion; portals were restored over subsequent days/weeks while supply services remained running.
example_incidents.data_impact: ALPHV claimed exfiltration of 150GB+ across 180,000+ files, published on its leak site July 29 — contracts, agreements, ID copies, invoices, and emails; analyses found 2,270+ files containing plaintext credentials/passwords and 100,000+ documents marked confidential.

example_incidents.summary: Romania's national oil-pipeline transport operator detected a cyberattack on Feb 3, 2026 affecting its business IT infrastructure. Crucially, OT systems — SCADA and telecommunications — stayed fully functional and pipeline transport continued. Qilin claimed the attack and alleged theft of ~1TB of data. Root cause was an infostealer on an IT administrator's personal device; with valid WSUS credentials attackers abused Conpet's own update infrastructure to push a malicious 'fake update' delivering Qilin ransomware.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly quantified; company emphasized transport operations were unaffected, limiting operational/financial disruption.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Business IT systems were isolated in response; SCADA/telecom and pipeline transport operations remained operational throughout (no OT downtime reported). IT recovery/remediation ongoing after Feb 2026 disclosure.
example_incidents.data_impact: Qilin alleged exfiltration of ~1TB including financial records, personnel data, and passport scans, and published sample images; Conpet confirmed data was stolen.

example_incidents.summary: Ecopetrol, Colombia's state-controlled national oil company and one of Latin America's largest energy firms, was listed as a victim by the 'TheGentlemen' ransomware group on ransomware.live (attack date 2026-07-17). Included as a recent, geographically diverse, large-state-oil-company data point from the ransomware.live Energy sector feed. Detailed public reporting was not yet available at research time (July 19, 2026).
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed at time of research.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed at time of research.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Not publicly disclosed at time of research.
example_incidents.data_impact: Claimed on ransomware.live leak-tracking; specifics of stolen data not independently confirmed at time of research.

example_incidents.summary: On October 29, 2024, Newpark Resources, Inc. detected a ransomware incident where an unauthorized third party accessed its internal information systems. The company activated its cybersecurity response plan and is investigating the incident with external advisors.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The incident caused disruptions and limitation of access to certain information systems, but manufacturing and field operations continued utilizing established downtime procedures.

example_incidents.summary: The Gentlemen ransomware gang has been linked to the compromise of the Romanian energy provider Oltenia. They utilize a suite of EDR killers, including a tool named GentleKiller, to disable defenses during attacks, allowing for unimpeded data theft or encryption processes.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: South Staffordshire Water Plc was fined $1.3 million by the Information Commissioner's Office after a cyberattack exposed the personal data of 663,887 customers and employees. The breach, which began in September 2020 and escalated between May and July 2022, was linked to the Cl0p ransomware gang, although the company initially dismissed these claims. The leaked data included sensitive personal information and was published on the dark web.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 663,887 customers and employees; full names, physical addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, customer account credentials, bank account details, employee HR data such as National Insurance numbers

example_incidents.summary: The Gentlemen ransomware group compromised Oltenia Energy Complex, one of Romania's largest energy providers, in December 2025. The attack utilized a botnet of over 1,570 hosts, indicating a focus on corporate victims. The ransomware employs advanced techniques for encryption and lateral movement within networks.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Conpet S.A., Romania's national oil pipeline operator, confirmed that the Qilin ransomware gang stole company data in a recent attack. The breach involved data exfiltration, with the attackers claiming to have stolen nearly 1TB of documents, including sensitive personal and financial information. The company is collaborating with the Romanian National Cyber Security Directorate to investigate the incident.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: operations remained unaffected
example_incidents.data_impact: nearly 1TB of documents, including financial information and passport scans; personal information such as names, postal addresses, personal identification numbers, and bank account numbers

example_incidents.summary: Southern Water, a UK water supplier, suffered a ransomware attack by the Black Basta group in February 2024, incurring costs of £4.5 million. The attack involved the theft of data from a limited part of their server estate, prompting the company to engage cybersecurity experts and legal advisers.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Initial demand of $3,500,000; proposed payment of $750,000
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: Limited part of server estate stolen; personal data may have been at risk

example_incidents.summary: The Lynx ransomware gang breached Electrica Group, a major electricity supplier in Romania, prompting an investigation in collaboration with national cybersecurity authorities. While critical power supply systems remained operational, the company is currently assessing the impact of the ongoing ransomware attack.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: In April 2020, the Chinese cybersecurity firm Sichuan Silence was involved in a series of Ragnarok ransomware attacks targeting U.S. critical infrastructure, including an energy company. The attackers exploited a zero-day vulnerability in Sophos XG firewalls to deploy malware and attempted to activate ransomware on victims' networks.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: approximately 81,000 firewalls compromised, including over 23,000 in the U.S.

example_incidents.summary: Evolution Mining, one of Australia's largest gold producers, was targeted by a ransomware attack on August 8, 2024, impacting its IT systems. The company has engaged external cybersecurity experts for remediation and reports that mining operations should continue uninterrupted, indicating that critical systems were likely not affected.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The attack is now fully contained, and the company does not anticipate any material impact on operations.

example_incidents.summary: The APT INC ransomware group, previously known as SEXi, has targeted IxMetro Powerhost, a Chilean hosting provider, encrypting their VMware ESXi servers. The group has been using the Babuk and LockBit 3 encryptors, demanding ransom payments in bitcoins for the decryption of affected files.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: PSI Software SE, a German software developer for critical infrastructure, confirmed a ransomware attack that impacted its internal systems. The company disconnected several IT systems to prevent data loss and is currently investigating the incident with assistance from authorities.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: IT systems, including email, were disconnected as a measure to mitigate the risk of data loss.

example_incidents.summary: Cactus ransomware claims to have stolen 1.5TB of data from Schneider Electric, threatening to leak it unless a ransom is paid. The group leaked 25MB of allegedly stolen data as proof, including sensitive documents. Schneider Electric's Sustainability Business division was breached on January 17, 2023.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 1.5TB of data, including sensitive information about customers' industrial control and automation systems and information about environmental and energy regulations compliance

example_incidents.summary: The ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware gang has claimed responsibility for a network breach at Trans-Northern Pipelines, which is currently under investigation. The U.S. State Department is offering rewards for information on the gang's leaders and affiliates, highlighting the group's significant impact on various sectors, including energy.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Trans-Northern Pipelines confirmed a breach of its internal network in November 2023, linked to claims of data theft by the ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware gang. The gang claims to have stolen 183GB of documents, which have been published on their data leak site, prompting TNPI to investigate the situation.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The incident was quickly contained and TNPI continues to safely operate its pipeline systems.
example_incidents.data_impact: 183GB of documents stolen, including company information and contact details of several TNPI employees.

example_incidents.summary: Veolia North America experienced a ransomware attack that affected its Municipal Water division and disrupted bill payment systems. The company implemented defensive measures and took some systems offline to contain the breach, but confirmed that water treatment operations were not impacted. They are currently assessing the extent of the attack's impact with third-party forensics experts.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Some systems were temporarily taken offline for restoration, but are now back online.
example_incidents.data_impact: Limited number of individuals' personal information may have been impacted.

example_incidents.summary: Slovenia's largest power provider, HSE, suffered a ransomware attack that compromised its systems and encrypted files. The attack did not disrupt electric power production, and the organization is currently engaged in system cleanup while remaining on high alert for potential ransom demands.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: IT systems and files were locked, but power generation operations remained unaffected.

example_incidents.summary: BHI Energy, a US energy services firm, was attacked by the Akira ransomware gang, which breached their network and stole sensitive data before deploying ransomware to encrypt files. The company managed to recover its systems without paying a ransom and has since enhanced its security measures.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The threat actor's foothold on BHI's network was removed on July 7, 2023. The company was able to recover data from a cloud backup solution that hadn't been affected by the ransomware attack, so they were able to restore their systems without paying a ransom.
example_incidents.data_impact: 767,000 files containing 690 GB of data, including employees' personal information such as full name, date of birth, Social Security Number (SSN), and health information.

example_incidents.summary: Siemens Energy confirmed a data breach resulting from the Clop ransomware data-theft attacks exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in the MOVEit Transfer platform. Although data was stolen, the company stated that no critical data was compromised and their operations remained unaffected.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: business operations were not impacted

example_incidents.summary: Hitachi Energy confirmed it suffered a data breach after the Clop ransomware gang stole data using a zero-day vulnerability in the GoAnywhere platform. The Clop gang has shifted its focus to extorting victims by threatening to publish stolen data rather than encrypting it.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Empresas Públicas de Medellín (EPM), a Colombian energy company, suffered a ransomware attack attributed to the BlackCat/ALPHV group. The attack disrupted the company's operations and affected its online services.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: disrupting the company's operations and taking down online services
sources: The Week in Ransomware - December 16th 2022 - Losing Trust

example_incidents.summary: Tata Power, India's largest integrated power company, was attacked by the Hive ransomware gang, which claimed to have stolen data from the company's networks. The attack exploited vulnerabilities in the Boa web server, which is still used in IoT devices, leading to a breach of Tata Power's IT infrastructure.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: The BlackCat/ALPHV ransomware gang claimed responsibility for an attack on Italy's energy agency GSE, resulting in the theft of approximately 700GB of confidential data. GSE's systems were taken down to prevent further access, and the website remains down as investigations continue into the compromised data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: GSE's website and systems were taken down to block the attackers; the website is still down almost a week after the incident.
example_incidents.data_impact: approximately 700GB of files stolen, including contracts, reports, project information, accounting documents, and other internal documentation.

example_incidents.summary: DESFA, Greece's largest natural gas distributor, confirmed a limited scope data breach and IT system outage following a ransomware attack attributed to LockBit. The incident led to disruptions in their operations.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: limited scope data breach and IT system outage
sources: The Week in Ransomware - August 26th 2022 - Fighting back

example_incidents.summary: South Staffordshire Water experienced IT disruption due to a cyberattack, but their water supply systems remained operational. The Clop ransomware gang initially misidentified Thames Water as their victim but later corrected this to South Staffordshire Water, claiming to have exfiltrated data and threatening to leak it after negotiations failed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: IT disruption reported, but water supply remains operational
example_incidents.data_impact: 5TB of data exfiltrated, including passports, driver's licenses, and SCADA system screenshots

example_incidents.summary: Creos Luxembourg S.A., a natural gas pipeline and electricity network operator, was targeted in a ransomware attack claimed by the ALPHV ransomware gang, also known as BlackCat. The attack resulted in partial encryption of the company's network.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

Fell back successfully to the public HTML activity page https://www.ransomware.live/activity/Energy, which returned 826 total Energy-sector victims and a list of notable organizations (Ecopetrol, Petrobras, Engie, Aramco, Eni, Creos, Conpet, etc.). Alternate hosts api-pro.ransomware.live returned 404. STEP 2 supplemental sources: ransomlook.io/api/search returned HTTP 400 Bad Request (failed). ransomwhat.telemetry.ltd/posts.json returned a 302 redirect to a landing page (ransomwatch.telemetry.ltd/) rather than the JSON feed (effectively unavailable via WebFetch). Both supplemental corroboration sources were therefore not usable; incident corroboration was instead done via WebSearch against mainstream press and vendor breach reporting, which was ample. STEP 3-5: All example-incident details, taxonomy grounding, and aggregate stats were sourced from named news outlets and authoritative annual reports; where a figure (ransom, downtime, financial loss, record count) was not publicly reported it is explicitly marked 'not publicly disclosed' rather than estimated. Ecopetrol is included as a recent large-state-oil victim drawn from the ransomware.live feed with details openly noted as not-yet-public. No rate-limit (429) errors were encountered on the endpoints that responded.

data_source_notes:
Primary source (ransomware.live API v2): The literal endpoint given in the task, /v2/victims/sector/..., 302-redirected to the HTML docs page rather than returning JSON; the correct working endpoint (confirmed via the site's own API docs and a third-party MCP server implementation) is GET /v2/sectorvictims/<sector>. Using https://api.ransomware.live/v2/sectorvictims/Financial%20Services successfully returned 100 victim records (apparently capped/paginated at 100, most recent first, spanning roughly 2026-04-16 to 2026-07-18) with fields victim, country, attackdate, group; per-record activity/press/ransom/data_size/url/claim_url detail was mostly null/not populated in the feed itself and was cross-checked via WebSearch instead for the notable incidents below. No rate-limit (429) errors were encountered on this endpoint.

Supplementary source 1 (ransomlook.io): FAILED. The task-specified query pattern /api/search?query=... returned HTTP 400; a corrected guess at the path (/api/search/bank) returned HTTP 404. The site's real API documentation lives behind /doc/ (Swagger) and its exact search route could not be resolved within the research pass, so this source could not be used to corroborate victims.

Supplementary source 2 (ransomwhat.telemetry.ltd/posts.json): FAILED/UNAVAILABLE. The URL 302-redirects to https://ransomwatch.telemetry.ltd/, whose landing page states the project "has been archived and is no longer actively maintained" with no live posts.json feed reachable through the redirect target.

Given both supplementary sources were unavailable, corroboration for individual notable incidents was instead done via targeted WebSearch against news/security-press coverage (Bloomberg, Reuters-adjacent trade press, The Record, TechCrunch, BleepingComputer, Cybernews, industry blogs, and the ransomware.live victim-detail pages themselves), as permitted by the task's fallback instructions. All financial/impact figures cited below are attributed to the specific article they came from; where no public figure exists this is stated explicitly rather than estimated.

Aggregate industry statistics (Sophos, IBM, Coveware, Verizon DBIR) were all retrieved successfully via WebSearch; no rate limiting encountered.
