example_incidents.summary: One of the most consequential OT-impacting ransomware attacks in manufacturing history; the global aluminum producer was forced into manual/paper-based operations across dozens of plants after LockerGoga encrypted IT systems that also touched production processes. Norsk Hydro refused to pay the ransom and publicly disclosed the incident in near-real time, becoming a widely cited case study in transparent incident response.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Total financial impact reached approximately $70-75 million, per Norsk Hydro's own quarterly financial disclosures; initial Q1 2019 losses were estimated at $35-41 million with additional Q2 losses of $23-29 million.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Ransom amount not publicly disclosed by attackers in a fixed figure; Norsk Hydro refused to pay the ransom entirely and rebuilt systems from backups instead.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Several aluminum extrusion plants were forced to switch to manual operations for an extended period; full IT recovery took multiple weeks, with the company reporting it was still not at 100% normal operations several weeks after the attack. Microsoft's incident response team was brought in to assist recovery.
example_incidents.data_impact: Primarily an availability/encryption event rather than a large-scale data-exfiltration/extortion case (LockerGoga predates widespread double-extortion); no large trove of stolen customer data was reported leaked.

example_incidents.summary: EKANS ransomware, one of the first ransomware strains purpose-built to target ICS/OT process-control software, hit Honda's internal network, forcing production and sales halts at multiple plants worldwide (Japan, US, UK, Turkey, Brazil, India, and elsewhere). Likely initial access was via an exposed RDP connection.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a specific dollar figure by Honda; industry analyses characterize the loss as significant given multi-day, multi-plant global production stoppage but no official cost figure was released.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed; no confirmed ransom payment reported.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Production and sales of cars, motorcycles, and power/marine products was suspended at plants across multiple countries for several days before systems were restored; exact recovery timeline varied by site.
example_incidents.data_impact: Primarily an OT/production-availability event; no large confirmed customer data leak was publicly reported in connection with this specific 2020 incident.

example_incidents.summary: Electronics-manufacturing giant Foxconn's Mexico facility was hit over the Thanksgiving 2020 weekend; attackers encrypted roughly 1,200 servers, exfiltrated data, and destroyed a large volume of backups before demanding a very large ransom.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as an official incident-cost figure by Foxconn; the destruction of 20-30 TB of backup data materially increased recovery cost and complexity beyond the ransom figure itself.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: DoppelPaymer demanded 1,804.0955 BTC, reported at the time as approximately $34 million (some sources cite ~$32.97 million); Foxconn did not pay, and stolen data was later published on the dark web.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Foxconn confirmed the ransomware disrupted production operations at the affected Mexico facility; precise recovery timeline in days not independently confirmed in public reporting beyond confirmation that normal operations were eventually restored.
example_incidents.data_impact: Approximately 100 GB of unencrypted files were stolen prior to encryption (double-extortion); 20-30 TB of backup data was deliberately deleted by the attackers to hamper recovery.

example_incidents.summary: The Snatch ransomware/extortion group claimed to have breached a Volvo Cars file repository and stole a portion of the automaker's proprietary R&D data, leaking sample files as proof. Volvo disputed being a 'victim of ransomware' per se, framing it as unauthorized third-party access to one file server, but confirmed R&D data theft.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; Volvo did not report a specific financial cost figure for the incident.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed; no confirmed ransom demand amount or payment reported. Volvo stated it maintained control of its data and did not indicate paying any ransom.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No significant production/operational downtime was publicly reported; this was primarily a data-theft/extortion event rather than an OT-disruptive encryption event.
example_incidents.data_impact: Snatch leaked approximately 35.6 MB of sample stolen R&D files as proof of the larger theft; Volvo stated it saw no indication of impact to customer safety, vehicle security, or personal customer data.

example_incidents.country: United States (Latin America/North America plants affected)
example_incidents.summary: The tire and rubber manufacturer detected a security incident in late February 2022; LockBit 2.0 claimed responsibility on March 11, 2022, and threatened to publicly release stolen business and customer data unless a ransom was paid. Bridgestone proactively disconnected manufacturing and retreading facilities across North and Latin America to contain the incident.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as an official total-cost figure; Bridgestone engaged Accenture Security for incident response, adding external forensic/recovery costs on top of ~10 days of idled production across ~30 plants.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Specific ransom demand amount not publicly disclosed; Bridgestone did not confirm payment, and LockBit proceeded to leak stolen data after the deadline passed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Approximately 30 plants across North America and Latin America were shut down for about 10 days; all plants had resumed normal operations by March 9, 2022.
example_incidents.data_impact: Business records were accessed and stolen, including files containing Social Security numbers, bank information, and other sensitive data belonging to some customers.

example_incidents.summary: The German automotive-parts giant was breached via an employee's browser download; LockBit gained access to internal systems and, after negotiations broke down, publicly offered the stolen dataset for sale on its leak site for a headline figure of $50 million (later reduced to $40 million).
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as an official incident-cost figure by Continental beyond confirming systems access occurred; no confirmed operational-loss figure released.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: LockBit publicly listed the stolen data for sale at $50 million on November 9, 2022, reduced to $40 million by November 29, 2022; negotiation transcripts published by LockBit show discussions beginning September 23, 2022, but Continental has stated it aborted contact with the group rather than paying.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No major manufacturing/plant downtime was publicly reported; this was chiefly a data-exfiltration/extortion event rather than an OT-encryption event.
example_incidents.data_impact: Attackers claimed to have stolen roughly 40 terabytes of internal files (some early reports mis-stated this as 40 GB), including technical documents and source code, based on screenshots published on the leak site.

example_incidents.summary: A single server managed by Yamaha's Philippines motorcycle-manufacturing/sales subsidiary was breached and hit with ransomware; INC Ransom added the company to its leak site roughly three weeks later and published stolen employee and corporate data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Yamaha stood up a countermeasures team and launched an investigation; no specific downtime duration was publicly disclosed, and the impact was described as limited to one server.
example_incidents.data_impact: Approximately 37 GB of allegedly stolen data was published, including employee ID information, backup files, and corporate/sales information; partial leakage of employees' personal information was confirmed by Yamaha.

example_incidents.summary: Nissan detected an intrusion into its Australian division's network in December 2023; the Akira ransomware gang claimed responsibility and, after negotiations reportedly failed, threatened to leak stolen business and personal data. Nissan confirmed in 2024 that the breach affected roughly 100,000 individuals across Australia and New Zealand, including customers, dealers, and current/former employees.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as an official cost figure by Nissan.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Specific dollar ransom demand not publicly disclosed; negotiations with Nissan reportedly failed and the company did not pay, after which Akira threatened to leak the data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No major production-line/OT downtime was publicly reported; primarily a data-breach/extortion event rather than an operational-disruption event.
example_incidents.data_impact: Approximately 100 GB of documents stolen, affecting an estimated 100,000 individuals; exposed data included around 4,000 Medicare card numbers, 7,500 driver's license numbers, 220 passport numbers, and 1,300 tax file numbers, alongside employee personal information, NDAs, and partner/client details.

example_incidents.summary: MKS Instruments, Inc. experienced a ransomware incident identified on February 3, 2023, which disrupted their operations. The company reported that they have restored global operations and are on track to recover revenue by the end of the second quarter of 2023.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Global operations restored following ransomware incident

example_incidents.summary: On February 11, 2023, Gates Industrial Corporation plc reported being the target of a ransomware attack. The company activated its incident response plans and engaged cybersecurity experts to assess and remediate the situation, which temporarily disrupted production and shipping operations.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The attack resulted in the temporary inability of most facilities to produce and ship products. Production and shipping have been restored at some facilities, with full restoration expected in the coming days.
example_incidents.data_impact: It is possible that personally identifiable information (PII) was accessed, but the extent is not yet determined.

example_incidents.summary: Tecogen Inc. experienced a ransomware attack on April 28, 2023, which was identified as a spear phishing attack targeting the company's VPN. The company took immediate action to limit access, investigate the threat, and restore affected files, successfully returning to full operational status by May 1, 2023.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The Company's network was fully operational on May 1, 2023, after restoring files from the previous evening's back-up.

example_incidents.summary: Hillman Solutions Corp. experienced a ransomware attack in May 2023, which resulted in direct and indirect costs associated with the incident. The company is also expecting insurance receivables related to this cybersecurity incident.

example_incidents.summary: PGT Innovations, Inc. reported that their fourth quarter financial results were impacted by a ransomware incident, which affected their ability to expand gross margin. The incident, along with Hurricane Ian, resulted in a revenue impact of approximately $15 million.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: HanesBrands Inc. announced that it experienced a ransomware attack on May 31, 2022. The incident raised concerns regarding the adequacy and security of their information technology systems.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The incident has temporarily impacted operations, including shipping, receiving, and manufacturing production. The timeline for full restoration is not yet known.

example_incidents.summary: Mueller Water Products, Inc. experienced a cybersecurity incident involving unauthorized access and deployment of ransomware, which disrupted access to business applications and limited the ability to take orders and ship products. example_incidents.summary: Johnson Controls International plc experienced a ransomware incident that disrupted portions of its internal IT infrastructure and applications. example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The company has largely restored the impacted applications and systems and continues to execute business continuity and restoration plans for the remaining impacted applications and systems.

example_incidents.summary: Hillman Group experienced a ransomware attack in May 2023, which has had direct and indirect costs associated with the incident. The company has mentioned the receipt of expected insurance receivables related to this cybersecurity incident.

example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Emergency measures, including shutting down the affected server and network, were taken to prevent the spread of the damage.

example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.data_impact: Employee contact information and some encrypted and hashed passwords; no customer or supplier data identified as obtained.

example_incidents.summary: Keytronic, an electronic manufacturing services provider, reported losses exceeding $17 million due to a ransomware attack detected on May 6, 2023. The attack, attributed to the Black Basta ransomware gang, resulted in the theft of personal information and significant operational disruptions at its facilities in the U.S. and Mexico.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: shut down domestic and Mexico operations for two weeks

example_incidents.summary: Ransomware gangs are exploiting a VMware ESXi authentication bypass vulnerability (CVE-2024-37085) to escalate privileges and deploy ransomware, including Black Basta. The vulnerability allows attackers to gain full administrative access to ESXi hypervisors, enabling them to steal sensitive data and encrypt the hypervisor's file system. The Storm-0506 group has been identified as deploying Black Basta ransomware in attacks on a North American engineering firm after exploiting this vulnerability.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Northern Minerals, an Australian mining company, disclosed a cybersecurity breach where data was stolen and published on the dark web. The BianLian ransomware group claimed responsibility for the attack, which involved the exfiltration of corporate, operational, and financial information, as well as personal data of employees and shareholders.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: OmniVision, a California-based imaging sensors manufacturer, suffered a ransomware attack by the Cactus group in 2023, resulting in the encryption of certain systems and a data breach. The attackers stole personal information and leaked various sensitive documents, but ultimately released all data they held for free.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Nexperia confirmed a data breach after the Dark Angels ransomware gang leaked samples of allegedly stolen data. The hackers claimed to have stolen 1 TB of confidential information and threatened to leak more if a ransom was not paid. The company has taken steps to contain the incident and is investigating the breach with third-party experts.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Nexperia shut down IT systems and launched an investigation to determine the scope of impact.
example_incidents.data_impact: 1 TB of confidential data, including 371 GB of design and product data, 246 GB of engineering data, 96 GB of commercial and marketing data, 41.5 GB of corporate data, 109 GB of client and user data, and 121.1 GB of various files.

example_incidents.summary: Hoya Corporation was targeted by the Hunters International ransomware group, which demanded a $10 million ransom to prevent the release of stolen files. The cyberattack affected production and order processing, leading to IT outages across several divisions, while the company investigates the potential exfiltration of sensitive information.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Production and order processing impacted; IT outages experienced in several business divisions.
example_incidents.data_impact: 1.7 million stolen files, amounting to 2 TB of data.

example_incidents.summary: Nissan Oceania confirmed a ransomware attack by the Akira group that exposed data of approximately 100,000 individuals. The stolen data includes personal information of current and former employees, as well as customers, with a significant portion of government identification compromised. Akira has leaked the stolen data on the dark web, prompting Nissan to offer support services to affected individuals.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 100,000 individuals affected; includes personal employee information, NDAs, project data, and information on partners and clients; compromised government IDs include approximately 4,000 Medicare cards, 7,500 driver's licenses, 220 passports, and 1,300 tax file numbers

example_incidents.summary: Duvel Moortgat Brewery experienced a ransomware attack that halted beer production in its bottling facilities. The Stormous ransomware group claimed responsibility, stating they hold 88 GB of stolen data and threatened to leak it if a ransom isn't paid by March 25, 2024. Despite the attack, the brewery has enough stock to maintain distribution.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Production was immediately stopped; it is not yet known when it could restart, but they hope to restart today or tomorrow.
example_incidents.data_impact: 88 GB of data stolen; specific records or people affected not disclosed.

example_incidents.summary: Hyundai Motor Europe suffered a ransomware attack by the Black Basta group, which claimed to have stolen three terabytes of corporate data. The company initially reported IT issues but later confirmed the cyberattack and is investigating the unauthorized access to its network.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 3 terabytes of corporate data, including legal, sales, human resources, accounting, IT, and management data

example_incidents.summary: Johnson Controls International confirmed that a ransomware attack in September 2023 cost the company $27 million and resulted in a data breach. The Dark Angels ransomware gang was responsible for the attack, which involved unauthorized access, data exfiltration, and deployment of ransomware, leading to significant service disruptions.

example_incidents.data_impact: over 27 TB of confidential data stolen

example_incidents.summary: Nissan Australia is investigating a cyberattack that targeted its systems, potentially allowing hackers to access personal information. The attack has been claimed by the Akira ransomware gang.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Austal USA, a shipbuilding contractor for the U.S. Department of Defense, confirmed a cyberattack by the Hunters International group, which leaked some information as proof of the breach. The company is investigating the incident and has stated that no personal or classified information was accessed or taken by the threat actor.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: no impact on operations

example_incidents.summary: The Qilin ransomware gang has developed a sophisticated Linux encryptor targeting VMware ESXi servers, allowing extensive customization for file encryption. example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: ranging from $25,000 to millions of dollars
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: The Qilin ransomware group claimed responsibility for a cyber attack on Yanfeng Automotive Interiors, a major automotive parts supplier. example_incidents.summary: Boeing was targeted by the LockBit ransomware gang, which exploited the Citrix Bleed vulnerability to gain access to its network. After refusing to pay the ransom, 43GB of data was leaked on the dark web. The incident highlights the ongoing threat posed by the exploitation of this vulnerability.

example_incidents.data_impact: 39,111 individuals affected; personal information including full names and Social Security Numbers (SSNs)

example_incidents.summary: Seiko confirmed it suffered a ransomware attack by the Black Cat gang, leading to a data breach that exposed sensitive customer, partner, and personnel information. example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

The breaches involved multiple ransomware attacks that resulted in data encryption and significant operational disruption as the victim organization attempted to restore systems while facing simultaneous attacks.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: ABB confirmed a ransomware attack that impacted some of its systems and involved data theft. The Black Basta ransomware gang was identified as the attacker, and while the breach has been contained, ABB is working with law enforcement and advisors to mitigate the impact.

example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Nichirin-Flex U.S.A, a subsidiary of the Japanese automotive hose maker Nichirin, was hit by a ransomware attack on June 14, 2022, causing significant disruptions in product distribution and order fulfillment. The company is investigating the unauthorized access and has temporarily taken down its website while prioritizing system recovery.

exposure_categories.description: Physical production infrastructure that, unlike pure IT, ties ransomware impact directly to safety and physical output — the defining exposure that differentiates manufacturing from most other insured industries.
subcategories: Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and Distributed Control Systems (DCS)
SCADA/HMI supervisory systems
Industrial IoT (IIoT) sensors and connected machinery
Robotics and automated assembly-line controllers
Building/plant management systems (HVAC, energy, safety interlocks) converged with IT networks
Legacy/unpatched OT systems with long refresh cycles (10-20+ year equipment lifespans)

exposure_categories.description: Software layers that plan, schedule, and track physical production — encryption or corruption here halts output even if OT hardware itself is untouched.
subcategories: Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES)
ERP systems tied to production scheduling and inventory (SAP, Oracle, etc.)
Quality-control and batch/lot-tracking systems
Warehouse management and inventory-control systems
Historian/data-collection servers bridging IT and OT

exposure_categories.description: Proprietary design, engineering, and process data that is high-value theft/extortion leverage distinct to manufacturers, especially in automotive, aerospace, electronics, and industrial-equipment segments.
subcategories: CAD/CAM design files and product blueprints
Source code for embedded/firmware systems in products
R&D data and pre-release product specifications
Proprietary manufacturing process/recipe data
Patents and trade-secret documentation

exposure_categories.description: Manufacturing's deep tiered-supplier interdependency means exposure extends well beyond the insured entity's own network perimeter.
subcategories: Tier 1/2/3 supplier and subcontractor network connections (EDI, VPN, shared portals)
Just-in-time (JIT) logistics and shipping/freight coordination systems
Contract manufacturers and OEM/ODM partners
Third-party MSPs/OT integrators with remote access credentials
Raw material and component sourcing platforms

exposure_categories.description: Conventional back-office systems that remain a primary initial-access and extortion target even in OT-heavy environments.
subcategories: Employee PII/HR records (payroll, SSNs, government ID data — as seen in Bridgestone, Nissan incidents)
Financial and banking data
Customer and dealer/distributor records
Email and collaboration systems
Backup and disaster-recovery infrastructure (frequently targeted for deletion, as in the Foxconn Mexico case)

exposure_categories.description: Geographically distributed physical facilities whose network segmentation (or lack thereof) determines how far a single compromise can spread.
subcategories: Multiple manufacturing plants/sites on shared corporate networks
Regional/subsidiary networks with varying security maturity (e.g., overseas subsidiaries)
Industrial network segmentation boundaries (IT/OT air gaps or lack thereof)
Remote/unmanned facility connections

hazard_categories.description: How ransomware actors first breach manufacturing environments; in this sector, exposed remote-access infrastructure and unpatched perimeter/OT-adjacent systems dominate over other industries' typical phishing-first patterns, though phishing remains prevalent too.
subcategories: Exposed/unsecured RDP and remote-access services (documented initial vector in the Honda/EKANS 2020 case)
Exploited public-facing vulnerabilities (leading root cause per Sophos 2025, 32% of manufacturing incidents; e.g., Citrix NetScaler CVE exploited by INC Ransom)
Phishing/spearphishing and malicious email attachments (Norsk Hydro's LockerGoga entry point)
Compromised/stolen credentials, including via infostealer malware
Malicious browser downloads by employees (Continental AG 2022 vector)
Third-party/vendor/MSP remote-access compromise

hazard_categories.description: The mechanisms attackers use to monetize a manufacturing compromise, increasingly shifting from pure encryption toward data theft as manufacturers improve encryption-prevention (per Sophos 2025: encryption success dropped from 74% to 40% YoY).
subcategories: Encryption of production/IT systems (traditional single-extortion, e.g. Norsk Hydro, Honda)
Data exfiltration and double-extortion (leak-site publication threats, e.g. Continental, Nissan, Yamaha)
Backup destruction to eliminate recovery options and increase payment pressure (Foxconn Mexico: 20-30TB of backups deleted)
Deadline-driven public leak-site pressure campaigns
Triple extortion (secondary harassment of customers/partners named in stolen data, or DDoS layered on top)
Direct sale of stolen IP/data to third parties independent of ransom negotiation (Continental data offered for sale at $50M/$40M)

hazard_categories.description: Manufacturing's unique bifurcated risk profile — attacks can remain IT-contained (data theft) or cross into OT (halting physical production), with dramatically different loss profiles.
subcategories: Pure-IT compromises with data-theft-only impact and limited production disruption
IT-to-OT lateral movement causing plant/production shutdowns
Purpose-built OT/ICS-targeting malware (e.g., Snake/EKANS designed to kill SCADA-associated processes)
Precautionary self-imposed shutdowns to contain spread (Bridgestone's proactive disconnection of ~30 plants)
Safety-system and physical-safety risk where OT compromise intersects with worker/product safety

hazard_categories.category: Supply Chain and Business Interruption Risk
hazard_categories.description: Because manufacturers sit inside just-in-time, tightly coupled supply chains, a single-site ransomware event can cascade into contingent business interruption for downstream customers and upstream suppliers well beyond the insured's own balance sheet.
subcategories: Contingent business interruption to downstream OEM customers relying on JIT delivery
Upstream supplier/sub-contractor compromise propagating into the manufacturer's network
Multi-plant/multi-region shutdowns from a single network-wide compromise (Bridgestone: ~30 plants, 10 days)
Extended full-recovery timelines (100+ days per Sophos 2024 data) prolonging revenue loss beyond initial outage

hazard_categories.description: Reliance on external integrators, MSPs, and cloud/SaaS platforms for both IT and OT management creates an attack surface outside the manufacturer's direct control.
subcategories: Compromise via managed service providers or OT system integrators with standing remote access
Shared/interconnected supplier portals and EDI systems as lateral-movement paths
Cloud ERP/MES vendor compromise cascading to multiple manufacturing clients
Sub-tier supplier ransomware indirectly halting the insured's production (contingent BI exposure)

hazard_categories.description: Human error and workforce-related exposure that manufacturers must underwrite alongside pure technical vulnerability.
subcategories: Employee-initiated compromise (malicious downloads, credential reuse, phishing susceptibility)
Insufficient in-house security expertise to detect/respond in time (cited by 42.5% of manufacturing ransomware victims per Sophos 2025)
Disgruntled or negligent insiders with OT/production-system access
Contractor and temporary-worker access-control gaps on factory floors

hazard_categories.description: Post-incident compliance and liability obligations that shape the insurable loss beyond the ransom/recovery cost itself, particularly where employee, customer, or government-ID data is exposed.
subcategories: Multi-jurisdictional breach-notification requirements for exposed employee/customer PII (e.g., Nissan's ~100,000-person notification across Australia/New Zealand)

Government-ID and financial-data exposure triggering elevated regulatory scrutiny (Medicare numbers, driver's licenses, passports, tax file numbers, SSNs, banking data seen across the example incidents)
Export-control and trade-secret protection obligations for defense/aerospace-adjacent manufacturers
Securities-disclosure obligations for publicly traded manufacturers (material incident/8-K-style disclosures)
Cross-border data-transfer and subsidiary-notification complexity for multinational manufacturers

overview: Manufacturing has been the single most-targeted sector by ransomware operators for five consecutive years through 2025, driven by a combination of high operational-downtime sensitivity (which pressures victims toward paying quickly), widespread reliance on legacy OT/ICS equipment with long refresh cycles, deep tiered supply-chain interdependency that multiplies contingent business-interruption exposure, and valuable intellectual property/trade-secret data. The ransomware.live "Manufacturing" sector tag alone contains 4,434 recorded victim postings, with year-over-year posting volume roughly quadrupling from 2021 (295) to 2025 (1,204), and the sector accounting for an estimated one in four ransomware attacks globally by 2025 per industry trackers. Attack economics are shifting: per Sophos's 2025 manufacturing-specific report, successful encryption rates have fallen sharply (74% to 40% YoY) as defenses improve, but attackers are compensating by shifting toward pure data theft and extortion, and average ransom demands against manufacturers have risen even as median demands/payments across all sectors trend down. High-profile incidents — from Norsk Hydro's ~$70M LockerGoga attack (2019) through Honda's global OT-targeted Snake/EKANS shutdown (2020), Foxconn Mexico's $34M DoppelPaymer demand (2020), Bridgestone's 30-plant, 10-day shutdown (2022), Continental's 40TB data-theft/$50M extortion (2022), and Nissan Australia's 100,000-person PII breach (2023) — illustrate the sector's dual exposure to both OT-driven physical-production disruption and conventional IT-driven data-theft/extortion, often within the same threat-actor toolkit.

industry: Professional, Scientific, Technical Services, Real Estate and Wholesale Trade
overview: This composite industry group spans consultancies, IT/managed services, law and accounting firms, engineering firms, staffing and BPO providers, travel management companies, commercial real estate services, and wholesale/logistics distributors. Ransomware.live's 'Business Services' sector tag is one of the most heavily populated on the platform, logging dozens of new claimed victims per week in mid-2026, with RaaS/extortion groups Qilin, DragonForce, INC Ransom, TheGentlemen, Akira, RansomHouse, Deadlock, and data-extortion crews like ShinyHunters posting new victims almost daily. The sector's risk profile is distinctive because these firms sit at a structural chokepoint: (1) they hold sensitive, often privileged or regulated client/third-party data (legal, financial, M&A, PII) that amplifies extortion leverage; (2) many are themselves suppliers/vendors (MSPs, SAP integrators, BPOs, staffing firms, travel managers) whose compromise cascades into downstream client organizations, making them attractive 'one-to-many' targets; and (3) wholesale trade/logistics operations depend on time-sensitive order, warehouse, and freight systems where even short outages create cascading supply-chain and revenue impact. Reported financial impact ranges enormously by incident type - from multi-hundred-million-dollar remediation and litigation costs at large diversified BPOs (Conduent) and IT consultancies (Cognizant, Sopra Steria) down to smaller professional firms where impact is mostly data-exposure/breach-notification driven rather than large ransom payments. Across the sector, exfiltration-only and SaaS/CRM (e.g., Salesforce) compromise via vishing/social engineering has become as common a threat vector as classic file-encryption ransomware.

WebSearch/news coverage for named incident verification (Bleeping Computer, SecurityWeek, Dark Reading, Cybersecurity Dive, Infosecurity Magazine, The Register, TechCrunch, CPO Magazine, Security Boulevard, Cyber Daily, etc.)
IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025
data_source_notes: STEP 1 (ransomware.live v2 API): The literal endpoint given in the task (/v2/victims/sector/Business%20Services) 302-redirected to the API docs page rather than returning JSON, indicating the actual current route is /v2/sectorvictims/<sector>. Using that corrected endpoint via WebFetch succeeded (no rate-limit/429 encountered), but WebFetch summarizes/truncates large JSON through a small model rather than returning raw records, so the tool only surfaced the most recent ~3 weeks of victims (2026-06-30 to 2026-07-19, 100+ records) plus a curated 'notable organizations' pull; it could not confirm total historical record count or full date range of the underlying dataset. No older (2020-2024) incidents were retrievable through this API for this sector, so all pre-2026 example incidents below were sourced via WebSearch/news archives rather than the API. STEP 2 supplemental sources both failed: ransomlook.io's search endpoint returned HTTP 400 Bad Request for the exact query string provided; ransomwhat.telemetry.ltd/posts.json 302-redirected to a different domain (ransomwatch.telemetry.ltd), which serves an HTML dashboard rather than the raw posts.json feed requested, so no corroborating group/victim posts were obtained from either supplemental source. No 429/rate-limit errors were encountered on any endpoint.

example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Attack occurred the evening of Oct 20, 2020; company reported 'differing levels of unavailability' of systems persisting for weeks afterward, driving the bulk of the cost.

example_incidents.group: ShinyHunters (vishing/Salesforce data theft) and Qilin (separate, coincidentally-timed claim)
example_incidents.summary: One of the world's largest commercial real estate services firms confirmed a 'limited' breach originating from a vishing (voice phishing) social-engineering attack that gave ShinyHunters access to its Salesforce CRM environment; Qilin separately listed the company on its ransomware leak site around the same time.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as of this research; company has not released cost estimates. A shareholder/customer lawsuit has been filed over the breach.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: ShinyHunters demanded an undisclosed ransom with a deadline of May 6, 2026, threatening to leak data; when negotiations reportedly stalled, the group published a 50GB dataset. No confirmation Cushman & Wakefield paid.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Company described the incident as 'limited' in scope; no significant operational downtime was publicly reported, consistent with a SaaS/CRM data-theft (non-encryption) incident rather than an operational-technology outage.
example_incidents.data_impact: Over 500,000 Salesforce records containing PII and internal corporate/client data claimed stolen; illustrates third-party/SaaS supply-chain exposure distinct from traditional on-prem ransomware.

example_incidents.summary: DragonForce ransomware utilized a custom malware named 'Backdoor.Turn' to exploit Microsoft Teams relays for command-and-control communications. The attack, which occurred in December 2025, involved the exfiltration of data and encryption of the victim's systems after establishing a foothold through an SQL server vulnerability.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.victim: multi-billion-dollar American defense contractor and IT services provider
example_incidents.summary: The Kyber ransomware gang has targeted Windows systems and VMware ESXi endpoints, deploying two distinct variants in March 2026. The attack involved encrypting files and defacing management interfaces, with claims of using post-quantum encryption that were found to be misleading. A multi-billion-dollar American defense contractor was identified as a victim on the Kyber data extortion portal.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: The State Bar of Texas reported a data breach after the INC ransomware gang claimed to have attacked the organization and leaked samples of stolen data. The breach occurred between January 28 and February 9, 2025, and was discovered on February 12, 2025, with the gang adding the organization to its dark web extortion page on March 9, 2025.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: CannonDesign experienced a data breach due to an Avos Locker ransomware attack, which resulted in the theft of sensitive data from over 13,000 employees. The breach was discovered on January 25, 2023, and involved unauthorized access and data exfiltration, with the stolen data later published online by various groups.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 13,000 current and former employees; names, addresses, social security numbers, driver s license numbers

example_incidents.summary: Fidelity National Financial confirmed a cyberattack on November 19, 2023, claimed by the BlackCat ransomware gang, which exposed the data of 1.3 million customers. The attackers accessed the network using stolen credentials and deployed non-propagating malware to exfiltrate data. The breach was contained within a week, and the company is providing support services to affected customers.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The breach was contained seven days later, with certain IT systems taken offline during containment measures.
example_incidents.data_impact: Data of 1.3 million customers was stolen.

example_incidents.summary: Spain's National Police has issued a warning about a sophisticated ransomware campaign targeting architecture companies through phishing emails. The attackers, using the 'LockBit Locker' ransomware, employ social engineering tactics to build trust with victims before executing the ransomware to encrypt their files.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: The Clop ransomware gang has begun leaking data stolen during the MOVEit Transfer attacks on clearweb sites, following a tactic previously used by the ALPHV gang. They created websites for various companies, including PWC, to pressure victims into paying ransom by making stolen data publicly accessible.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: HWL Ebsworth, a major Australian law firm, was targeted by the ALPHV ransomware gang, which leaked data they claim was stolen from the firm. The firm has refused to meet the extortion demands, emphasizing their commitment to ethical standards and the privacy of their clients.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 1.45 terabytes of data containing over a million documents

example_incidents.summary: Capita, a business process outsourcing firm, warned customers to assume their data was stolen following a cyberattack in early April. The Black Basta ransomware gang claimed to have stolen sensitive data, including personal bank account details and passport scans, affecting over 500,000 members of the Universities Superannuation Scheme.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Capita experienced a weekend-long outage due to the cyberattack, with the breach discovered on March 31.
example_incidents.data_impact: approximately 470,000 members' personal information including names, dates of birth, National Insurance numbers, and USS member numbers

example_incidents.summary: NCR suffered an outage on its Aloha point of sale platform after being hit by a ransomware attack claimed by the BlackCat/ALPHV gang. This incident highlights the ongoing threat of ransomware targeting critical business operations.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
sources: The Week in Ransomware - April 21st 2023 - Macs in the Crosshairs

example_incidents.summary: The Trigona ransomware operation has been active since late October 2022, utilizing a new Tor negotiation site for ransom payments in Monero. Victims, including a real estate company, have been targeted with file encryption and ransom notes, although the exact ransom amounts and data theft claims remain unverified.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

hazard_categories.description: How ransomware/extortion actors first get in, tailored to how this sector's workforce and infrastructure typically operate.
subcategories: Voice phishing (vishing) targeting IT helpdesk/employees to obtain SaaS/CRM credentials (Cushman & Wakefield/ShinyHunters pattern)
Business email compromise / spear-phishing against client-facing consulting, legal, and accounting staff
Exploited VPN/RDP and edge-device vulnerabilities into MSP and IT-services provider networks
Infostealer malware harvesting employee and third-party credentials (RedLine, Lumma, generic stealers observed heavily across ransomware.live Business Services listings)
Compromise of exposed EDI, order-processing, and warehouse-management portals in wholesale/distribution firms
Compromised MSP/RMM tooling providing one-to-many access into multiple downstream client environments

hazard_categories.description: How attackers monetize access once obtained, and how these tactics manifest specifically in professional/technical services, real estate, and wholesale trade.
subcategories: Double extortion: encryption plus exfiltration threat of client/case data (law, accounting, consulting firms)
Pure data-exfiltration extortion without encryption, increasingly common via SaaS/CRM compromise (no file-encryption downtime, but reputational/regulatory leverage)
Leak-site 'countdown' publication of stolen client and employee data to pressure payment
Multi-group/competing extortion claims on the same victim (seen with Cushman & Wakefield, claimed by both ShinyHunters and Qilin) complicating incident response and negotiation
Harassment of downstream clients/customers whose data was exposed, used as secondary leverage against the professional-services victim
DDoS as an auxiliary pressure tactic during negotiation stand-offs

hazard_categories.description: This sector is disproportionately exposed because many of its firms are themselves vendors, integrators, or outsourced back-office providers to other companies.
subcategories: MSP/IT-services compromise cascading into many downstream client organizations (Cognizant, Accenture, Sopra Steria pattern)
SAP/ERP consultancy and implementation-partner compromise exposing multiple enterprise clients' back-office systems (e.g., Megawork/SAP consultancy incident)

BPO/back-office outsourcing compromise exposing data the vendor processes on behalf of many end clients across other regulated industries (Conduent processing healthcare claims and payments for numerous government/commercial clients)
SaaS/CRM platform (e.g., Salesforce) compromise via a single vendor or employee credential exposing aggregated client contact/PII data across an entire real estate or professional-services portfolio
Franchise, staffing-agency, and subcontractor network risk in wholesale distribution and real estate where security posture varies widely by location

hazard_categories.description: Professional/technical services firms hold sensitive third-party information whose exposure carries outsized legal and reputational consequences.
subcategories: Attorney-client privileged case files and litigation strategy documents (law firms)
M&A due-diligence, financial audit, and pre-earnings material non-public information (accounting/consulting firms)
Engineering drawings, architectural plans, and technical IP (engineering/technical consultancies)
Aggregated multi-client PII/PHI held by BPOs and claims processors, creating breach exposure that multiplies across every underlying client

hazard_categories.description: Hazards specific to wholesale trade and logistics operations where system downtime directly halts physical goods movement.
subcategories: Warehouse management system (WMS) and inventory database encryption halting order fulfillment
Freight/transportation management system (TMS) and dispatch/scheduling outages delaying deliveries

Customer-facing portal outages (e.g., MyToll-style portals) degrading service visibility even when core freight movement continues

subcategories: Multi-state breach notification obligations when a single incident exposes data spanning many client industries and jurisdictions (Conduent: multi-state AG enforcement, ~10+ class actions)
Contractual indemnification and liability clauses with enterprise clients whose data was exposed via the vendor
