data_source_notes: Step 1 succeeded but required correcting the endpoint path: the literal URL given in the task (/v2/victims/sector/Consumer%20Services) 302-redirected to API docs rather than returning data. The correct current endpoint, per https://www.ransomware.live/apidocs, is /v2/sectorvictims/<sector> (e.g. https://api.ransomware.live/v2/sectorvictims/Consumer%20Services), which returned a clean JSON array of ~120 victim records with all requested fields (activity, attackdate, country, description, group, press, ransom, victim, data_size, url, claim_url). No rate-limiting (429) was encountered on this call. Nearly all records had ransom=null and data_size=null (leak-site postings essentially never disclose ransom amounts publicly), and only 3 of ~120 records had a populated "press" field with a corroborating news link (Karl Chevrolet/RansomHouse, pchome.com.tw/Settra, Au Vieux Campeur/TheGentlemen) - these were used directly. The API snapshot only covered a roughly 2-month recent window (~May 20-Jul 19, 2026); it does not appear to expose full historical depth via this endpoint, so it was supplemented heavily with WebSearch for older/larger notable incidents (2023-2025) that are known to be classified under this sector (M&S, Co-op, MGM, Caesars, CDK Global, ShinyHunters/Salesforce campaign victims). Step 2 supplements both failed gracefully as anticipated: ransomlook.io's /api/search endpoint returned HTTP 400 for both a URL-encoded sector-name query and a plain "retail" query (endpoint/parameter format likely differs from what was specified), and ransomwhat.telemetry.ltd redirected to ransomwatch.telemetry.ltd, which is explicitly marked as an archived, unmaintained project with no live/queryable post data - so no corroborating group/victim posts were obtained from either secondary source. IBM's Cost of a Data Breach report page returned HTTP 403 on WebFetch (likely bot/WAF blocking), so no IBM-specific retail breach-cost figure could be verified this session; it was omitted rather than quoted from memory. The WebSearch tool budget for this session (200 calls) was exhausted partway through Step 5, after the Sophos and Coveware figures were already secured; remaining supplementary searches (e.g., Verizon DBIR retail-specific ransomware figures, a second Ahold Delhaize/Sobeys grocery-ransomware example, Chainalysis retail-specific figures) were not performed, and no numbers for those were fabricated from training memory.

example_incidents.group: DragonForce (attack attributed to the "Scattered Spider" affiliate cluster)
example_incidents.summary: One of the most disruptive retail ransomware incidents on record. Attackers used social-engineering (help-desk/Active Directory compromise) to encrypt core systems; DragonForce contacted M&S's CEO directly via a hacked employee email account. M&S was forced to shut down automated ordering, stock and click-and-collect systems for weeks, reverting to pen-and-paper processes for fresh food and clothing supply.
example_incidents.financial_impact: M&S disclosed total incident costs of £101.6 million (£82.7m incident response/recovery, £18.9m third-party costs); the company guided to roughly £300 million of lost operating profit for FY2025/26; statutory pre-tax profit fell from £391.9m to £3.4m over the affected half-year; the attack wiped an estimated £750 million off M&S's market capitalization at its worst point.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly confirmed whether M&S paid; DragonForce publicly claimed the encryption/extortion but no verified payment amount has been disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Online ordering and click-and-collect were suspended for roughly 6-7 weeks; full operational recovery of automated stock/ordering systems took months.
example_incidents.data_impact: Customer personal data (names, contact details, order history, dates of birth) was confirmed stolen; M&S stated payment card details were not compromised.

example_incidents.date: April 2025 (disclosed publicly in stages through mid-2025)
example_incidents.summary: Part of the same UK retail campaign that hit M&S and Harrods. DragonForce exfiltrated data via third-party/network access, then escalated to a direct extortion threat via Microsoft Teams and a phone call to Co-op's head of security. Co-op proactively disconnected systems to head off a ransomware deployment, which limited operational disruption relative to M&S but did not stop the data theft.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Co-op reported £206 million in lost revenue attributable to the incident in its official earnings disclosure.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: DragonForce demanded payment for the stolen member data; Co-op has not disclosed paying a ransom, and the UK National Crime Agency arrested four suspects (aged 17-20) in July 2025 on Computer Misuse Act, blackmail, and money-laundering charges.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Systems were proactively taken offline to contain the threat; the company described a multi-week restoration process for affected back-office and membership systems.
example_incidents.data_impact: Personal data of all 6.5 million Co-op members was confirmed stolen (names, dates of birth, emails, phone numbers, home addresses); no financial/payment card data was taken.

example_incidents.victim: CDK Global (SaaS/DMS provider to ~15,000 US/Canada auto dealerships - third-party supply-chain incident affecting the retail auto sector broadly)
example_incidents.summary: BlackSuit ransomware hit CDK Global, the dominant dealer management system (DMS) provider for North American car dealerships, forcing an industry-wide outage. A second attack during initial recovery on June 19 further delayed restoration. Nearly 15,000 dealerships had to revert to manual, paper-based sales, financing, and service workflows for close to two weeks - a textbook example of concentrated third-party/supply-chain risk in the retail sector.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Anderson Economic Group estimated total financial damage to dealers at just over $600 million in the first two weeks of the shutdown alone - roughly 24 times the ransom paid.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Attackers initially demanded $10 million, escalating to $50 million; blockchain analysis (TRM Labs) traced approximately 387 BTC (~$25 million) to a BlackSuit-linked wallet on June 21, 2024, consistent with a paid ransom, though CDK never officially confirmed payment.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Dealer systems were down for nearly two weeks; CDK restored services in a phased rollout through late June/early July 2024.
example_incidents.data_impact: Not publicly detailed at the individual-record level; primary reported impact was operational (sales, financing, service scheduling) rather than a disclosed mass PII leak.

example_incidents.summary: Scattered Spider used a 10-minute vishing call to MGM's IT help desk (via LinkedIn-sourced employee impersonation) to obtain Okta admin credentials, then handed off to ALPHV/BlackCat for ransomware deployment. MGM chose not to pay and rebuilt systems from backups, causing days of casino, hotel, and slot-machine outages across its Las Vegas properties.
example_incidents.financial_impact: MGM disclosed a $100 million negative impact on Q3 2023 results, comprising approximately $84 million in lost revenue (from disrupted hotel, casino and online operations) and $10 million in one-time technology consulting, legal, and third-party advisory expenses.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: MGM stated it never considered paying and did not pay a ransom.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Core systems (reservations, digital key cards, slot machines, ATMs) were down for roughly 10 days; full operational recovery took several weeks.
example_incidents.data_impact: Customer personal information (names, contact details, dates of birth, driver's license and Social Security/passport numbers for some customers) was confirmed stolen.

example_incidents.summary: Scattered Spider socially engineered a third-party IT support vendor for Caesars' identity provider (Okta) to gain network access, exfiltrating loyalty-program customer data before deploying an extortion threat. Unlike MGM, Caesars opted to negotiate and pay, prioritizing avoiding a public data leak and minimizing operational disruption.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not broken out publicly as a discrete total-cost figure (unlike MGM); reported impact centered on the ransom payment and associated incident-response/legal costs, which were not separately quantified in public filings.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Attackers initially demanded $30 million; Caesars paid approximately $15 million in cryptocurrency to prevent publication of stolen data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Caesars avoided the extended, highly visible operational outages MGM experienced, largely because it paid quickly and did not have hotel/casino systems encrypted in the same way.
example_incidents.data_impact: Loyalty program (Caesars Rewards) database exposed, including driver's license numbers and, for a significant number of members, Social Security numbers.

example_incidents.date: Compromise reported mid-2025; extortion/leak threats through June 2026
example_incidents.summary: Part of a broad ShinyHunters campaign that used voice-phishing (vishing) against corporate help desks to trick employees into authorizing a malicious connected app in Salesforce, then exfiltrated data via a modified Salesforce Data Loader - a pure data-extortion attack with no encryption payload, illustrating the sector's growing SaaS/CRM exposure.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed by Ralph Lauren as a discrete cost figure.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: ShinyHunters issued a public leak deadline as extortion leverage; no confirmed ransom payment amount has been reported.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No significant operational/store downtime reported - this was a data-theft/extortion event rather than an encryption/availability incident.
example_incidents.data_impact: More than 220 GB of data claimed stolen, including customer information, transaction records, and documents related to unreleased future product lines.

example_incidents.victim: Madison Square Garden Sports Corp. (parent of the New York Knicks; consumer/entertainment services)
example_incidents.summary: Same ShinyHunters Salesforce-vishing campaign as Ralph Lauren/JCPenney. Attackers socially engineered access to MSG's client/talent CRM database using the old-fashioned vishing technique, then claimed a very large-scale data theft spanning customers, staff, and celebrities/former players.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Extortion/leak-deadline threat issued by ShinyHunters; no confirmed payment reported.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No reported operational outage - data-theft/extortion event, not an encryption event.
example_incidents.data_impact: ShinyHunters claimed roughly 26 million records, including 9.8 million emails, ~9,500 dates of birth, and close to 5 million street addresses/full names/phone numbers; a leaked "Talent" file reportedly included former Knicks players/coaches, MSG executives' family members, and celebrities.

example_incidents.date: Unauthorized access before March 27, 2026; discovered April 4, 2026
example_incidents.summary: A regional single-location car dealership example (contrasted with the CDK/M&S/MGM enterprise-scale cases) illustrating that ransomware targets consumer-services retailers across the full size spectrum, not just national chains. RansomHouse claimed encryption of dealership systems.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not disclosed by RansomHouse or the dealership; Karl Auto Group stated it "did not pay ransom money."
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Phone and computer systems were unavailable over the Easter weekend (roughly April 4-8, 2026 and reportedly beyond, per public customer-facing social media posts); an outside forensic firm was engaged and the FBI/FTC were notified.
example_incidents.data_impact: Data exposed reportedly included full names, Social Security numbers, driver's license/government ID numbers, financial account information, and passport numbers/images; the number of affected individuals was not disclosed.

example_incidents.victim: PChome (pchome.com.tw) / NetHome Group and subsidiary Bibian
example_incidents.date: Claimed June 10, 2026; disclosed publicly late June 2026
example_incidents.summary: A major Taiwanese e-commerce/payment platform targeted by the emerging Settra group, illustrating ransomware risk to online-retail and embedded-payment infrastructure outside the US/UK. The parent company publicly disputed that its core systems were breached, while an affiliated subsidiary (Bibian) confirmed a related, separate data breach - a useful example of attacker claims vs. victim denial/dispute dynamics common in this sector.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: PChome stated its main platforms and payment channels continued operating normally with no evidence of an actual breach to core systems; no confirmed outage was reported.
example_incidents.data_impact: Settra claimed approximately 102GB of internal data stolen, including personal information for roughly 3.5 million members, nine years of operational records, system architecture diagrams, and employee personnel files; subsidiary Bibian separately confirmed exposure of member names, phone numbers, addresses, and purchase history, which reportedly led to follow-on phishing campaigns against customers.

example_incidents.summary: Citi Trends, Inc. experienced a disruption of its back office and distribution center IT systems due to Hive ransomware on January 14, 2023. The FBI provided tools to help restore affected systems, and the company's stores and financial systems remained operational throughout the incident.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The Company activated its incident response and business continuity plan to support the restoration of affected systems. Critical operating systems were restored, and the flow of merchandise to stores began to normalize during the third week of February 2023.
example_incidents.data_impact: Sensitive customer data is not retained on its systems.

example_incidents.summary: Marks Spencer suffered a ransomware attack attributed to the DragonForce group, disrupting various online services. The attack utilized tactics associated with Scattered Spider, leading to significant operational disruptions.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: disrupted online orders, contactless payments, and Click Collect service

example_incidents.summary: Ahold Delhaize confirmed a data theft incident following a cyberattack attributed to the ransomware group INC Ransom. The company stated that certain files were taken from its U.S. business systems, and the investigation is ongoing to determine the extent of the data affected.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: IT systems taken offline for protection

example_incidents.summary: Fourlis Group, the operator of IKEA stores in Eastern Europe, suffered a ransomware attack just before Black Friday on November 27, 2024, leading to estimated losses of $23 million. The attack primarily impacted IKEA's business operations, causing temporary disruptions in store replenishment and e-commerce, but no evidence of data theft or leaks was found.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Temporary disruptions in store replenishment and e-commerce operations from December 2024 through February 2025; systems restored with external cybersecurity experts' help.

example_incidents.summary: Sam's Club is investigating claims of a ransomware breach by the Clop group, which has added the company to its dark web leak site. The company has not confirmed the breach but is prioritizing the security of its members' information.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Avery Products Corporation reported a data breach after its website was hacked to steal customers' credit card and personal information. The breach occurred between July 18, 2024, and December 9, 2024, affecting 61,193 customers. Avery is offering free credit monitoring services to impacted individuals and has set up a dedicated assistance line for inquiries.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 61,193 customers affected; first and last names, billing and shipping address, email address, phone number, payment card number, CVV code, expiration date, purchase amount

example_incidents.summary: AutoCanada experienced a ransomware attack in August 2023, claimed by the Hunters International gang, which may have exposed employee data. The company is notifying affected individuals and has implemented measures to enhance security and minimize future risks.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Operational disruptions occurred, but business continued at AutoCanada's 66 dealerships with some customer service operations impacted by delays.
example_incidents.data_impact: Employee data including full names, addresses, dates of birth, payroll information, social insurance numbers, bank account numbers, and scans of government-issued identification documents.

example_incidents.summary: MarineMax, the world's largest recreational boat and yacht retailer, experienced a data breach impacting over 123,000 individuals. The Rhysida ransomware gang claimed responsibility for the attack, which involved the theft of personal data from the company's systems. The breach was detected on March 10, 2024, after the attackers gained access to the network on March 1, 2024.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Rite Aid reported a data breach impacting 2.2 million customers, where personal information was stolen after attackers breached their network using an employee's credentials. The RansomHub ransomware gang claimed responsibility for the breach, stating they obtained over 10 GB of customer information and threatened to leak it if ransom negotiations failed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 2.2 million customers' personal information including name, address, date of birth, and driver's license number

example_incidents.summary: LockBit ransomware claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on Canadian pharmacy chain London Drugs in April 2024. The FBI has recovered over 7,000 decryption keys from LockBit, which can help victims recover their encrypted data. Despite law enforcement efforts to disrupt LockBit's operations, the group remains active and continues to target organizations worldwide.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: VF Corporation, the owner of brands like Vans and The North Face, reported a ransomware attack that affected over 35 million customers. The breach involved the encryption of IT systems and the theft of personal data, although sensitive information like social security numbers and payment details were not compromised. The company has restored most of its systems but continues to face operational challenges as it investigates the incident.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: VF has substantially restored the IT systems encrypted in the incident but continues to work through minor operational impacts.
example_incidents.data_impact: approximately 35.5 million individual consumers' personal data
sources: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing

example_incidents.summary: AutoZone experienced a data breach due to the Clop ransomware gang's exploitation of a MOVEit vulnerability, affecting the data of 184,995 individuals. The breach was reported on May 28, 2023, and the gang published the stolen data on July 7, 2023, which included sensitive employee information but no customer data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed
example_incidents.data_impact: 184,995 people; full names, social security numbers, employee names, email addresses, parts supply details, tax information, payroll documents, Oracle database files, data about stores, production and sales information
sources: Office of the Maine Attorney General

example_incidents.summary: The ALPHV ransomware gang, also known as BlackCat, has introduced a new API for their data leak site to increase pressure on victims to pay ransoms. This follows their breach of Est e Lauder, which ignored the gang's ransom demands, prompting the group to mock the company's security measures.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Shutterfly, an online retail and photography manufacturing platform, was hit by a Clop ransomware attack. The company stated that the attack did not impact customer data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: The Clop ransomware gang claims to have attacked Saks Fifth Avenue, threatening to leak data if a ransom is not paid. The retailer has stated that mock data was stolen, but the specifics of the breach remain unclear.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Indigo Books Music, the largest bookstore chain in Canada, was struck by a cyberattack that caused the company to shut down its website and only accept cash payments. The incident occurred on February 9th, 2023, and the details regarding the financial impact and ransom are not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The website was made unavailable to customers and only cash payments were accepted.
sources: The Week in Ransomware - February 10th 2023 - Clop's Back

example_incidents.summary: Arnold Clark, Europe's largest independent car retailer, experienced a cyberattack on December 23, 2022, claimed by the Play ransomware group. The attack resulted in the theft of personal information from customers, prompting the company to notify affected clients and take measures to secure their systems.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The company's systems were disconnected from the Internet on December 24, and they are working on restoring the compromised systems in a new segregated environment.
example_incidents.data_impact: Personal information including names, contact details, dates of birth, vehicle details, ID documents (such as passports and driver's licenses), National Insurance numbers (in limited cases), and bank account details were stolen.

example_incidents.summary: Sobeys, a Canadian food retail giant, has been experiencing IT systems issues due to a ransomware attack attributed to the Black Basta group. The attack has affected grocery stores and pharmacies under the Sobeys brand.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: IT systems issues since last weekend

example_incidents.summary: Pendragon Group, a U.K. car dealer, was targeted by the LockBit ransomware gang, who demanded a ransom of $60 million to decrypt files and prevent the leak of stolen data. The company confirmed the breach but stated that it did not affect their operations and they have chosen not to pay the ransom. Pendragon reported the incident to law enforcement and the data protection office in the U.K.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: no impact on operations

example_incidents.summary: Damart, a French clothing company, was hit by a ransomware attack from the Hive gang, demanding a ransom of $2 million. The attack led to the encryption of some systems and significant operational disruptions, affecting 92 stores and customer services since August 15, 2022.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Operations disrupted since August 15; 92 stores impacted and customer support unavailable.

example_incidents.summary: 7-Eleven Denmark confirmed a ransomware attack that led to the closure of 175 stores across the country. The attack prevented stores from using cash registers or accepting payments, prompting an investigation in cooperation with the police. While there is no evidence of customer data being affected, the potential for data theft remains a concern.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: All 7-Eleven stores in Denmark were shut down while the company investigated the incident. Some stores have resumed operations using local solutions.

example_incidents.summary: Walmart has denied being attacked by the Yanluowang ransomware gang, which claimed to have encrypted between 40,000 and 50,000 of their computers. The gang demanded a ransom of $55 million but stated they did not receive a response from Walmart, which maintains that no successful attack occurred.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Fast Shop, one of Brazil's largest retailers, has suffered an extortion cyberattack that led to network disruption and the temporary closure of its online store. The details regarding the ransom demanded or paid have not been disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: network disruption and temporary closure of its online store

example_incidents.summary: Shoprite Holdings, Africa's largest supermarket chain, was hit by a ransomware attack. The RansomHouse group extorted the company, leading to significant operational disruptions.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

exposure_categories.description: In-store POS terminals, payment gateways/processors, e-commerce checkout flows, and PCI-scoped cardholder data environments. Encryption or manipulation of these systems can halt in-store sales entirely; breach of stored/tokenized card data drives PCI-DSS liability.
subcategories: In-store POS terminals and card readers
Payment gateway / processor integrations
E-commerce checkout and shopping-cart platforms
Tokenization/PCI cardholder data environments
Gift card and loyalty-point redemption systems

exposure_categories.description: Centralized repositories of customer PII, purchase history, and loyalty-program data, increasingly hosted in third-party SaaS/CRM platforms (e.g., Salesforce) that have become a primary extortion target independent of on-prem encryption.
subcategories: Loyalty/membership program databases (names, DOB, contact info)
CRM/SaaS platforms (e.g., Salesforce instances, connected apps/OAuth grants)
Marketing and email/SMS platforms
Customer service and call-center/ticketing systems
Website account credentials and stored preferences

exposure_categories.category: Supply Chain, Inventory, and Store Operations Systems
exposure_categories.description: ERP, warehouse management, automated ordering, and inventory/replenishment systems whose disruption forces retailers back to manual, paper-based operations - the single biggest driver of revenue loss in major incidents like M&S.
subcategories: ERP / enterprise resource planning platforms
Warehouse management and logistics/routing systems
Automated stock replenishment and ordering systems
Store network and in-store IT infrastructure (self-checkout, digital signage)
Click-and-collect / omnichannel fulfillment systems

exposure_categories.description: Retail and consumer-services businesses depend heavily on shared platforms (DMS/SaaS providers), franchise networks, and outsourced IT help desks, creating single points of failure that can cascade an attack on one vendor into thousands of affected businesses.
subcategories: Shared SaaS/dealer-management-system providers (e.g., DMS platforms for auto dealers)
Franchise and multi-location operator networks
Outsourced/third-party IT help desks and identity providers (Okta and similar)
Payment processors and financial intermediaries
Marketing, loyalty, and analytics vendors with data-sharing access

exposure_categories.description: Large, often lower-wage, high-turnover workforces mean retailers and consumer-services firms hold extensive employee PII, frequently a secondary but highly damaging data-theft target.
subcategories: Social Security numbers and government ID scans
Payroll and W-2/tax records
Benefits and background-check data
Time-and-attendance / scheduling system data

exposure_categories.description: Consumer-services subsectors (grocery, hospitality, fitness, healthcare-adjacent services) operate physical/IoT systems whose disruption creates safety and spoilage risk beyond pure data loss.
subcategories: Refrigeration/HVAC and building management systems (grocery, food service)
Digital key/access-card systems (hospitality/casino)
Warehouse robotics and automated fulfillment hardware
Fitness/wellness facility access and scheduling systems

exposure_categories.category: Brand, Product, and Intellectual Property Data
exposure_categories.description: Unreleased product designs, pricing strategy, and brand assets are targeted for extortion leverage distinct from customer-data theft, particularly in fashion/apparel and consumer product goods.
subcategories: Unreleased product designs and merchandising plans
Pricing and promotional strategy documents
Supplier/vendor contracts and cost data
Brand and marketing creative assets

hazard_categories.description: How attackers first get in; retail/consumer-services shows a disproportionate reliance on social-engineering of people and processes rather than pure technical exploitation, reflecting large, distributed, high-turnover workforces and heavy reliance on outsourced IT support.
subcategories: Help-desk/service-desk vishing and impersonation (Scattered Spider-style)
Third-party IT vendor or identity-provider (Okta/SSO) compromise
Exploited public-facing vulnerabilities (VPN, web app, edge devices)
SaaS/OAuth and connected-app abuse (e.g., fake Salesforce Data Loader)
Phishing/credential theft against store, warehouse, or corporate staff
Compromised franchise or dealer-network credentials

hazard_categories.description: The dominant tactic in this sector is shifting from encryption toward pure data-theft extortion, but encryption-driven operational shutdown remains the most financially destructive variant when it occurs.
subcategories: Traditional encryption of ERP/POS/inventory systems (operational shutdown)
Extortion-only data exfiltration with no encryption (fastest-growing tactic)
Double extortion (encrypt + threaten to leak)
Direct executive/leadership harassment (calls, Teams messages, emails to C-suite)
Deadline-based public leak-site threats naming victims before payment
Threats against downstream customers/members directly (name-and-shame of loyalty program members)

hazard_categories.description: Because retail margins depend on continuous inventory flow and point-of-sale availability, ransomware's operational-availability impact (not just data loss) is often the largest cost driver in this industry.
subcategories: Store-wide or chain-wide POS outages halting sales
Automated ordering/replenishment failure forcing manual (paper) processes
E-commerce/website downtime and lost online revenue
Warehouse and logistics disruption causing stockouts
Shared-platform outages cascading across many independent locations (franchise/dealer model)

hazard_categories.description: Concentration risk in a small number of shared SaaS, DMS, payment, and identity-provider vendors means a single compromise can simultaneously affect thousands of retail/consumer-services businesses.
subcategories: Compromise of shared SaaS/DMS/CRM platforms serving many retailers at once
IT help-desk/outsourced support vendor compromise
Payment processor or gateway compromise
Franchise/multi-brand holding-company shared infrastructure
Fourth-party risk from vendors' own vendors

hazard_categories.description: Sophos data shows retail has the highest rate of any surveyed sector attributing root cause to "lack of in-house security expertise," reflecting thin IT/security staffing relative to large distributed physical footprints.
subcategories: Under-resourced in-house security teams relative to store/location count
Susceptibility of frontline/call-center/help-desk staff to social engineering
High employee turnover complicating access management and training
Malicious or negligent insider access at franchise/third-party locations

hazard_categories.description: Consumer-facing businesses face a dense, overlapping set of breach-notification, payment-card, and consumer-protection obligations that amplify post-incident cost and litigation risk beyond the direct technical recovery.
subcategories: PCI-DSS liability for payment card data exposure
State/federal breach-notification requirements (and UK/EU GDPR for multinational retailers)
Securities disclosure obligations for public companies (SEC 8-K, equivalent UK/other filings)
Class-action and consumer-litigation exposure over PII/loyalty-data theft
Regulatory scrutiny of ransom payments (OFAC-type sanctions risk on payment recipients)

hazard_categories.description: Because purchase decisions in retail and consumer services are discretionary and brand-sensitive, publicized ransomware incidents translate directly into measurable revenue and market-value loss, distinct from the direct IR/ransom cost.
subcategories: Customer churn and reduced footfall/online conversion post-incident
Stock price / market capitalization impact for public companies
Loyalty-program member attrition after data-theft disclosure
Franchise/brand-license reputational spillover across independently owned locations

overview: Retail Trade and Consumer Services (ransomware.live's "Consumer Services" sector tag) is one of the highest-volume ransomware targeting categories, spanning everything from single-location dealerships, gyms, and jewelry shops up to multinational department-store chains, casino/hospitality operators, and the shared SaaS platforms (CRM, dealer-management systems) that underpin the industry. A live pull of the ransomware.live sector feed (~120 victim postings across roughly a 2-month window in mid-2026) shows the sector is dominated by high-volume, opportunistic ransomware-as-a-service groups (Qilin, TheGentlemen, SafePay, DragonForce, Akira, Nova, Settra) hitting mostly small/mid-size retailers, HVAC/home-services firms, funeral homes, and franchise operations, alongside a smaller number of large, named-brand victims. Layered on top of this baseline is a distinct and increasingly dominant pattern: pure data-extortion campaigns against enterprise SaaS/CRM platforms (the ShinyHunters Salesforce-vishing campaign hit Ralph Lauren, JCPenney/Catalyst Brands, and Madison Square Garden Sports Corp. in 2025-2026) that steal customer and employee data without ever deploying encryption. The sector's most financially destructive incidents, however, remain operational-shutdown events: Marks & Spencer's 2025 DragonForce/Scattered Spider attack cost over £100m directly and roughly £300m in lost operating profit after weeks of manual, pen-and-paper store operations; the 2024 CDK Global (BlackSuit) attack on a shared auto-dealer platform caused an estimated $600m in dealer losses against a reported $25m ransom; and the 2023 MGM Resorts/Caesars Entertainment (Scattered Spider/ALPHV) attacks on hospitality/gaming caused a combined $100m+ loss and a confirmed $15m ransom payment, respectively. Sophos's 2025 retail-specific survey confirms the trend lines visible in these cases: 58% of retailers paying when hit, rising ransom demands (median $2M) alongside a falling encryption rate (48%, a five-year low) as attackers shift toward pure exfiltration, and the highest "lack of in-house security expertise" root-cause rate of any sector surveyed - consistent with a highly distributed, thin-security-staff, high-turnover industry that is unusually exposed to help-desk social engineering and third-party/franchise concentration risk.

aggregate_stats.metric: Telecom sector ransomware victims listed (all-time, ransomware.live)
aggregate_stats.value: 357 victims listed under 'Telecommunication' sector tag as of July 2026; 124 posted in 2025 alone (peak year to date), 62 already in partial-year 2026
aggregate_stats.source: ransomware.live API (api.ransomware.live/v2/sectorvictims/Telecommunication)

aggregate_stats.metric: Top threat actor groups targeting telecom (by victim count, ransomware.live dataset)
aggregate_stats.value: Qilin (25), Akira (22), LockBit3 (17), Play (12), Clop (12), LockBit2 (10), BianLian (10), DragonForce (9), ALPHV/BlackCat (9), INC Ransom (8)
aggregate_stats.source: ransomware.live API (author's own aggregation of the pulled dataset)

aggregate_stats.metric: Telecom ransomware attack volume growth
aggregate_stats.value: Ransomware attacks on telecom companies grew nearly 4x from 24 in 2022 to 90 in 2025; 444 telecom data-theft incidents identified with 133 stolen-database listings; ~70% of 2025 telecom attacks targeted the Americas; Qilin, Akira and Play were the leading groups (corroborates ransomware.live figures above)
aggregate_stats.source: Cyble research via Cybersecurity Dive

aggregate_stats.metric: Ransomware presence in breaches / median payout (all sectors, 2025)
aggregate_stats.value: Ransomware present in 44% of breaches overall; median ransomware payout fell to $115,000 and 64% of victims refused to pay; third-party involvement was a factor in 30% of all breaches (up from ~15% the prior year) - relevant to telecom's heavy vendor/reseller/MVNO dependence; edge/VPN device exploitation as an initial-access vector rose 8x, with only 54% patched (median 32 days to patch)
aggregate_stats.source: Verizon 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR)

aggregate_stats.metric: Average/median ransom payment (all sectors, 2025)
aggregate_stats.value: Mean ransom payment fell from $2M (2024) to $1M (2025); by sector, state/local government paid the highest median ($2.5M) and healthcare the lowest ($150K); telecom not broken out separately in public summary
aggregate_stats.source: Sophos State of Ransomware 2025

aggregate_stats.metric: Quarterly average/median ransom payments, 2025
aggregate_stats.source: Coveware Quarterly Ransomware Reports

aggregate_stats.metric: Global data breach cost by industry, 2025
aggregate_stats.value: Global average cost of a data breach: $4.44M (down 9% YoY). By industry: Healthcare $7.42M (highest, 14th year running), Financial Services $5.56M, Industrial $5M, Energy $4.83M, Technology $4.79M. Telecommunications/Communications was not broken out as a distinct line item in the public summaries reviewed - noted as a data gap
aggregate_stats.source: IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025

aggregate_stats.metric: Global on-chain ransomware payments, 2025
aggregate_stats.value: Ransomware actors received more than $820M in on-chain payments in 2025, an 8% YoY decline from $892M in 2024; median payment per victim rose 368% (from $12,738 in 2024 to $59,556 in 2025) even as total payments fell, and eCrime.ch-tracked claimed victims rose ~50% YoY to the most active year on record - consistent with 'more attacks, fewer big payouts, higher per-incident asks' dynamic seen in telecom cases like Colt and WOW!
aggregate_stats.source: Chainalysis 2025/2026 Crypto Crime Report

data_source_notes:
Primary source (ransomware.live) worked but required discovery: the documented endpoint pattern /v2/victims/sector/{sector} 302-redirects to /apidocs/ and does not return data on the current v6.0-beta ('Aegis') API; the working endpoint is /v2/sectorvictims/Telecommunication (confirmed against /v2/sectors, which lists 'Telecommunication': 357). Also hit the stated 1-req/min rate limit once (got {"message":"1 per 1 minute"}) and succeeded on retry after waiting ~65s. Full 357-record JSON was pulled and parsed locally with jq for group/country/year aggregation.

Supplement 1 (ransomlook.io): partially worked. The documented `?query=` param returned "Query must be at least 2 characters" regardless of input; switching to `?q=` returned valid group-profile JSON with useful corroborating detail (used to confirm Arkana Security's WOW! attack and Babuk-Locker's telecom targeting).

Supplement 2 (ransomwhat.telemetry.ltd/posts.json): failed - the ransomwatch/ransomwhat project has been archived and the endpoint now serves a static "this project has been archived" HTML page rather than JSON, so no data was available from this source.

All 8 example incidents and the aggregate stats were corroborated via WebSearch/WebFetch against independent news and vendor reporting (BleepingComputer, The Record, SecurityWeek, TechCrunch, Bloomberg, Cybersecurity Dive, Coveware, Sophos, Verizon, IBM, Chainalysis, SEC filings, etc.) rather than relying on ransomware.live alone. Where a reported figure could not be corroborated (e.g., WOW!/Cincinnati Bell/Colt precise financial cost), this is stated explicitly as "not publicly disclosed" rather than estimated.
data_sources_used: WebSearch/WebFetch news and vendor reporting (BleepingComputer, The Record, SecurityWeek, TechCrunch, Bloomberg, Cybersecurity Dive, Security Affairs, Infosecurity Magazine, Computer Weekly, SC Media, Trinidad Express, Wikipedia)
IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025

example_incidents.summary: Argentina's largest telecom operator was hit by REvil ransomware that spread via a phishing email to a hijacked internal Domain Admin account, ultimately encrypting more than 18,000 workstations and disrupting internal systems including Office 365, OneDrive, corporate VPN, Citrix, Genesys and customer/field-service virtual machines.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: $7.5 million in Monero demanded, rising to $15 million after a 48-hour deadline passed. Telecom Argentina stated it contained the attack and regained access without paying.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Internal corporate systems (not customer-facing telecom/internet service) were disrupted; company said it isolated affected systems and restored operations using backups, without paying the ransom. Precise recovery timeline/cost not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed beyond the ransom demand itself; no confirmed customer-facing outage cost figures reported.
example_incidents.data_impact: Internal corporate/IT systems affected; no large-scale confirmed customer PII leak was publicly documented.

example_incidents.summary: US regional telecom/broadband provider Cincinnati Bell was listed as a victim on the Yanluowang ransomware group's leak site; the company publicly refused to pay the ransom.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Ransom amount not publicly disclosed; company confirmed it did not pay.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Specific downtime duration and recovery cost not publicly disclosed in available reporting.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; no SEC filing or press disclosure of a specific dollar cost was located.
example_incidents.data_impact: Scope/type of data exfiltrated by Yanluowang not publicly detailed in available sources.

example_incidents.victim: Telecommunications Services of Trinidad and Tobago (TSTT)
example_incidents.summary: The Caribbean nation's state-owned telecom provider had an administrator's credentials compromised (October 3), leading to a security breach on October 9 that affected its internal virtual infrastructure/private cloud. RansomEXX later released a CSV of customer data on the dark web as proof of the hack.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: TSTT reported the breach affected availability of internal virtual infrastructure/private cloud; full recovery timeline not publicly quantified. CEO Lisa Agard was subsequently fired following the incident.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Trinidad and Tobago has no mandatory breach-notification law, which delayed and limited public cost disclosure.
example_incidents.data_impact: Over 1.2 million customer records (mobile, fixed line, broadband) leaked, including full names, emails, national ID numbers, phone numbers and ID scans; the leaked CSV was downloaded 13,000+ times within two weeks; TSTT internal GitLab projects and database dumps were also exposed.

example_incidents.summary: A newly-emerged data-extortion group, Arkana Security, breached major US cable/ISP WOW! after an employee's device was infected with infostealer malware in September 2024, harvesting credentials for backend platforms Symphonica and AppianCloud that gave attackers alleged full backend control (they released a demo video). This was Arkana's debut, high-profile attack.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: WOW! was given a deadline to negotiate or the data would be sold/leaked; specific dollar ransom demand not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No confirmed customer-facing service outage reported; incident was primarily a backend data-access/exfiltration event rather than an encryption/downtime event.
example_incidents.financial_impact: In its March 28, 2025 SEC Form 8-K, WideOpenWest stated the incident had not had a material impact on operations and it did not believe it was reasonably likely to materially affect financial condition or results; the company also disputed that sensitive personal information was accessed, contrary to the attacker's claims.
example_incidents.data_impact: Arkana claimed theft of 403,000 WOW! user account records (names, usernames, salted passwords, emails, login histories, security Q&As) plus a separate CSV of 2.2 million records (names, addresses, phone numbers, device data).

example_incidents.group: Attributed on ransomware.live to 'coinbasecartel' data-extortion listing; technical intrusion used BPFDoor malware (attribution to a distinct ransomware crew is contested/unclear in public reporting)
example_incidents.summary: South Korea's largest mobile carrier (~23M subscribers) disclosed a breach of its Home Subscriber Server after detecting unusual traffic on April 22, 2025. Investigation found BPFDoor malware present undetected on at least 28 servers (33 variants) since as early as 2022, exfiltrating USIM authentication keys and other subscriber identifiers.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: No ransom payment publicly reported; this was primarily treated as a state-linked/criminal espionage-style data breach rather than a classic encryption ransomware case, though listed as a data-leak/extortion incident by dark-web trackers.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No major network outage; SK Telecom offered free SIM replacements to all customers as remediation.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Record $97.2 million (KRW 134.8 billion) fine from South Korea's Personal Information Protection Committee, plus a ~$7,000 fine for late breach reporting; the Korea Consumer Agency separately ordered SK Telecom to pay ~$67 (100,000 won) compensation to each of the 23 million affected users; SK Telecom committed roughly $514 million to a security-overhaul 'Accountability and Commitment Program,' plus bill discounts, fee waivers and free data.
example_incidents.data_impact: 25 types of personal information for 23.2 million subscribers exposed, including phone numbers, IMSI numbers, and USIM authentication keys - raising SIM-swap and surveillance risk.

example_incidents.summary: Global business telecom provider Colt was breached via exploitation of the SharePoint remote-code-execution vulnerability CVE-2025-53770, leading to a multi-day (ultimately multi-week/multi-month) outage of Colt Online customer portal, hosting APIs, and Voice API/porting platforms; core network infrastructure reportedly remained largely unaffected. Colt publicly attributed responsibility to the WarLock ransomware group.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: WarLock demanded $200,000 for the stolen data cache and posted samples on dark-web forums as proof.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Outage began August 12, 2025; Colt stated the majority of recovery would take 8-10 weeks, with customer portal, hosting APIs and voice-on-demand tools still offline in early October 2025 - a multi-month recovery, unusually long for a major telecom provider.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Specific dollar cost of the incident not publicly disclosed by Colt; impact described qualitatively as affecting 27,000+ customers across ~40 countries.
example_incidents.data_impact: WarLock claimed theft of over one million documents including employee salary data, customer contact information, internal executive personal information, and confidential emails.

example_incidents.victim: Orange S.A. (Orange Group, incl. Orange Belgium subsidiary)
example_incidents.summary: French telecom giant Orange disclosed a security incident at the end of July 2025 involving internal systems, using the same SharePoint exploitation chain (webshells, Group Policy abuse, credential theft, lateral movement) attributed to WarLock. The group publicly claimed the attack on August 17, 2025 and released roughly 4GB of data. A separate, related incident hit Orange Belgium, affecting 850,000 customer accounts.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Specific ransom amount not publicly disclosed for the Orange S.A. incident.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Orange stated the attacker had only limited access and exfiltrated mostly 'outdated or low-sensitivity data'; no major prolonged network outage reported (unlike Colt).
example_incidents.data_impact: ~4GB of internal data published on the dark web by WarLock; Orange characterized the exposed data as largely outdated/low-sensitivity. The related Orange Belgium breach separately impacted 850,000 customer accounts.

example_incidents.summary: One of the world's largest cell-tower/telecom infrastructure REITs was breached in a 'pay-or-leak' extortion campaign by ShinyHunters. After American Tower did not pay by the group's June 15, 2026 deadline, the attackers published the stolen files - notable for exposing physical-security data (tower gate/access codes) rather than just customer records, illustrating the physical-infrastructure risk unique to telecom tower operators.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Extortion demand made; American Tower did not comply and data was leaked. Specific dollar figure not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No network/tower service outage publicly reported; incident was a data-exfiltration/extortion event rather than an encryption/availability event.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as of this research.
example_incidents.data_impact: Attackers claimed over 5.2 million records including customer and landowner PII, records referencing other companies' infrastructure (T-Mobile, Verizon, US DHS), tower asset records with GPS coordinates, and plaintext physical access/gate codes for cell tower compounds; 216,601 accounts were added to Have I Been Pwned on June 26, 2026.

example_incidents.summary: On March 27, 2023, Lumen Technologies announced two cybersecurity incidents. A ransomware attack affected a limited number of the Company’s servers, degrading operations for some enterprise customers. Additionally, a separate intrusion involved unauthorized access to internal IT systems, including data extraction.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The Company implemented business continuity plans to restore functionality to its customers’ operational and business systems.
example_incidents.data_impact: A limited amount of data was extracted, but the specific number of records or individuals affected is not publicly disclosed.
sources: United States Securities and Exchange Commission

example_incidents.summary: Ascom, a Swiss telecommunications company, confirmed a cyberattack by the HellCat hacking group that targeted its Jira servers. The hackers claimed to have stolen 44GB of sensitive data, including source code and confidential documents, but the company stated that the incident did not impact its business operations.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: no impact on the company s business operations
example_incidents.data_impact: 44GB of data stolen, including source code, project details, invoices, confidential documents, and issues from the ticketing system

example_incidents.summary: BT Group's BT Conferencing division experienced a breach by the Black Basta ransomware gang, which claimed to have stolen 500GB of sensitive data. Although the company stated that the incident did not impact their operations, they took certain servers offline as a precaution. The attackers threatened to leak the stolen data on their dark web site.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Some servers were taken offline and isolated, but BT Conferencing services remained fully operational.
example_incidents.data_impact: 500GB of data allegedly stolen, including financial and organizational data, users data and personal documents, NDA documents, and confidential information.

example_incidents.summary: Frontier Communications reported a data breach affecting 750,000 customers after a cyberattack attributed to the RansomHub ransomware group. The breach exposed personal information, including full names and Social Security Numbers, and the attackers threatened to leak additional data unless their demands were met.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Some systems were shut down to contain the attack; customers reported Internet connection issues during the attack.
example_incidents.data_impact: 751895 customers' full names and Social Security Numbers (SSNs) were confirmed as breached; 5GB of data allegedly stolen containing information of 2 million customers.

example_incidents.summary: Tigo Business, the largest mobile carrier in Paraguay, suffered a ransomware attack attributed to the Black Hunt group, impacting their cloud and hosting services. The attack reportedly encrypted over 330 servers and compromised backups, affecting more than 300 associated companies.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: Chilean telecom giant Grupo GTD was hit by a ransomware attack on October 23, 2023, impacting its Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) platform and disrupting various online services. The attack involved the Rorschach ransomware gang, which utilized DLL sideloading vulnerabilities to execute the ransomware payload.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Partial impact on services, including IaaS platform and shared services; specific services like IP telephony and VPNs were affected.
sources: Chile's Computer Security Incident Response Team (CSIRT)

example_incidents.summary: Royal Ransomware claimed responsibility for a cyber attack on telecommunications provider Intrado, demanding a ransom of $60 million after stealing sensitive data. The attack coincided with a significant outage affecting Intrado's services, and the group threatened to leak the stolen data unless the ransom is paid.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Intrado experienced a widespread outage impacting all services, including Unified Communication Services and Healthcare, starting December 1. Most services have been restored, but healthcare services were still experiencing intermittent issues as of December 21.
example_incidents.data_impact: Internal documents, passports, and employee driver's licenses

example_incidents.summary: The Hive ransomware gang claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on Bell Technical Solutions, a subsidiary of Bell Canada. The details regarding the extent of the attack and the data affected have not been disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: The Hive ransomware gang claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on Bell Technical Solutions, a subsidiary of Bell Canada. The attack, which occurred on August 20, 2022, resulted in the encryption of BTS' systems and unauthorized access to operational company and employee information, as well as customer details. Bell Canada has since alerted customers and is investigating the incident with law enforcement.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: BTS' website is currently inaccessible; immediate steps were taken to secure affected systems.
example_incidents.data_impact: operational company and employee information; names, addresses, and phone numbers of residential and small business customers in Ontario and Quebec who booked a technician visit

example_incidents.summary: Hackers exploited a zero-day vulnerability in Mitel MiVoice VOIP appliances, believed to be part of a ransomware attack. Although the attack was stopped, the vulnerability allowed for remote code execution and potential lateral movement within the network.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

exposure_categories.description: The 'OT-equivalent' layer for telecom - subscriber and routing infrastructure whose compromise or outage disrupts service for large customer populations rather than just exposing records.
subcategories: Home Subscriber Server (HSS) / HLR subscriber databases (e.g., SK Telecom)
USIM/SIM authentication keys and IMSI/IMEI identifiers
BSS/OSS (billing and operations support systems)
BGP/RIPE routing account credentials and DNS infrastructure (Orange Spain-style hijack risk)
SS7/signaling systems
5G core network functions and voice/SMS switching platforms (Cellcom-style voice-network compromise)
E911/emergency call routing systems

exposure_categories.description: The high-volume personal data telecom operators uniquely hold by virtue of serving as national-scale identity and communications intermediaries.
subcategories: Names, addresses, dates of birth, national ID/passport/driver's license scans
Call Detail Records (CDRs) - who called whom, when, duration, cell-tower location metadata
Billing, payment card and bank account data
Login credentials, security questions, and account history (WOW!-style)
Device/handset data and device financing records

exposure_categories.description: The corporate IT layer - often the actual initial-access and lateral-movement surface even when the attacker's goal is subscriber or infrastructure data.
subcategories: CRM and customer-support/ticketing portals (Colt Online-style customer portals)
Third-party SaaS/backend platforms integrated into telecom operations (e.g., AppianCloud, Symphonica)
VPN/remote-access and SharePoint/collaboration infrastructure (CVE-2025-53770-style exploitation)
Employee HR, payroll and executive personal data
Internal source code, GitLab/CI-CD repositories and database dumps

exposure_categories.description: Telecom's unusual exposure of physical assets and access controls alongside digital ones - a hazard largely absent in pure IT/software industries.
subcategories: Cell tower compounds and physical access/gate codes (American Tower incident)
Colocation and data center facility access systems
Field service technician and subcontractor credentials/networks (Bell Technical Solutions-style)
Tower/asset GPS location data

exposure_categories.description: Data and access that telecom operators hold on behalf of, or shared with, other organizations - amplifying blast radius beyond the operator's own customers.
subcategories: MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) and reseller partner data
Interconnect/roaming carrier data and industry-association data (e.g., GSMA)
Data belonging to enterprise customers hosted, routed, or processed by the telecom (managed services, hosting, colocation)
References to other companies' infrastructure held incidentally (e.g., tower records referencing other carriers' equipment)

exposure_categories.description: Government-facing and critical-infrastructure-designated systems that create outsized regulatory and national-security exposure when compromised.
subcategories: Lawful intercept and law-enforcement request-handling systems
Critical infrastructure/national security designated network segments
Breach-notification and regulatory reporting systems (subject to GDPR, PIPC, FCC, Ofcom, etc.)

hazard_categories.description: How ransomware and extortion actors most commonly get into telecom environments, per the incidents and DBIR/Cyble data reviewed.
subcategories: Infostealer-harvested employee/admin credentials (WOW!/Arkana; Orange Spain RIPE-account takeover)
Exploitation of internet-facing edge devices, VPNs and collaboration platforms (Colt/Orange - SharePoint CVE-2025-53770; DBIR notes 8x rise in edge/VPN exploitation, only 54% patched)
Phishing and social engineering leading to hijacked Domain Admin accounts (Telecom Argentina/REvil)
Compromised third-party/vendor or subcontractor credentials (Bell Technical Solutions/Hive)
Rapid weaponization of zero-day/critical vulnerabilities in internet-facing network equipment (Cyble finding)
Stolen or weak administrative credentials (TSTT/RansomEXX)

hazard_categories.description: The spectrum of pressure techniques used against telecom victims, which increasingly skew toward pure data extortion over encryption.
subcategories: Double extortion: encryption plus data exfiltration (RansomEXX/TSTT, Yanluowang/Cincinnati Bell)
Pure data-leak/'pay-or-leak' extortion with no encryption (Arkana/WOW!, ShinyHunters/American Tower, ShinyHunters/Charter)
Public shaming, 'wall of shame' and doxxing tactics (Arkana Security's stated model)
Proof-of-hack demonstration videos and backend-access showcases (Arkana/WOW!)
Reupload/re-extortion of previously leaked data by a different or same group (SK-Telecom 'data reuploaded' listing)
Deadline-driven negotiation windows escalating ransom demands over time (Telecom Argentina's $7.5M to $15M escalation)

hazard_categories.description: Telecom's version of OT/ICS risk - attacks that threaten service availability at national or regional scale rather than just confidentiality.
subcategories: Voice/SMS/data network outages from ransomware or intrusion (Cellcom's week-long voice/SMS blackout)
BGP hijacking / routing manipulation causing internet outages (Orange Spain)
Sabotage-style attacks without malware causing multi-day national outages (Vodafone Portugal, 4.7M mobile + 1M fixed customers affected)
Customer-portal and OSS/BSS downtime cascading into business-customer disruption (Colt's multi-month portal outage)
Emergency-services (911/E911) disruption risk given telecom's critical-infrastructure designation

hazard_categories.description: Telecom's dense web of vendors, resellers, field-service contractors, and shared industry infrastructure creates outsized supply-chain blast radius (DBIR: third-party factor rose to 30% of breaches).
subcategories: Compromise via subcontracted field-service/technical-solutions providers
Compromise of shared backend SaaS platforms used across the operator's business (AppianCloud/Symphonica-style)
MVNO/reseller relationship exposure
Industry-body/association compromise with cross-member blast radius (GSMA/Qilin)
Downstream exposure of other carriers' data held incidentally (American Tower's records referencing T-Mobile/Verizon/DHS)

hazard_categories.description: Human-layer risk distinct from bulk phishing - individual employee/admin compromise with outsized consequences given telecom's centralized subscriber-identity role.
subcategories: Single-employee infostealer infection cascading to full backend compromise (WOW!)
Reused/weak passwords on high-privilege admin or registry accounts (Orange Spain RIPE account)
SIM-swap-enabling data theft (USIM keys, IMSI) creating downstream account-takeover risk for subscribers (SK Telecom)
Insider-facilitated or insider-adjacent credential sale enabling initial access

hazard_categories.description: Telecom's status as a heavily regulated, often critical-infrastructure-designated sector amplifies post-incident financial and legal consequences beyond the ransom/attack itself.
subcategories: Data-protection regulator fines (SK Telecom's $97.2M PIPC fine; Cosmote/OTE's combined ~$9.25M Greek DPA fines for a related breach)
Mandatory consumer compensation schemes (SK Telecom's per-subscriber payout order)
Breach-notification law gaps/delays in some jurisdictions (Trinidad and Tobago's lack of mandatory notification law)
Securities disclosure obligations for public telecom operators (WideOpenWest 8-K materiality determination)
Executive/leadership accountability actions (TSTT CEO's dismissal post-breach)
National security and critical-infrastructure regulatory scrutiny given telecom's designation in most jurisdictions

overview: The telecommunications sector - internet service providers, mobile network operators, fixed-line/cable carriers, tower/infrastructure companies, and satellite/media-adjacent telecom firms - has become an increasingly frequent ransomware and data-extortion target. Ransomware.live's own sector tracker lists 357 telecom-sector victims (tag "Telecommunication") with a pronounced acceleration in 2025-2026 (124 posted in 2025 alone, the sector's most active year on record, plus 62 more in the first ~7 months of 2026), corroborated by Cyble/Cybersecurity Dive research showing telecom ransomware attack volume grew roughly fourfold from 24 in 2022 to 90 in 2025. The threat-actor landscape is dominated by prolific double-extortion RaaS groups (Qilin, Akira, LockBit variants, Play, Clop) alongside a newer wave of pure data-extortion/leak-only crews with no encryption capability (Arkana Security, ShinyHunters, DragonForce) that specifically target telecom's dense stores of subscriber PII, SIM/USIM credentials, and call-detail metadata. What distinguishes telecom from most other industries in this taxonomy is the sector's dual exposure: (1) a large, regulated subscriber-PII attack surface comparable to healthcare or financial services, and (2) an "OT-equivalent" core-network/availability layer (HSS/HLR, BGP routing, voice/SMS switching, physical tower infrastructure) where a successful intrusion can cascade into regional or national service outages - as seen in incidents ranging from Vodafone Portugal's multi-day national outage to Cellcom's week-long US regional voice/SMS blackout. Third-party and supply-chain exposure is also unusually acute, given telecom's dependence on field-service subcontractors, MVNO/reseller relationships, shared backend SaaS platforms, and industry bodies - Verizon's 2025 DBIR found third-party involvement in 30% of all breaches, up sharply from roughly 15% the year before. Regulatory consequences have grown correspondingly severe, exemplified by SK Telecom's record $97.2M Korean privacy-regulator fine and mandated per-subscriber compensation after its 2025 USIM-data breach.
