aggregate_stats.source: ransomware.live sector activity feed (Transportation/Logistics)

data_source_notes:
Base incident data (Step 1): The documented API v2 sector endpoint returned by ransomware.live's own docs (`/v2/victims/sector/{sector}` and variants like `/v2/sector/{sector}`) 404-redirected to the docs page. Cross-referencing the ransomware.live MCP server source code revealed the true route is `/v2/sectorvictims/{sector}`. However, this sector's tag literally contains a slash — "Transportation/Logistics" — and every encoding attempt tried (`%2F`, double-encoded `%252F`, `--path-as-is` curl flag, dash-substituted slug `Transportation-Logistics`, bare `Transportation`) either 404'd with the sector value truncated at the slash (server/router decodes %2F before route matching, so only "Transportation" reached the handler and no sector by that exact name exists) or hit the endpoint's "1 per 1 minute" rate limit (confirmed via a 429 `{"message":"1 per 1 minute"}` response on one attempt). Given the instructed retry-once-then-fallback policy, I fell back to WebFetching the equivalent live website page (https://www.ransomware.live/activity/Transportation-Logistics), which successfully returned real, current victim/group/date/country rows (500+ entries noted as available, ~20 most-recent shown) and served as the functional substitute for the raw API pull. The `/v2/sectors` list endpoint (a different, non-rate-limited path) did work and confirmed "Transportation/Logistics" as the exact registered sector tag.

Step 2 supplements: ransomlook.io's `/api/search` endpoint returned HTTP 400 Bad Request for the query attempted (likely a different expected query-parameter format not documented publicly) — treated as unavailable, skipped gracefully. ransomwhat.telemetry.ltd/posts.json redirected to ransomwatch.telemetry.ltd, which turned out to be an archived/no-longer-maintained project page with no live claim data — also skipped gracefully; noted as unavailable rather than fabricated.

All 8 example incidents were independently verified via multiple WebSearch queries and cross-referenced against named news/breach-tracking sources (Forbes, CNBC, TechTarget, SEC EDGAR filings for Expeditors, The Record, BleepingComputer, TechRadar, The Register, ClassAction.org, CNN, Maritime Executive, therecord.media) rather than relying solely on ransomware.live's short descriptions. Aggregate stats were pulled via WebSearch against Sophos, Coveware, Verizon DBIR, Comparitech, and Zscaler ThreatLabz reporting; IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 was checked but did not surface a clean global (non-India-specific) transportation-industry cost figure in available search snippets, so it was omitted rather than approximated.
data_sources_used: ransomware.live website sector activity feed (https://www.ransomware.live/activity/Transportation-Logistics) — substituted for the rate-limited/routing-broken API sector endpoint
ransomware.live /v2/sectors API endpoint (confirmed sector tag naming)
WebSearch (general news, breach trackers) for incident verification
Zscaler ThreatLabz 2025 Ransomware Report / Mobile, IoT & OT Report
ransomlook.io API — attempted, returned HTTP 400, not usable
ransomwhat.telemetry.ltd / ransomwatch.telemetry.ltd — attempted, project archived/no live data, not usable

example_incidents.group: NotPetya (masqueraded as Petya ransomware; attributed to Sandworm/Russian military intelligence, not a typical criminal ransomware gang)
example_incidents.summary: The NotPetya wiper, disguised as ransomware, spread globally via a compromised Ukrainian accounting software update (M.E.Doc) and crippled Maersk's global IT infrastructure, forcing the reinstallation of roughly 4,000 servers and 45,000 PCs and halting container booking and port operations across multiple countries.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Maersk publicly estimated total costs of $200-300 million (lost revenue, IT restoration, and extraordinary operating costs), disclosed in investor communications; widely cited as one of the costliest cyber incidents in history at the time.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not applicable in the traditional sense — NotPetya had no functioning decryption mechanism; no ransom was viably payable or paid despite a nominal $300 in Bitcoin demanded on-screen.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Core systems were down for roughly 10 days; a full IT rebuild (including a 'miracle' surviving domain controller found in Ghana) took an emergency response team working around the clock roughly a week to restore booking systems, with normal port operations taking longer to stabilize.
example_incidents.data_impact: Primarily an operational/availability impact (systems wiped) rather than a data-exfiltration/breach event; no large-scale customer PII exposure was reported.

example_incidents.group: Mailto (Netwalker family) initially; Nefilim in the second, follow-on attack
example_incidents.summary: Australian freight and logistics giant Toll Group was hit by ransomware twice within three months in 2020. The first attack infected roughly 1,000 servers and forced a full network shutdown; the second (Nefilim, a double-extortion group) again took down the MyToll customer portal and stole and threatened to leak data.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a specific dollar figure by Toll Group; operational disruption affected freight booking, invoicing, and customer service for weeks across both incidents.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed; Toll Group stated it did not pay.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: First attack: core IT systems and ~1,000 servers taken offline, with a multi-week recovery of booking/tracking portals. Second attack (three months later): MyToll portal and other systems again disrupted for an extended period while freight shipments continued via manual workarounds.
example_incidents.data_impact: Nefilim attackers stole and published approximately 220GB of data from at least one server, including current and former employee information.

example_incidents.group: Not publicly attributed to a named ransomware group in company disclosures
example_incidents.summary: Global freight forwarder Expeditors International proactively shut down most of its global operating systems after detecting a cyberattack, disrupting its ability to move shipments through ports and process customer orders for weeks, with effects disclosed as materially impacting quarterly results in SEC filings.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Per SEC 10-K/8-K filings: approximately $62 million in incremental demurrage charges (inability to timely move shipments through ports) and approximately $28 million in investigation, recovery, and remediation expenses in H1 2022 — commonly summarized in press coverage as roughly $60 million in total incident-related costs; company also disclosed lower shipment volumes and revenue impact as customers shifted to competitors during the outage.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Systems were shut down company-wide starting February 20, 2022; recovery of operating and accounting systems extended over several weeks, with the company still describing 'material adverse impact' months later in its Q1 2022 disclosures.
example_incidents.data_impact: Not detailed in public filings as a large-scale data breach; disclosures focused primarily on operational/financial impact rather than confirmed record counts of exposed data.

example_incidents.victim: Port of Nagoya (Nagoya Harbor Transportation Association / Nagoya United Terminal System)
example_incidents.group: LockBit 3.0 (claimed credit; not officially confirmed by port authorities)
example_incidents.summary: Japan's largest and busiest cargo port (handling ~10% of Japan's trade volume, including Toyota vehicle exports) suffered a ransomware attack on its Nagoya Port Unified Terminal System (NUTS), the central OT/IT system managing container terminal operations, halting all container loading/unloading operations.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly quantified in dollar terms; impact described qualitatively as significant given the port's role in ~10% of Japan's total trade volume and its handling of major automotive exports (Toyota).
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Container operations were fully suspended for roughly 2-3 days (attack detected July 4, most terminals resumed by July 6) after servers were isolated and systems restored from backup.
example_incidents.data_impact: Primarily an OT/operational-availability incident (terminal management system encrypted); no large-scale personal data exposure was publicly reported.

example_incidents.summary: Akira ransomware operators brute-forced a weak employee password (no MFA in place) to breach 158-year-old UK haulage firm KNP Logistics, encrypting critical systems and data. The already financially strained company was unable to secure emergency investment in the aftermath and entered administration roughly three months later.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not disclosed as a precise incident-remediation cost; the ultimate financial outcome was total business collapse — KNP Logistics Group entered insolvency/administration, with the ransomware attack cited by administrators as a decisive contributing factor alongside pre-existing market pressures.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Ransom demand reported at approximately GBP 5 million (some reporting cites GBP 5-6 million); not paid.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Critical operational and financial systems were encrypted and unusable; the company was unable to recover operationally and ceased trading roughly three months after the attack rather than completing a technical recovery.
example_incidents.data_impact: Financial and operational data was encrypted/compromised; approximately 730 employees lost their jobs when the company subsequently collapsed into administration.

example_incidents.summary: Major North American less-than-truckload (LTL) freight carrier Estes Express Lines was breached by the LockBit ransomware gang, which stole personal data and later published it on its leak site after Estes declined to pay. Estes disclosed the breach to regulators and affected individuals over the following months, triggering a class-action lawsuit.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a specific dollar figure; costs would include forensic investigation, legal defense of the resulting class action, and regulatory notification expenses.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Estes publicly stated it refused to pay the ransom; specific demand amount not disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Forensic investigation concluded November 7, 2023; notification to affected individuals began December 4, 2023 — roughly ten weeks after initial network access. Operational downtime specifics were not detailed in public reporting.
example_incidents.data_impact: Breach affected 21,184 individuals per filing with the Maine Attorney General; compromised data included names and Social Security numbers of current/former employees, job applicants, and/or customers. LockBit published the stolen data on its leak site November 13, 2023.

example_incidents.country: United States (impact felt across the broader North American trucking industry as a third-party/supply-chain event)
example_incidents.group: Not publicly attributed to a named group in available reporting
example_incidents.summary: ORBCOMM, a major provider of Electronic Logging Device (ELD) and fleet-tracking technology used by numerous trucking companies, suffered a ransomware attack that took down its FleetManager platform and BT500/BT504 ELD hardware line, forcing truckers using affected devices to revert to paper logs. Illustrates concentrated third-party/supply-chain risk in transportation: a single vendor outage cascaded across many downstream carriers and triggered a federal regulatory response.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed by ORBCOMM; downstream financial impact on the many trucking companies dependent on the affected ELD/FleetManager services was not separately quantified in public reporting.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Outage began September 6, 2023; ORBCOMM targeted September 28, 2023 for full restoration of impacted services — an outage window of roughly three weeks.
example_incidents.data_impact: Primarily an availability/operational-technology impact (fleet tracking and ELD compliance systems down) rather than a disclosed data-exfiltration event; the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) issued a temporary enforcement waiver allowing affected carriers to use paper logs beyond the normal 8-day limit.

example_incidents.country: United States (global freight-forwarding operations, headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia)
example_incidents.group: Not officially attributed by JAS in public statements; some industry reporting associated the incident with the broader RansomHub-era wave of attacks, though this was not confirmed by the company
example_incidents.summary: Global freight forwarder JAS Worldwide suffered a ransomware/malware attack that disrupted core operating systems, customer service, billing/payment systems, and its central operations platform (C1) and customer-facing JAS SmartHub portal.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Disruption began August 27, 2024; the company reported most core systems restored and functioning normally within days, with full recovery and resumption of pre-incident business levels across most geographies described as substantially complete within roughly two weeks.
example_incidents.data_impact: JAS disclosed a leak of over 400 data records; the majority of its contract logistics business and several entities were reported unaffected.

example_incidents.summary: On September 19, 2025, RTX Corporation reported a ransomware incident affecting its Multi-User System Environment (MUSE) passenger processing software. The company activated its incident response plan and is investigating the incident with the help of cybersecurity experts while communicating with affected airlines and airports.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Customers have shifted to back-up or manual processes and have experienced certain flight delays and cancellations.
sources: United States Securities and Exchange Commission

example_incidents.summary: Manchester Airports Group disclosed that hackers breached its systems and stole customer data, including Wi-Fi sign-ups and details related to car park, lounge, and Fast Track bookings. The attack did not access payment details and had no impact on airport operations, but MAG has temporarily suspended its online Manage My Booking service as a precaution.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The incident has not resulted in any operational disruption, and customer parking services continue to operate normally.
example_incidents.data_impact: Potentially 8.9 million travelers' data including email addresses, phone numbers, vehicle registration numbers, and postcodes.

example_incidents.summary: The Port of Seattle experienced a ransomware attack in August 2024, impacting the personal information of roughly 90,000 individuals. The Rhysida ransomware group was identified as the perpetrator, and the Port refused to pay the ransom despite threats to publish stolen data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: disrupted multiple services and systems, including reservation check-in systems, passenger display boards, the Port of Seattle website, and delayed flights
example_incidents.data_impact: approximately 90,000 individuals affected; data types include names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, and some medical information

example_incidents.summary: Cold storage giant Americold confirmed a data breach after an April attack claimed by Cactus ransomware, affecting over 129,000 employees and their dependents. The attackers stole personal information and leaked a 6GB archive of sensitive documents, prompting Americold to shut down its IT network to contain the breach.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Americold had to shut down its IT network to contain the breach and rebuild the impacted systems.
example_incidents.data_impact: Over 129,000 employees and their dependents had their personal information stolen, including names, addresses, Social Security numbers, driver's license/state ID numbers, passport numbers, financial account information, and employment-related health insurance and medical information.

example_incidents.summary: The Allied Pilots Association, representing 15,000 American Airlines pilots, experienced a ransomware attack that encrypted certain systems. The union is currently investigating the incident and working to restore affected systems with the help of cybersecurity experts.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The IT team and outside experts are working on restoring systems impacted by the ransomware attack from backups, focusing on pilot-facing products and tools.

example_incidents.summary: The BianLian extortion group claims to have breached the network of Air Canada, stealing 210GB of data. As a result, they are extorting the airline, threatening to leak the stolen data if their demands are not met.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: ORBCOMM, a trucking and fleet management solutions provider, confirmed a ransomware attack on September 6, 2023, causing significant service outages for customers. The attack has impacted their FleetManager platform and Blue Tree product line, preventing trucking companies from managing their fleets effectively.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Service restoration expected by September 29, 2023

example_incidents.summary: Auckland Transport in New Zealand is experiencing a widespread outage due to a suspected ransomware attack, affecting various customer services including the HOP integrated ticketing system. Investigations are ongoing, and while there are concerns about potential data exposure, AT believes the incident is isolated and that no personal or financial data has been accessed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: AT's website and HOP services might return to normal operations early next week.

example_incidents.summary: The Port of Nagoya, Japan's largest port, was hit by a ransomware attack on July 4, 2023, disrupting container terminal operations. The attack caused significant financial losses and halted all container loading and unloading operations.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Operations planned to resume by 08:30 AM the day after the attack.

example_incidents.summary: The Money Message ransomware group has emerged, targeting victims globally and demanding million-dollar ransoms to prevent data leaks and provide decryptors. They have claimed to have stolen files from an Asian airline, which has annual revenue close to $1 billion, and have provided proof of the breach through screenshots of the accessed file system.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: The LockBit ransomware gang claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on Royal Mail that disrupted international shipping services. The attack was detected on January 10, 2023, and Royal Mail is investigating the incident with external forensic experts and UK security agencies. LockBit has threatened to publish stolen data if their ransom is not paid.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Royal Mail experienced severe service disruption to its international export services but has resumed some services as of February 3, 2023.

example_incidents.summary: Wabtec Corporation experienced a data breach following a ransomware attack by LockBit, which exposed sensitive personal information. The breach was detected on June 26, 2022, and data was leaked on August 20, 2022, after a ransom was presumably not paid.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: The LockBit ransomware gang claimed an attack on the Port of Lisbon Administration on Christmas day, threatening to leak stolen data unless a ransom of $1,500,000 is paid. The port's operations were reportedly unaffected, but the official website is currently offline, and the gang has already published samples of the stolen data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The port's official website remains offline, but operations were not impacted according to the company statement.
example_incidents.data_impact: Financial reports, audits, budgets, contracts, cargo information, ship logs, crew details, customer PII, port documentation, email correspondence.

example_incidents.summary: New ransomware attacks in Ukraine have been linked to the Russian military threat group Sandworm, utilizing a new ransomware named RansomBoggs. The malware encrypts files using AES-256 and appends a .chsch extension, with ransom notes referencing the character James P. Sullivan from Monsters Inc.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.victim: transportation and logistics organizations in Ukraine and Poland
example_incidents.summary: A series of ransomware attacks targeting transportation and logistics organizations in Ukraine and Poland have been linked to the Russian Sandworm threat group. The attacks, utilizing Prestige ransomware, have been noted for their sophisticated deployment methods and are part of a broader pattern of Russian state-aligned cyber activity in the region.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: not publicly disclosed

example_incidents.summary: TAP Air Portugal was targeted by the Ragnar Locker ransomware gang, which claimed to have attacked the airline's systems. Although TAP stated that the attack was blocked and no customer data was accessed, the ransomware group threatened to release evidence contradicting this claim, suggesting that significant amounts of customer data may have been compromised.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The website and app experienced instability and were unable to function properly due to the cyberattack.
example_incidents.data_impact: Hundreds of Gigabytes of data might have been compromised, including customer information such as names, dates of birth, emails, and addresses.

example_incidents.summary: SpiceJet, a low-cost Indian airline, faced an attempted ransomware attack that impacted its systems and caused significant flight delays. The IT team managed to contain the attack, restoring normal operations, but customer reports indicated ongoing issues with service availability and booking systems.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Flights experienced delays ranging from two to five hours, with some cancellations due to operational restrictions.

exposure_categories.description: The operational core of transportation/warehousing firms — systems whose downtime directly halts the physical movement of goods, distinguishing this industry's ransomware exposure from purely data-centric sectors.
subcategories: Electronic Logging Devices (ELD) and telematics/fleet-tracking platforms (e.g., ORBCOMM FleetManager, Samsara, Omnitracs)
Transportation Management Systems (TMS) and Warehouse Management Systems (WMS)
Port/terminal operating systems (TOS), crane and gate-automation control systems, and container-yard management platforms (e.g., Nagoya Port's NUTS)
Dispatch, routing, and load-planning software
Fuel management, weigh-station, and vehicle-maintenance scheduling systems
Warehouse automation, conveyor/sortation controllers, and robotics/IoT sensors on the OT side of distribution centers

exposure_categories.description: Sensitive business and transactional data whose exposure drives breach-notification duties and extortion leverage even when operations aren't disrupted.
subcategories: Bill of lading, manifest, and customs/trade-compliance data (HS codes, import/export declarations)
EDI (Electronic Data Interchange) transaction streams with shippers, carriers, and customs brokers
Freight billing, invoicing, and payment/AP-AR financial data
Customer shipment and pricing/contract data (competitively sensitive)
Employee, driver, and job-applicant PII (names, SSNs, driver's license/CDL numbers) — as seen in the Estes Express Lines breach

exposure_categories.description: Transportation/warehousing firms rely heavily on shared vendor platforms and interconnected partner networks, concentrating risk in a small number of upstream providers.
subcategories: ELD/telematics hardware and software vendors (single-vendor outages cascade across many downstream carriers, as in the ORBCOMM incident)
Freight-forwarding and customs-broker software platforms shared across multiple shipping lines
Cloud-hosted logistics SaaS (booking portals, customer self-service platforms like MyToll or JAS SmartHub)
Interconnected partner/customer networks (3PLs, drayage carriers, warehouse operators) that can propagate an intrusion or be disrupted by a partner's outage
Payment processors and financial clearinghouses for freight settlement

exposure_categories.description: Because transportation is designated critical infrastructure in most jurisdictions, exposure extends beyond data to physical assets and public safety/regulatory systems.
subcategories: Ports, container terminals, and intermodal rail yards
Vehicle fleets rendered inoperable when dispatch/ELD/telematics systems are locked
Cold-chain and hazmat tracking systems where downtime creates spoilage or safety risk
Cross-border/customs clearance systems whose outage can halt trade flows nationally
Airport ground-handling and cargo-processing systems

hazard_categories.description: How ransomware actors most commonly gain a foothold in transportation/warehousing environments, shaped by the industry's mix of legacy OT, distributed fleet/warehouse sites, and often-thin IT security staffing relative to operational scale.
subcategories: Weak/brute-forced credentials and absent MFA on remote-access or VPN accounts (e.g., KNP Logistics/Akira — single weak password, no MFA)
Exploited public-facing vulnerabilities in logistics/ERP software and edge devices
Phishing and stolen-credential campaigns targeting dispatch, billing, and operations staff
Compromise of a shared/upstream software vendor whose platform many carriers depend on (supply-chain trojan, e.g., NotPetya's spread via M.E.Doc)
Legacy or unpatched OT/ICS components in port terminal and warehouse-automation systems with long refresh cycles

hazard_categories.description: The specific leverage mechanisms ransomware groups use against transportation/logistics targets, reflecting a broader industry shift toward data theft and multi-pronged pressure over pure encryption.
subcategories: Traditional file/system encryption halting dispatch, billing, and tracking operations
Double extortion — data theft plus threatened leak (Nefilim/Toll Group, LockBit/Estes)
Extortion-only attacks with no encryption payload, relying purely on stolen shipment/customer/financial data (a rising share industry-wide per Sophos 2025)
Harassment of customers, partners, or drivers via leaked contact data to pressure payment
Wiper malware disguised as ransomware for disruption rather than profit (NotPetya/Maersk)

hazard_categories.description: Transportation/warehousing uniquely blends conventional IT (billing, CRM, EDI) with operational technology controlling physical movement of goods — an intrusion in either domain can halt the other.
subcategories: Port/terminal operating systems and crane/gate automation as single points of failure (Nagoya Port)
Fleet telematics/ELD systems whose compromise removes real-time visibility and regulatory compliance capability (ORBCOMM)
Warehouse robotics, conveyor, and sortation-system control networks
IT/OT network convergence enabling lateral movement from a compromised office network into operational control systems
Safety and regulatory fallback processes (e.g., manual/paper logging) that partially mitigate but don't eliminate business impact during OT outages

hazard_categories.description: Because logistics networks are inherently interconnected, an attack on one node (a carrier, a software vendor, a port) propagates operational and reputational damage across partners and customers.
subcategories: Concentration risk in dominant ELD/telematics or TMS/WMS software vendors serving many carriers simultaneously
Cascading customer-service disruption when a shared customer portal or booking platform goes down
Cross-organizational data exposure when EDI/partner data feeds are compromised
Regulatory/compliance cascade — e.g., FMCSA having to issue nationwide ELD enforcement waivers after a single vendor's outage

hazard_categories.description: Distributed, high-turnover workforces (drivers, warehouse staff, seasonal labor) and thin security-awareness investment create human-factor exposure distinct from office-centric industries.
subcategories: Credential reuse/weak passwords among widely distributed field and warehouse staff
High employee/contractor turnover complicating access-deprovisioning
Limited security-awareness training budgets relative to operational/safety training priorities
Malicious or coerced insiders with access to dispatch or customs-clearance systems

hazard_categories.description: Transportation's critical-infrastructure designation and highly interconnected, low-margin business model amplify the downstream consequences of an incident beyond the direct IT-remediation cost.
subcategories: Critical-infrastructure sector status triggering mandatory incident reporting (e.g., CISA/TSA requirements in the US)
State/federal breach-notification laws when driver, employee, or customer PII is exposed (Estes Express Lines — 21,184 individuals, Maine AG filing)
Class-action litigation risk following notification delays or inadequate security practices
SEC disclosure obligations for material incidents at public logistics companies (Expeditors International 8-K/10-K)
Thin operating margins meaning even moderate incident costs or demurrage/detention penalties can threaten solvency (KNP Logistics collapse)
Sector-specific safety regulator waivers/interventions (FMCSA ELD enforcement relief after the ORBCOMM outage)

overview: Transportation and Warehousing (ransomware.live sector tag "Transportation/Logistics") is a high-frequency, high-consequence ransomware target because it sits at the intersection of critical infrastructure, thin operating margins, and deeply interconnected IT/OT systems. The sector has seen some of history's costliest cyber incidents (Maersk/NotPetya, ~$300M) as well as cases where a ransomware attack directly caused a long-established company's insolvency (KNP Logistics, ~730 jobs lost). Live ransomware.live tracking shows a very high and steadily growing victim count across trucking, freight forwarding, maritime/port operators, warehousing, and fleet-technology vendors, spanning dozens of active ransomware groups and dozens of countries. Industry reporting for 2025 shows both attack frequency (+34% YoY) and average ransom demands (+685% YoY, to $2.19M) rising sharply, with third-party/supply-chain exposure (shared ELD, TMS, and port-terminal software) acting as a key amplifier — a single vendor compromise can cascade operational disruption across many otherwise-unrelated carriers simultaneously.
